name: academic-paper-search
text:
---
name: academic-paper-search
description: Use when the user wants scholarly papers found or summarized: "find papers on", "what does the research say", "get me citations", "summarize this arXiv paper", "make a reading list in APA".
---

# Academic Paper Search

## When to use

- Finding peer-reviewed papers, preprints or reviews on a topic.
- Summarizing a specific paper from a title, DOI or arXiv link.
- Building a reading list or bibliography in a chosen citation style (APA, MLA, Chicago, IEEE, BibTeX).
- Not for a broad report mixing papers, news and data: use `deep-research`.
- Not for checking one claim: use `fact-checking`.

## Steps

1. Turn the request into 2 or 3 search phrasings with the key terms and synonyms. Note any year range or field the user gave.
2. Search OpenAlex first (free, no key, covers most journals). Add `mailto` so requests go to the polite pool:
   `curl -s "https://api.openalex.org/works?search=sleep%20deprivation%20memory&filter=from_publication_date:2019-01-01,type:article&sort=cited_by_count:desc&per-page=25&mailto=helper@example.com" -o tmp/openalex.json`
3. For computing, physics and math, also search arXiv:
   `curl -s "http://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all:%22diffusion%20models%22&sortBy=submittedDate&max_results=20" -o tmp/arxiv.xml`
4. For citation counts and influential citations, Semantic Scholar works without a key at low rates:
   `curl -s "https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/search?query=sleep+memory&fields=title,year,authors,venue,citationCount,externalIds,openAccessPdf,tldr&limit=20" -o tmp/s2.json`
5. Merge results into `tmp/papers.csv` (`title,year,authors,venue,doi,arxiv_id,citations,open_pdf,source`). Deduplicate by DOI, then by lowercase title.
6. Rank: relevance to the question first, then reviews and meta-analyses, then citation count adjusted for age, then recency. Keep 5 to 15.
7. For each kept paper, read the abstract (OpenAlex gives `abstract_inverted_index`; rebuild it in python). Read the full text only when an open PDF exists (`open_access.oa_url` or `openAccessPdf.url`).
8. Write `output/papers-<topic>.md`: a short overview of what the papers agree on, then one entry per paper with the citation, a 2 to 3 sentence plain summary (question, method, main result, sample size), and a link.
9. If the user asked for a style, format every citation in it. Also write `output/papers-<topic>.bib` when they want BibTeX or a reference manager.

## Tools on a Mac

- `curl` plus `python3 -m json.tool tmp/openalex.json | head -80` to inspect results.
- Rebuild an OpenAlex abstract:

```python
import json
works = json.load(open("tmp/openalex.json"))["results"]
for work in works:
    index = work.get("abstract_inverted_index") or {}
    positions = sorted((pos, word) for word, plist in index.items() for pos in plist)
    print(work["display_name"], work["publication_year"], work.get("doi"))
    print(" ".join(word for _, word in positions)[:600], "\n")
```

- arXiv XML: `python3 -c "import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET;..."` with namespace `{http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom}`.
- BibTeX from a DOI: `curl -sLH "Accept: application/x-bibtex" https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12373`.
- Formatted citation from a DOI: `curl -sLH "Accept: text/x-bibliography; style=apa" https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12373` (also `modern-language-association`, `chicago-author-date`, `ieee`).
- PDFs: `python3 -m pip install --user pypdf` to extract text.

## Quality checklist

- Every paper listed exists: its DOI or arXiv link resolves.
- Authors, year and venue come from the API data, never from memory.
- Summaries state the study type (trial, observational, review, preprint) and sample size where given.
- Preprints are labeled as not peer reviewed.
- Retracted papers are dropped or flagged (OpenAlex `is_retracted`).
- Citation style is consistent across the whole list.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: how many papers, the one-line takeaway, and the path, for example "I found 12 papers; most trials show a moderate memory drop after one night without sleep. The list with summaries and APA citations is in output/papers-sleep-memory.md."

## Pitfalls

- Making up citations. Never write a reference that did not come from an API result or a page you opened.
- Search by full title when the user names a paper; keyword search may return a lookalike.
- Citation counts favor old papers; do not rank a 2024 paper below a 2009 one on count alone.
- Semantic Scholar returns HTTP 429 when hit fast. Wait a few seconds between calls and keep to about one per second.
- arXiv asks for no more than one request every three seconds.
- Do not download paywalled PDFs from unofficial mirrors. Use open versions or the abstract.

text:
---
name: apple-shortcuts
description: Use when the user mentions their Shortcuts: "run my shortcut", "what shortcuts do I have", "use my Log Water shortcut", or wants a new shortcut designed for them to build in the Shortcuts app.
---

# Apple Shortcuts

## When to use

- Listing the user's shortcuts or folders.
- Running a shortcut, with or without input, and capturing its output.
- Describing step by step a new shortcut the user can build, when no existing one does the job.
- Not for scripting app data directly (reminders, events, Finder): use `mac-automation-applescript`.
- Shortcuts can't be created or edited from the shell. You describe; the user builds.

## Steps

1. List what exists: `shortcuts list` (names) and `shortcuts list --folders`. For one folder: `shortcuts list --folder-name "Home"`.
2. Match the user's words to a name. Names are case and space sensitive; quote them. If two could fit, ask which one.
3. Before running, think about what the shortcut does. If its name suggests it sends, posts, buys, pays, deletes or controls home devices, ask the user first.
4. Run it:
   - No input: `shortcuts run "Log Water"`
   - Input from a file: `shortcuts run "Resize Image" --input-path tmp/photo.jpg`
   - Text input: `printf '%s' "250 ml" > tmp/in.txt && shortcuts run "Log Water" --input-path tmp/in.txt`
   - Capture output: `shortcuts run "Get Weather" --output-path tmp/out.txt --output-type public.plain-text`
5. Read the output file and check it makes sense. A zero exit code only means it did not crash.
6. If the shortcut asks a question (Ask for Input, Choose from Menu), it will wait on the Mac's screen. Tell the user it is waiting for them instead of retrying.
7. To design a new one, write a short recipe in `output/<name>-shortcut.md`: the name, the trigger (run by voice, from the menu bar, an automation), then the actions in order with the exact action names as they appear in the Shortcuts app ("Get Contents of URL", "Get Dictionary Value", "Show Result"), and what to set in each.
8. After the user builds it, run it once with them and adjust.

## Tools on a Mac

- `shortcuts list`, `shortcuts list --folders`, `shortcuts list --folder-name "X"`
- `shortcuts run "Name" [--input-path file] [--output-path file] [--output-type UTI]`
- `shortcuts view "Name"` opens it in the Shortcuts app for the user to look at or edit.
- `shortcuts sign --mode anyone --input tmp/x.shortcut --output output/x.shortcut` signs a shortcut file for sharing (only if the user exported one).
- Useful output types: `public.plain-text`, `public.png`, `public.jpeg`, `com.adobe.pdf`, `public.json`.
- `open "shortcuts://run-shortcut?name=Log%20Water"` runs it through the app instead of the CLI (shows UI).
- `pbpaste` / `pbcopy` when a shortcut reads from or writes to the clipboard.
- `shortcuts list | grep -i water` to find a name when the user only remembers part of it.
- Check the result type with `file tmp/out.txt` when you asked for one type and might have got another.
- `shortcuts help run` prints the flags this macOS version supports.

## Quality checklist

- The shortcut name matched exactly what `shortcuts list` printed.
- Shortcuts with outside effects ran only after the user's yes.
- Output was read and checked, not just the exit code.
- Recipes use real action names and say which inputs and variables connect.
- Nothing personal (passwords, card numbers) put into a shortcut recipe.

## Reply to the user

One sentence on what ran and what came back, for example "I ran Log Water with 250 ml; it says today's total is 1.5 liters." For a design: "I wrote the steps for a Morning Brief shortcut in output/morning-brief-shortcut.md; it's six actions."

## Pitfalls

- A shortcut that runs fine in the app can fail from the CLI when it needs a permission it never asked for before; the prompt appears on the Mac. Tell the user to check the screen.
- Shortcuts that show a result with "Show Result" print nothing to the CLI; use "Stop and Output" in the design for anything that should return text.
- `--input-path` passes a file, so text must be written to a file first.
- iCloud-synced shortcuts can be edited on the iPhone between runs; list again if a name fails.
- Long-running shortcuts have no timeout from the CLI; macOS has no `timeout` command, so use `gtimeout 120` only if `coreutils` is already installed, otherwise run it in the background and check on it.
- Don't invent action names. If unsure an action exists on this macOS version, say so in the recipe.

name: brainstorming-before-building
text:
---
name: brainstorming-before-building
description: Use when the user has a vague idea to build ("make me an app that...", "I want a tool for...", "help me design") and no agreed design yet. Turn it into a short design.md before any code.
---

# Brainstorming Before Building

## When to use

- The user asks for something to be built but the goal, users, inputs or limits are fuzzy.
- The request could be read two or more ways and the readings lead to different code.
- A new project, feature or script that will take more than about 30 minutes of work.

Do not use when:

- The task is a small, clear change ("rename this function", "fix this typo"). Just do it, following careful-coding-rules.
- A design already exists and the user wants the work split into steps. Use writing-plans.
- Something is broken. Use systematic-debugging.

## Steps

1. Look before asking. Read what is already in the folder (`ls -la`, any README, package.json, pyproject.toml, Package.swift) so you do not ask questions the files already answer.
2. Write down, for yourself, what you think the user wants in one sentence. Note the gaps: who uses it, what goes in, what comes out, where it runs, what "done" looks like.
3. Ask one question at a time. Your reply is shown in a small notch card and may be read aloud, so each question is one short sentence. Prefer multiple choice: "Should it run as (a) a menu bar app, (b) a command line script, or (c) a web page?"
4. Ask the most important unknown first: purpose and success criteria, then constraints (platform, language, offline, budget), then nice-to-haves. Stop asking when the remaining gaps would not change the design. Three to five questions is usually enough.
5. If the user says "you decide", pick the simplest option that meets the stated goal and say which one you picked.
6. Propose 2 or 3 approaches. For each give: one line on how it works, the main trade-off, and rough effort (small, medium, large). Lead with the one you recommend and say why in one sentence.
7. Once the user picks (or agrees with your pick), write `output/design.md` with these sections:
   - Goal: one or two sentences.
   - Users and use: who runs it and how.
   - Scope: what is in, and an explicit "Not in this version" list.
   - Approach: the chosen design, main parts and how data flows between them.
   - Interfaces: commands, file formats, screens or API shapes, with one concrete example each.
   - Risks and open questions.
   - Success criteria: checks that prove it works (a command and its expected output, a file that must exist).
8. Keep design.md under about 100 lines. If it grows past that, the scope is too big; split off a later version.
9. Ask the user to confirm the design before writing any code. Do not start building in the same turn unless they already said "go ahead and build it".
10. When confirmed, hand off to writing-plans to turn design.md into plan.md.

## Tools on a Mac

- Look at the folder: `ls -la`, `find . -maxdepth 2 -type f | head -50`, `cat README.md`.
- Check what is installed before proposing it: `which python3 node swift git`, `python3 --version`, `node --version`, `swift --version`.
- Check macOS version when it matters for an approach: `sw_vers -productVersion`.
- Quick research on an unfamiliar library or API: use web search, then read the official docs page with web fetch or `curl -sL <url>`.
- Preview the design file: `open output/design.md` (opens in the default text editor) or `qlmanage -p output/design.md`.
- Copy a short summary for the user: `pbcopy < output/design.md`.

## Quality checklist

- Every question you asked was one question, short enough to hear in one breath.
- At least two real approaches were offered, with an honest trade-off for each.
- design.md has a "Not in this version" list and measurable success criteria.
- No code, scaffolding or installs happened before the user agreed.
- Assumptions you made on the user's behalf are written in design.md under Risks and open questions.

## Reply to the user

While gathering requirements: just the one question, with options if possible.
When done: "I wrote the design to output/design.md. I recommend <approach> because <reason>. Want me to plan the build?"

## Pitfalls

- Asking five questions in one reply. The user hears a wall of text and answers only the last one.
- Asking things you could have found by reading the folder or the docs.
- Offering fake alternatives where two options are the same idea with different names.
- Gold-plating the design with accounts, settings screens and sync when the user asked for a script.
- Skipping the design because the idea "seems obvious", then rebuilding after the first demo.
- Treating "you decide" as permission to pick the most interesting option instead of the simplest.

text:
---
name: brand-guidelines
description: Use when the user wants to capture a brand (colors, fonts, logo rules, tone of voice) into a brand file, or apply their brand to a doc, deck, site, post or graphic so it looks and sounds on-brand.
---

# Brand Guidelines

## When to use

- "Make a brand guide", "pull the colors and fonts from my site", "write down our brand", "make this match our brand".
- Any design or writing task where the user has a brand: check for `brand.md` in the working folder, `output/`, or the skills library first.
- Not for designing a new web page or image from scratch: do the work with `frontend-design`, `landing-page` or `poster-and-graphics`, using this skill's `brand.md` as the source of truth.

## Steps

### Capture a brand

1. Collect sources: the user's website URL, logo files, existing decks or docs, screenshots. Work only from what they give or what is public.
2. Colors: for a site, fetch the HTML and CSS (`curl -sL <url> -o tmp/site.html`, then the linked stylesheets) and pull hex values and CSS variables (`grep -oE '#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}\b' tmp/*.css | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20`). For a logo or image, sample dominant colors (see Tools). Pick 1 primary, 1 or 2 secondary, 2 or 3 neutrals, plus success/warning/error if used.
3. Fonts: read `font-family` and Google Fonts links in the CSS. Note heading font, body font, weights, and a free fallback for each.
4. Logo: list each file, its versions (full, mark only, light, dark), minimum size, clear space (e.g. the height of the mark's letter), and don'ts (no stretching, recoloring, shadows, busy backgrounds).
5. Voice: read 3 to 5 pieces of their copy. Describe the tone in 3 adjectives, each with a "this, not that" pair, plus words they use and words they avoid. Add 2 short example lines.
6. Write `output/brand/brand.md` with sections: Name and one-line description, Colors (table: name, hex, RGB, use), Typography (font, weights, sizes for H1, H2, body, caption), Logo (files and rules), Imagery (photo style, illustration style), Voice and tone, Do and don't, Ready-made tokens (a CSS `:root` block).
7. Copy logo files to `output/brand/assets/` and make a one-page preview `output/brand/brand-preview.html` showing swatches, type samples and the logo on light and dark.
8. Check every color pair you recommend for text against WCAG contrast and note it in the table.

### Apply a brand

1. Read `brand.md` fully before starting.
2. Use only its colors (via tokens), its fonts (or the listed fallbacks), its logo files untouched, and its voice.
3. For Office files, set theme colors and fonts in the template, not per text box (see `word-documents` and `slide-decks`).
4. Before finishing, compare the result against the "Do and don't" list.

## Tools on a Mac

- Fetch a site: `curl -sL https://example.com -o tmp/site.html`.
- Dominant colors from an image: `magick logo.png -resize 200x200 -colors 6 -unique-colors txt:- ` (`brew install imagemagick`). Python fallback: `python3 -m pip install --user pillow`, then `Image.quantize(colors=6)`.
- Image info: `sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight -g space logo.png`; `mdls logo.svg`.
- Fonts installed: `system_profiler SPFontsDataType | grep -i "Family:" | sort -u | head -50`.
- Contrast ratio: compute in `python3` with the WCAG relative luminance formula.
- SVG to PNG preview: `qlmanage -t -s 800 -o tmp logo.svg`.
- Preview: `open output/brand/brand-preview.html`.

## Quality checklist

- Every hex in `brand.md` came from a real source (site, file, user), not guessed.
- Text color pairs listed as allowed pass 4.5:1 contrast.
- Fonts named with a free fallback that is actually available.
- Logo rules include clear space, minimum size and at least 3 don'ts.
- Voice section has concrete examples, not only adjectives.
- The CSS tokens block matches the color table exactly.
- When applying: no off-brand colors or fonts slipped in.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: what you captured or applied and where, e.g. "I wrote your brand guide to output/brand/brand.md with 6 colors, 2 fonts and voice notes. A visual preview is in output/brand/brand-preview.html."

## Pitfalls

- Picking up random colors from third-party widgets, ads or cookie banners on the site.
- Treating a paid font as free; always give a free fallback.
- Recoloring or redrawing the logo instead of using the supplied files.
- Voice rules so vague ("friendly, professional") that they guide nothing.
- Downloading assets from sites the user doesn't own for anything beyond reference.

name: careful-coding-rules
text:
---
name: careful-coding-rules
description: Use for any coding task, big or small ("write code", "change this", "add", "fix", "refactor"). Think first, do the simplest thing, change only what was asked, and define success before starting.
---

# Careful Coding Rules

## When to use

- Every time you write or change code. These are working habits, not a separate phase.
- Especially in someone else's project, where unasked changes cost them review time.

For bigger work, pair with brainstorming-before-building (unclear goal), writing-plans (many steps), test-driven-development (behavior to check) and verification-before-done (finishing).

## Steps

1. Think before typing. Restate the request to yourself in one sentence. If it has two plausible meanings that lead to different code, ask the user one short question instead of guessing. If the meanings lead to the same code, pick one and note it.
2. State your assumptions. Write down what you are assuming about inputs, environment and scope. Put non-obvious ones in your reply.
3. Define success before starting. Turn the request into checks: "running `python3 convert.py in.csv` writes out.json with 120 records", "the test `test_rejects_empty_name` passes". You are done when the checks pass, not when the code looks finished.
4. Read the surrounding code. Match its style, naming, error handling and libraries. Use what the project already has before adding a dependency.
5. Do the simplest thing that meets the checks. No extra options, layers, abstractions, config flags or "future-proofing" nobody asked for. Three similar lines are better than a premature helper.
6. Make surgical changes. Touch only the lines the task needs. Do not reformat files, rename things, reorder imports, fix unrelated warnings or "clean up" nearby code. If you spot a real problem elsewhere, mention it in the reply instead of fixing it.
7. Clean up only your own mess: remove imports, variables and files your change made unused. Do not remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.
8. Keep the diff readable: `git diff` should read like a direct answer to the request. If the diff contains a change you cannot tie to the request, revert it.
9. Run the checks from step 3 and read the output (verification-before-done).
10. Stop when the checks pass. Do not keep polishing.

A worked example. Request: "make the export skip empty rows".
- Ambiguous? "Empty" could mean all cells blank, or the first cell blank. Ask: "Skip rows where every cell is blank, or where the name is blank?"
- Success: `python3 export.py sample.csv` on a file with 2 blank rows out of 10 writes 8 rows; existing tests still pass.
- Simplest change: one `if not any(cell.strip() for cell in row): continue` in the existing loop.
- Not done: renaming `export_rows`, switching to pandas, adding a `--skip-empty` flag.

## Tools on a Mac

- See what you changed: `git diff`, `git diff --stat`, `git status --short`.
- Undo changes to a file you did not mean to touch: `git restore path/to/file` (only for files with no edits of the user's).
- Check you did not reformat a file: `git diff --ignore-all-space --stat` compared with `git diff --stat`; a big gap means whitespace churn.
- Find existing helpers before writing new ones: `grep -rn "def parse\|function parse\|func parse" .`
- Check for an existing dependency: `grep -n '"dependencies"' -A 30 package.json`, `cat requirements.txt`, `python3 -m pip show <pkg>`.
- Formatters only if the project already uses them: `npx prettier --check <changed files>`, `ruff format <changed files>`, never on the whole repo.

## Quality checklist

- Success checks were written down before coding and all pass now.
- Every line in `git diff` traces back to the request.
- No new dependency, file, option or abstraction that the task did not need.
- Style matches the surrounding code.
- Assumptions and anything you noticed but did not fix are in the reply.

## Reply to the user

"Done: <what changed, in one sentence>. Checked with <command>: <result>." Add one sentence for any assumption or an issue you noticed but left alone.

## Pitfalls

- Silently choosing one meaning of an ambiguous request and building a lot on it.
- Rewriting a working function "while you are there".
- Running a formatter over the whole file or repo, burying a 3-line fix in 300 lines of diff.
- Adding a settings option instead of making a decision.
- Adding a library for something the standard library does in five lines.
- Declaring done because the code compiles.
- Fixing a neighboring bug you noticed without telling the user, so the change does more than they reviewed.

name: charts-and-dashboards
text:
---
name: charts-and-dashboards
description: Use when the user wants a chart, graph, plot or small dashboard made from data: "chart this", "make a graph of", "visualize these numbers", "build me a dashboard page".
---

# Charts and Dashboards

## When to use

- Turning numbers into a PNG/SVG chart or a single-file HTML dashboard the user can open in a browser.
- Restyling or fixing a chart that is hard to read.
- Not for exploring an unknown dataset: use `csv-data-analysis` first, then this skill for the final visuals.

## Steps

1. Get the data into a tidy table (one row per observation, one column per variable) in `tmp/data.csv`. Check totals against the source.
2. Decide the one message each chart should carry and write it as the title, for example "Signups doubled after the March launch".
3. Pick the chart by the question:
   - Change over time: line chart (bars if fewer than about 8 periods).
   - Compare categories: horizontal bar chart, sorted by value.
   - Part of a whole: stacked bar, or a pie only with 2 to 4 slices.
   - Relationship between two numbers: scatter plot, with a trend line if it helps.
   - Distribution: histogram or box plot.
   - A single headline number: a big-number tile, not a chart.
4. Choose the output:
   - Static image for documents and messages: matplotlib PNG at 200 dpi, or SVG for print.
   - Interactive page: one HTML file using Chart.js from a CDN, data embedded inline as JSON.
5. Label everything: title, axis titles with units, readable tick labels, source note under the chart. Start bar axes at zero. Use thousands separators.
6. Use a colorblind-safe palette. Okabe-Ito: `#E69F00 #56B4E9 #009E73 #F0E442 #0072B2 #D55E00 #CC79A7 #000000`. Use one strong color for the series that matters and gray for the rest. No more than 6 colors in one chart.
7. For a dashboard: a row of 2 to 4 number tiles at top, then 2 to 4 charts in a responsive grid, a date of the data, and a source line. Keep it to one screen when possible.
8. Save to `output/` (`output/signups-by-month.png`, `output/dashboard.html`) and render a check: `qlmanage -t -s 1200 -o tmp output/signups-by-month.png` or open the HTML headless (see Tools).

## Tools on a Mac

- `python3 -m pip install --user matplotlib pandas`.

```python
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5), dpi=200)
axis.bar(months, signups, color="#0072B2")
axis.set_title("Signups doubled after the March launch", loc="left")
axis.set_ylabel("Signups per month")
axis.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.text(0.01, 0.01, "Source: app analytics, Jan-Jun 2026", fontsize=8, color="gray")
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig("output/signups-by-month.png")
```

- Chart.js in one HTML file: `<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js@4.4.1/dist/chart.umd.min.js"></script>`, a `<canvas id="signups">`, and `new Chart(document.getElementById("signups"), {type: "bar", data: {...}, options: {...}})`. Pin the version.
- Respect dark mode in HTML with `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` and set Chart.js `color` and grid colors from CSS variables.
- Screenshot an HTML page to check it: `python3 -m pip install --user playwright && python3 -m playwright install chromium`, then `page.screenshot(path="tmp/dash.png", full_page=True)`.
- `sips -Z 1600 output/chart.png` to shrink an image; `open output/dashboard.html` only if the user asks to see it.

## Quality checklist

- The title states the finding, not just the variables.
- Axes are labeled with units; bar charts start at zero; dates are in order.
- Colors pass for colorblind viewers and the important series stands out.
- Values in the chart match the source table (spot-check three).
- Text is readable at the size it will be seen (no tick labels under 8 pt).
- The HTML file works offline except for the pinned CDN script, and the page has a `<title>`.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences: what the chart shows and where it is, for example "The bar chart shows signups doubling after the March launch; it's in output/signups-by-month.png."

## Pitfalls

- Dual y-axes mislead; use two charts side by side.
- 3D charts, heavy gridlines and gradients make values harder to read.
- Pie charts with many slices; use sorted bars.
- Truncated y-axis on bars exaggerates differences.
- Red and green as the only distinction fails for the most common color blindness.
- Loading an unpinned CDN URL (`chart.js@latest`) can break the page later.
- Do not publish or upload the dashboard; saving it in `output/` is the job.

name: code-review
text:
---
name: code-review
description: Use when asked to review code, a diff, a branch, a pull request or a folder ("review this", "is this safe to merge", "check my code"). Report findings ranked P0 to P3 with file:line.
---

# Code Review

## When to use

- The user asks for a review of uncommitted changes, a branch, a commit range, a PR or a folder.
- Before merging or shipping your own non-trivial change, as a second look.

Do not use when:

- The user wants a known bug fixed. Use systematic-debugging.
- The review is only about security. Use secure-coding for the deeper checklist, then come back for anything else.

## Steps

1. Pin down what to review. Uncommitted: `git diff` and `git diff --staged`. Branch: `git diff main...HEAD`. PR: `gh pr diff <number>` if gh is set up. Folder: list files with `git ls-files <folder>`.
2. Understand the intent first: commit messages (`git log main..HEAD --oneline`), PR description, linked design or plan. A review judges the code against what it is meant to do.
3. Read every changed file in full, not just the diff hunks, and the callers of changed functions (`grep -rn "funcName(" .`). Bugs often sit where the change meets unchanged code.
4. Run what exists: tests, type checker, linter. Note failures as findings; do not fix them unless asked.
5. Check, in this order:
   - Correctness: logic errors, off-by-one, wrong conditions, null or empty handling, error paths that swallow failures, races, wrong units or time zones, behavior the intent did not ask for.
   - Security: untrusted input reaching shell, SQL, HTML, file paths or eval; secrets in code; missing auth checks; unsafe deserialization.
   - Data safety: migrations that lose data, deletes without confirmation, writes without backups.
   - Performance: queries or network calls inside loops, unbounded memory, work repeated on every call, blocking the main thread.
   - Tests: new behavior covered, edge cases tested, tests that would actually fail if the code broke.
   - Readability: unclear names, dead code, duplicated logic, comments that lie, functions doing too much.
6. Rank each finding:
   - P0: will break production, lose data or open a security hole. Must fix before merge.
   - P1: real bug or risk in a likely path. Should fix before merge.
   - P2: edge-case bug, missing test, maintainability problem. Fix soon.
   - P3: nit or style suggestion. Optional.
7. Write each finding as: `[P1] src/api.ts:42 - <what is wrong>. <why it matters / when it fails>. Fix: <concrete suggestion>.`
8. Only report what you are confident about. If unsure, say "possible" and what would confirm it. Do not pad with nits to look thorough.
9. Save the full review to `output/code-review.md`: a one-line verdict (approve, approve with fixes, request changes), then findings grouped by priority, then what you checked and found fine.
10. Do not edit the code during a review unless the user asked for fixes.

## Tools on a Mac

- Diffs: `git diff --stat main...HEAD`, `git diff -U10 main...HEAD -- src/` (more context), `git show <sha>`.
- Line numbers for findings: `grep -n "pattern" file`, `nl -ba file | sed -n '30,60p'`.
- GitHub PRs (only if `gh auth status` succeeds): `gh pr view 123`, `gh pr diff 123`, `gh pr checks 123`. Do not post comments to a PR without the user's yes.
- Static checks: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx eslint .`, `python3 -m pip install --user ruff && ruff check .`, `swift build`.
- Dependency risk: `npm audit --omit=dev`, `python3 -m pip install --user pip-audit && pip-audit`.
- Secrets scan of the diff: `git diff main...HEAD | grep -nEi '(api[_-]?key|secret|token|password)\s*[:=]'`.

## Quality checklist

- Every finding has a priority, a file:line and a concrete fix.
- P0 and P1 findings are real, with a path that triggers them, not guesses.
- You read the full changed files and key callers, not just hunks.
- You ran the tests and type checks that exist and reported their result.
- The verdict matches the findings (no "approve" with an open P0).

## Reply to the user

"Review saved to output/code-review.md: <verdict>. <N> must-fix issues, the biggest is <one-line P0/P1>." If clean: "Looks good to merge; tests pass and I found only minor nits."

## Pitfalls

- Reviewing only the diff and missing that a changed function is called elsewhere with different assumptions.
- Burying one P0 among twenty style nits.
- Vague findings ("error handling could be better") with no line and no fix.
- Flagging the author's style choices as bugs when the project already does it that way.
- Approving because tests pass, when the tests do not cover the changed lines.
- Silently rewriting the code instead of reporting.

text:
---
name: commercial-script-and-shotlist
description: Use when the user wants a commercial, product ad, promo video or app demo spot planned: concept, script, voiceover, on-screen text and a timed shot list of what to record on the Mac.
---

# Commercial Script and Shot List

## When to use

- "Write a commercial for my app", "plan a 30-second ad", "make a promo video script", "what should I record for a product demo ad".
- The goal is selling or announcing one product or feature in a fixed length (6, 15, 30, 60 or 90 s).
- Not for creator videos (tutorials, vlogs): use `youtube-tiktok-scripts`.
- For editing the recorded footage: `screen-recording-edits`. For a still ad: `poster-and-graphics`.

## Steps

1. Brief, in `tmp/brief.md`: product, the one feature or promise, audience, where it runs (YouTube pre-roll, Instagram/TikTok, X, website hero, App Store preview), length, aspect ratio, tone, the CTA, and brand rules (`brand.md` if present). Use only facts the user gave or that are on their site.
2. Write 3 concepts, one line each plus a sentence on why it works:
   - Problem then solution (show the pain, then the product removing it).
   - Before and after (split screen or time jump).
   - Single magic moment (one jaw-drop interaction, repeated or slowed).
   Recommend one.
3. Time budget: about 2.3 spoken words per second for VO. 15 s is about 30 words, 30 s about 65. Leave the last 2 to 3 s for logo and CTA. App Store previews: 15 to 30 s, captured on the device, no hands or people.
4. Script: write `output/<slug>-commercial.md` with:
   - Title, length, aspect ratio(s), concept line.
   - Script table: Time (start-end), Visual, VO, On-screen text (max 6 words per card, readable for at least 1.5 s), Sound/music cue.
   - Opening 2 seconds must show the product or the problem with motion.
5. Shot list table, one row per shot: Shot #, Duration, Type (screen recording, UI close-up zoom, phone footage, title card, stock), Exactly what to do on screen (app state, window size, clicks, what to type), Setup notes, Status.
6. Mac recording plan for every screen shot:
   - Clean desktop: hide icons (`defaults write com.apple.finder CreateDesktop false; killall Finder`, revert with `true`), turn on Do Not Disturb, close unrelated apps, use demo data with no real names or emails.
   - Window size fixed per aspect: 1920x1080 for 16:9; for 9:16 record a narrower window centered so it crops cleanly.
   - Larger pointer if the cursor matters; slow, deliberate mouse moves; pause 1 s before and after each click.
   - Record each shot separately with 2 s of handle at both ends; name files `shot-01.mov`, `shot-02.mov` in `output/<slug>-footage/`.
7. Voiceover: final VO text in `output/<slug>-vo.txt`, plus a scratch read with `say` so the user hears the timing.
8. Deliverables list: master 16:9, cutdowns (15 s, 6 s bumper), vertical 9:16, square 1:1, captions SRT, thumbnail/end card.
9. Hand off to `screen-recording-edits` once footage exists.

## Tools on a Mac

- Scratch VO and timing: `say -v Samantha -r 165 -o tmp/vo.aiff -f output/<slug>-vo.txt && afinfo tmp/vo.aiff | grep duration`.
- Convert scratch VO for editing: `afconvert -f m4af -d aac tmp/vo.aiff output/<slug>-scratch-vo.m4a`.
- Screen recording (only after the user says go): `screencapture -v -C -V 12 output/<slug>-footage/shot-01.mov` (12-second cap, `-C` shows cursor).
- Window sizing: `osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to tell process "Safari" to set size of front window to {1920, 1080}'` (needs Accessibility permission).
- Do Not Disturb: suggest the user turns on a Focus; `shortcuts run "<their focus shortcut>"` if they have one.
- Word count: `wc -w output/<slug>-vo.txt`.
- Storyboard frames: quick HTML or SVG frames rendered to PNG (see `poster-and-graphics`), saved as `output/<slug>-storyboard/frame-NN.png`.

## Quality checklist

- The product appears in the first 3 seconds and the brand/logo at the end.
- One message only; the CTA is one action with the exact URL or store name.
- VO word count fits the length; on-screen text readable at phone size.
- Every shot in the script has a row in the shot list with concrete on-screen actions.
- Shot durations add up to the total length.
- No invented claims (awards, user counts, "number one"), no competitor names, no real personal data in demo screens.
- Works with sound off (captions or on-screen text carry the message).

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: the concept, the length, the paths, e.g. "Planned a 30-second 'single magic moment' ad with 7 shots and a 64-word voiceover. Script and shot list are in output/notes-ad-commercial.md; play tmp/vo.aiff to hear the timing."

## Pitfalls

- Too many features for the length; a 30 s ad sells one thing.
- Scripts where the visuals just repeat the VO word for word.
- Recording at different window sizes per shot, which makes crops jump.
- Shots with no handles, so cuts feel abrupt.
- Licensed music or stock assumed free; list them as to-license.
- Recording the screen, publishing or buying ads without the user's yes.

name: csv-data-analysis
text:
---
name: csv-data-analysis
description: Use when the user gives a CSV, TSV or Excel file and wants it understood: "analyze this spreadsheet", "what's in this data", "summarize sales.csv", "find anything weird", "clean this up".
---

# CSV Data Analysis

## When to use

- A table of data (CSV, TSV, XLSX, XLS, JSON lines) that needs summarizing, cleaning or exploring.
- Questions like "which month sold most", "is there a trend", "are there duplicates or bad rows".
- Not for making a polished chart or dashboard as the main deliverable: use `charts-and-dashboards` (this skill makes quick charts only).
- Not for collecting the data from websites: use `web-scraping-politely` first.
- Not for building or formatting a spreadsheet file as the deliverable: use `spreadsheets`.

## Steps

1. Copy the file into `tmp/` and work on the copy. Never modify the user's original.
2. Peek before loading: `head -5 tmp/data.csv` and `wc -l tmp/data.csv` to see the delimiter, header row, encoding problems and size.
3. Load with pandas. For CSV try `pd.read_csv(path)`; on errors try `sep=None, engine="python"` (sniffs the delimiter), `encoding="latin-1"`, or `skiprows` for title rows. For Excel, list sheets with `pd.ExcelFile(path).sheet_names` and load the one the user meant (ask only if it is truly ambiguous).
4. Profile: shape, `df.dtypes`, `df.isna().sum()`, `df.nunique()`, `df.describe(include="all")`, duplicated rows. Save to `tmp/profile.txt`.
5. Fix types: parse dates with `pd.to_datetime(errors="coerce")`, strip currency symbols and thousands separators before `pd.to_numeric`, trim whitespace in text, normalize obvious category spellings. Count what each fix changed.
6. Explore:
   - Distributions of numeric columns (median and quartiles, not only mean).
   - Top categories by count and by value.
   - Trends over time when there is a date column (`df.resample("M", on="date")`).
   - Correlations between numeric columns (`df.corr(numeric_only=True)`); report only strong ones (absolute value above 0.5) and say correlation is not cause.
   - Anomalies: values beyond 1.5 IQR, negative amounts where impossible, future dates, duplicates, sudden gaps.
7. Make 2 to 5 charts that answer the user's question, saved as PNG in `output/charts/` (150 dpi, labeled axes, title that states the finding).
8. Write `output/findings.md`: the question, 3 to 7 key findings with numbers, a data-quality section (rows dropped, fixes made, columns with missing values), and the chart images linked.
9. If you cleaned the data, save it as `output/<name>-clean.csv` and list every change in findings.md.

## Tools on a Mac

- `python3 -m pip install --user pandas matplotlib openpyxl` (openpyxl for .xlsx, add `xlrd` for old .xls).
- `head`, `wc -l`, `cut -d, -f1-5`, `sort | uniq -c` for a first look without Python.
- `file -I tmp/data.csv` shows the encoding.
- `qlmanage -p file.xlsx` previews a spreadsheet; `open -a Numbers file.csv` only if the user asks.
- Charts without a display: `import matplotlib; matplotlib.use("Agg")` before pyplot.

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("tmp/data.csv", sep=None, engine="python")
df.columns = df.columns.str.strip()
print(df.shape); print(df.dtypes); print(df.isna().sum())
print(df.describe(include="all").T.head(30))
```

## Quality checklist

- Row counts before and after cleaning are stated, with the reason for each dropped row.
- Every number in findings.md was computed by code you ran, not estimated.
- Units and currencies are named; totals and averages say over what period.
- Charts open, have titles and axis labels, and are referenced in findings.md.
- Findings answer the user's actual question first; side discoveries come after.
- The original file is untouched.

## Reply to the user

Two or three sentences with the headline numbers and the path, for example "Sales grew 18% from January to June, driven by the West region; 42 duplicate orders were removed. Findings and four charts are in output/findings.md."

## Pitfalls

- European CSVs use `;` as delimiter and `,` as decimal: `pd.read_csv(path, sep=";", decimal=",")`.
- Excel dates may arrive as serial numbers (like 45291); convert with `pd.to_datetime(col, unit="D", origin="1899-12-30")`.
- Leading zeros in IDs and ZIP codes vanish unless you load them as text: `dtype={"zip": str}`.
- Means hide skew. Report medians for money, time and counts.
- Large files (over about 1 GB): load selected columns with `usecols` or read in chunks.
- Do not fill missing values silently. Say how many and what you did.
- Do not send the data anywhere or upload it to online tools.

name: customer-support-replies
text:
---
name: customer-support-replies
description: Use when the user needs replies to their app's customers or users: "answer this support email", "reply to this review", "write support macros", "turn this complaint into a bug report".
---

# Customer Support Replies

## When to use

- Drafting replies to support emails, App Store or Play Store reviews, Discord or forum questions about the user's app or product.
- Writing a set of saved replies (macros) for common issues.
- Turning a user's report into a clean bug report for the developer.
- You draft; the user sends. Never send, post or reply on any account yourself.
- Not for marketing posts: use `social-media-content`.

## Steps

1. Read the whole message and any thread. Find: what the person wants, what they tried, device and app version, how upset they are.
2. Check what you know: the user's FAQ, docs, changelog or past replies in the folder (`grep -ril "keyword" .`). Don't guess at features or fixes; if you don't know, say what you need from the owner.
3. Decide the path:
   - **Solve**: you know the answer. Give the steps.
   - **Route**: it's a bug, a billing question, an account change or a legal or privacy request. Acknowledge, say what happens next, and produce a bug report or a note for the owner.
   - **Ask**: missing detail. Ask for the one or two things you need (version, device, screenshot), not a questionnaire.
4. Write the reply: thank or acknowledge in one line, answer in numbered steps if there are steps, close with what happens next. Aim for under 120 words. Match their language.
5. Refunds, credits, discounts, account deletion and promises of dates are the owner's decision only. Write "I've passed this to the team" unless the owner already said yes in this conversation.
6. Save drafts to `output/support-replies.md` with the original message quoted above each reply. Bug reports go to `output/bug-reports.md`.
7. Copy a single reply to the clipboard if asked: `pbcopy < tmp/reply.txt`.

## Tools on a Mac

- `pbcopy` / `pbpaste` to move text in and out of the clipboard.
- `grep -ril` to search the user's docs and past replies; `textutil -convert txt -stdout file.docx` to read docs in Word format.
- `open output/support-replies.md` to show drafts.
- Macro file format, one per issue in `output/support-macros.md`:

```
### Can't sign in
Trigger: "can't log in", "password reset not arriving"
Reply:
Sorry you're locked out. Two things usually fix it:
1. Check spam for the reset email from <sender>.
2. Request a new link; older links stop working after one hour.
If neither works, reply with the email you signed up with and we'll look into it.
```

- Bug report template for `output/bug-reports.md`:

```
### <short title: what breaks, where>
- Reported: <date>, <channel>
- App version / device / OS: <...>
- Steps to reproduce: 1. ... 2. ... 3. ...
- Expected: <...>
- Actual: <...>
- Frequency: always / sometimes / once
- Attachments: <screenshots, logs mentioned>
- User impact: <blocked / annoying / cosmetic>
```

## Quality checklist

- The reply answers the actual question in the first two sentences.
- Kind and plain: no blame, no jargon, no "as previously stated".
- Every step is something the app really has; no invented menus or features.
- No refunds, credits or dates promised without the owner's yes.
- No asking for passwords, full card numbers or codes. Only safe identifiers (account email, order number).
- Public replies (reviews, forums) contain no personal details of the customer.
- Under about 120 words unless steps require more.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences, for example "I drafted replies to all four emails in output/support-replies.md; two need your call on refunds." Flag anything that needs the owner's decision.

## Pitfalls

- Arguing with an angry review. Acknowledge, fix or route, move on.
- Copy-pasted macros that ignore what the person said. Adjust the first line to their message every time.
- Promising a fix "in the next update" when nobody committed to it.
- Asking for information they already gave.
- Closing a bug as user error without reproducing it.
- Legal threats, chargebacks, privacy or data-deletion requests: don't answer the substance; route to the owner.

name: deep-research
text:
---
name: deep-research
description: Use when the user wants a topic researched in depth across many sources: "research this", "dig into", "write me a report on", "what does the evidence say about". Produces a cited report.md.
---

# Deep Research

## When to use

- Open questions that need many sources weighed against each other: markets, history, technologies, policies, health or science topics.
- The user wants a written report with citations, not a one-line answer.
- Not for a single claim to verify: use `fact-checking`.
- Not for finding scholarly papers only: use `academic-paper-search` (and come back here if the papers feed a wider report).
- Not for a recurring update on a topic: use `news-briefing`.
- Not for a competitor or pricing table: use `pricing-and-competitor-research`.

## Steps

1. Restate the question in one sentence in `tmp/plan.md`. Note the scope the user gave (time range, region, audience) and assume sensible defaults when they gave none; write the assumptions down.
2. Break it into 4 to 8 sub-questions. Each must be answerable from sources, for example "What did the 2024 FDA guidance change?" rather than "Is it good?".
3. Search widely for each sub-question. Run at least two differently worded searches per sub-question, and include one search aimed at critics or opposing views.
4. Prefer primary sources: official statistics, laws and filings, original studies, company documentation, direct statements. Use news and blogs to find those, then cite the primary source.
5. Read the actual page, not the search snippet. Fetch it, save the readable text to `tmp/sources/NN-short-name.txt`, and note the publish date and author.
6. Track every claim in `tmp/claims.csv` with columns `claim,source_url,source_type,date,quote_or_number,sub_question`. One row per claim. Numbers get the exact figure and unit.
7. Look for disagreement. When sources conflict, record both sides with links and say which is stronger and why (newer data, larger sample, primary versus secondary, conflict of interest).
8. Stop searching when new sources only repeat what you have, or after about 25 sources read, whichever comes first. Note any sub-question you could not answer.
9. Write `output/report.md` (use a topic slug, for example `output/report-heat-pumps.md`):
   - Title and date.
   - Summary: 4 to 6 bullets with the main findings.
   - One section per sub-question, each claim followed by a numbered citation like `[3]`.
   - "Where sources disagree".
   - "Limits of this report": gaps, paywalled sources, things that may change soon.
   - "Sources": numbered list with title, publisher, date and URL.
10. Reread the report against `tmp/claims.csv`; every number and strong claim must trace to a row.

## Tools on a Mac

- Web search and web fetch tools of the helper are the main instruments.
- `curl -sL -A "Mozilla/5.0" "https://example.org/page" -o tmp/sources/01-page.html` when fetch fails.
- `textutil -convert txt -stdout tmp/sources/01-page.html` to strip HTML to text.
- PDFs: `python3 -m pip install --user pypdf`, then `python3 -c "import pypdf,sys;print('\n'.join(p.extract_text() or '' for p in pypdf.PdfReader(sys.argv[1]).pages))" tmp/sources/02-report.pdf`.
- `mdls -name kMDItemContentCreationDate file.pdf` sometimes recovers a document date.
- Optional: `brew install pandoc` and `pandoc output/report.md -o output/report.docx` when the user wants Word.
- `open output/report.md` only if the user asked to see it.

## Quality checklist

- Every factual sentence that is not common knowledge has a citation.
- Every citation number resolves to a real URL in the Sources list, and that URL was actually opened.
- Dates are given for statistics and for anything that changes over time.
- At least one opposing or skeptical source was looked for, and the report says what it found.
- Assumptions about scope are stated near the top.
- No source is cited for something it does not say; quotes are exact.
- The summary can be understood without reading the rest.

## Reply to the user

Two or three sentences: the main finding in plain words, how many sources it rests on, and the path, for example "Most studies find heat pumps cut heating bills by a third in mild climates, less in very cold ones; the full report with 18 sources is in output/report-heat-pumps.md."

## Pitfalls

- Citing a search result page or an aggregator instead of the original source.
- Treating a press release as independent evidence about the company that issued it.
- Old numbers presented as current. Always check the date of the figure, not the date of the article.
- Circular sourcing: five articles that all copy one original count as one source.
- Letting the first source frame the whole report. Plan sub-questions before reading deeply.
- Paywalls: do not try to get around them. Use the abstract or a free version and say so.
- Overlong reports. A focused 1,500 to 3,000 word report is better than an exhaustive one nobody reads.

name: doc-coauthoring
text:
---
name: doc-coauthoring
description: Use when the user wants to write a long document together over several rounds: a proposal, spec, essay, report, plan or guide. "help me write", "let's draft", "work on my doc with me".
---

# Doc Co-authoring

## When to use

- Long or important writing where the user's knowledge matters: proposals, design docs, grant applications, policies, reports, essays, guides.
- Work that will take several turns: outline, then sections, then revisions.
- Not for a quick message: use `email-drafting` or `internal-comms`.
- Not for file format work: once the text is done, use `word-documents`, `pdf-tools` or `slide-decks` to produce the file.

## Steps

Work in rounds. Each round ends with a short reply and one clear question, because the user hears your reply in a few sentences, not a page.

1. Frame (round 1). Find out the doc type, who reads it, what the reader should do or decide after reading, length, deadline, and any template. Ask at most three questions at once. Write the answers to `output/<slug>/brief.md`.
2. Gather context (round 1 to 2). Ask the user to point you at files, links or notes, or to just talk through what they know. Read everything they give. Keep a running list of facts, numbers and claims with their sources in `output/<slug>/notes.md`. List what is still missing.
3. Outline (round 2). Write `output/<slug>/outline.md`: section headings, and under each one sentence saying what that section must establish. Ask the user to confirm or reorder before drafting.
4. Draft one section at a time (rounds 3+). Start with the section the user knows best or the hardest one, not necessarily the first. Write it into `output/<slug>/draft.md`. For each section, offer 2 or 3 specific choices where you are unsure ("lead with the cost or the risk?") rather than asking "any thoughts?".
5. Revise from feedback. Change only what the user asked for; keep their own phrases. Keep a short `output/<slug>/changes.md` log so nothing silently disappears.
6. Reader test (last round). Reread the full draft as the target reader with no background. Check: can they say the main point after the first paragraph? Is every term defined? Is the ask clear? Is anything repeated? Write findings to `output/<slug>/reader-test.md` and fix the real ones.
7. Finish: one clean file `output/<slug>/<slug>.md`, and the requested format via the matching skill.

Folder layout for one document:

```
output/<slug>/
  brief.md         reader, goal, length, deadline
  notes.md         facts and sources gathered
  outline.md       agreed headings, one sentence each
  draft.md         the working text
  changes.md       what changed each round
  reader-test.md   gaps found by the cold read
```

## Tools on a Mac

- Files are plain Markdown; read with `cat`, search with `rg` (or `grep -rn`).
- Word count: `wc -w output/<slug>/draft.md`.
- Read the user's sources: `textutil -convert txt -stdout file.docx`, `pdftotext -layout file.pdf -` (`brew install poppler`), `curl -sL <url>` or the web fetch tool for pages.
- Compare versions: `diff -u old.md new.md` or `git diff --no-index old.md new.md`.
- Turn the final text into a file: `pandoc output/<slug>/<slug>.md -o output/<slug>/<slug>.docx` (`brew install pandoc`).
- Read a section aloud to check flow if the user asks: `say -f tmp/section.txt`.

## Quality checklist

- The first paragraph states the point and what the reader should do.
- Every section does what its outline sentence promised.
- Every number and claim traces to the user's material or a cited source; nothing invented.
- Headings are parallel and scannable; paragraphs under about 120 words.
- Terms and acronyms are defined on first use.
- The user's voice is kept: their phrasing and their opinions, not yours.
- Length is within the target.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: what you did this round, where it is, and the one question that moves things forward. For example: "Drafted the Budget section in output/grant-2027/draft.md. Should I put the cost table first or the justification first?" Do not paste the draft into the reply.

## Pitfalls

- Drafting the whole document before the outline is agreed wastes the user's time and buries their ideas.
- Filling gaps with plausible-sounding facts. Mark them `[TODO: need the real figure]` instead.
- Asking open questions ("what do you think?") instead of concrete choices.
- Rewriting sections the user already approved while fixing another.
- Long replies: the user hears them. Keep the substance in the files.
- Losing context between rounds: always reread `brief.md`, `notes.md` and `outline.md` at the start of a turn.

name: email-drafting
text:
---
name: email-drafting
description: Use when the user wants an email or reply written: "draft a reply to", "write an email to", "help me answer this", follow-ups, cold emails. Drafts only; never sends.
---

# Email Drafting

## When to use

- Writing a new email, a reply, a follow-up, a polite no, a request or an apology.
- Rewriting the user's rough draft to be clearer, shorter or warmer.
- Several versions of one message (formal and casual).
- Not for team-wide updates or announcements: use `internal-comms`.
- Not for long documents: use `doc-coauthoring`.

This skill never sends email. Sending is the user's action.

## Steps

1. Collect what you need: who it goes to, what the user wants to happen after they read it, the email being answered (pasted or in a file), and any facts to include. If the purpose is unclear, ask one short question.
2. Learn the user's voice. If they have earlier emails or a `voice.md` in the skills library or workspace, read them. Note greeting style, sign-off, length, formality, emoji or not. Otherwise default to plain, friendly and short.
3. Write the draft:
   - Subject line under 8 words that says what the email is about.
   - First line states the point or the ask.
   - Body: only what the reader needs to act; 3 short paragraphs at most.
   - A clear next step with a date if there is one.
   - The user's usual sign-off and name.
4. Replies: answer every question the sender asked, in their order. Quote nothing back unless it helps.
5. Save to `output/emails/<yyyy-mm-dd>-<recipient>-<topic>.txt` with `To:`, `Cc:`, `Subject:` lines on top, then a blank line, then the body.
6. If the user asks to put it in Mail, create an unsent draft with osascript (below). Only when asked, and never with `send`.
7. If the user asks, put the body on the clipboard: `pbcopy < file`.

## Tools on a Mac

- Save and copy: `pbcopy < output/emails/draft.txt`.
- Read a saved email file (.eml): `cat`, or `textutil -convert txt -stdout message.html` for HTML mail.
- Open a Mail draft only when the user asks (it appears in Drafts, not sent):

```bash
osascript <<'APPLESCRIPT'
tell application "Mail"
  set newMessage to make new outgoing message with properties {subject:"Quote for the kitchen job", content:"Hi Sam,

Here is the updated quote...", visible:true}
  tell newMessage to make new to recipient at end of to recipients with properties {address:"sam@example.com"}
end tell
APPLESCRIPT
```

- A `mailto:` link also works for short drafts: `open "mailto:sam@example.com?subject=Quote&body=Hi%20Sam"` (URL-encode with `python3 -c "import urllib.parse,sys;print(urllib.parse.quote(sys.argv[1]))" "text"`).
- Word count: `wc -w`.

## Quality checklist

- The ask or point is in the first two lines.
- Every question from the original email is answered.
- Names, dates, amounts and attachments mentioned are correct and match the user's facts.
- Tone fits the relationship (boss, client, friend) and the user's voice.
- Under 150 words unless the content truly needs more.
- No promises or commitments the user did not make.
- Nothing was sent; the draft is saved in `output/emails/`.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences: what the draft says in a phrase and where it is. For example: "Drafted a short reply to Sam accepting Thursday and asking for the final quote; it's in output/emails/2026-10-22-sam-quote.txt and on your clipboard." If you opened a Mail draft, say it is waiting in Mail for them to review and send.

## Pitfalls

- Never call Mail's `send`, never use command-line mail tools, never post to any service. The user sends.
- Do not invent facts, prices, availability or attachments to make the email complete. Use `[confirm date]` placeholders and mention them.
- Do not read the user's mailbox unless they asked you to look at a specific message.
- Overly formal or flowery language ("I hope this email finds you well") that the user would never write.
- Burying the ask at the end.
- AppleScript strings break on unescaped double quotes; escape them as `\"` or write the body to a file and read it in.
- Leaving out the subject line for a new email.

text:
---
name: fact-checking
description: Use when the user wants a claim, quote, statistic or article checked: "is this true", "fact-check this", "did X really say", "is this number right", "check this post before I share it".
---

# Fact Checking

## When to use

- One or a handful of specific claims: a statistic, a quote, a news story, a viral post, a line in the user's own draft.
- Checking whether information is still current (prices, laws, records, who holds a role).
- Not for open questions with no single claim to test: use `deep-research`.
- Not for finding scholarly literature in general: use `academic-paper-search`, then come back to rate claims against it.

## Steps

1. Pull out each checkable claim and write it in `tmp/claims.md` as a plain sentence. Split compound claims ("X rose 40% and is the highest ever" is two claims). Skip opinions; say they are opinions.
2. For each claim, decide what would settle it: an official dataset, the original study, a transcript or video, a law text, a company filing.
3. Search for that primary source directly. Use fact-checking sites (Snopes, PolitiFact, Full Fact, AFP Fact Check, Reuters Fact Check) as leads, then confirm against the original.
4. Open and read the source. Record the exact quote or figure, the URL, and the date it was published or last updated.
5. Check the date. If the claim was true once but has changed, mark it outdated and give the current value with its date.
6. Check context: is the number per year or total, in which country, which units, adjusted or nominal? Was the quote cut in a way that changes its meaning?
7. Rate each claim:
   - **True**: primary source confirms it as stated.
   - **Mostly true**: right in substance, a detail is off (rounding, date, wording).
   - **Misleading**: the facts are real but the framing gives a wrong impression.
   - **False**: primary sources contradict it.
   - **Outdated**: was true, no longer is.
   - **Unclear**: no reliable source either way, or good sources disagree.
8. Write `output/fact-check.md`: a table `Claim | Rating | What the source says | Source (link, date)`, then one short paragraph per claim that is not plainly true.

## Tools on a Mac

- The helper's web search and fetch tools.
- Older versions of a page (to see what it said when the claim was made): `curl -s "https://archive.org/wayback/available?url=example.com/page&timestamp=20230101"` returns the closest snapshot URL.
- `curl -sI https://example.com/page | grep -i last-modified` for a hint of when a page changed.
- Images: reverse search is not available offline; check `mdls -name kMDItemContentCreationDate -name kMDItemWhereFroms image.jpg` and `sips -g all image.jpg` for embedded dates and origin.
- PDFs and reports: `python3 -m pip install --user pypdf` to read the original document text.

## Quality checklist

- Every rating has at least one link to a primary or clearly authoritative source.
- The source actually contains the figure or quote; it was opened, not inferred from a snippet.
- Dates are given for each source and for each "current" value.
- "Unclear" is used honestly instead of forcing a verdict.
- The wording of each claim matches what the user gave; the check is not of a weaker or stronger version.
- Opinion, prediction and satire are named as such, not rated true or false.
- When the user's own draft is being checked, each fix suggests corrected wording they can paste in.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences with the verdicts in plain words and the path, for example "The 40% figure is true for 2022 but outdated; the 2024 number is 31%. The quote is real but cut short. Details and links are in output/fact-check.md." For a single claim, the verdict and one link in the reply is enough.

## Pitfalls

- Trusting a fact-check site's verdict without reading its sources.
- Rating a claim false because one source disagrees, when better sources support it.
- Missing that a statistic is real but for a different country, year or group.
- Quotes attributed to famous people are often invented; look for the original speech, book or recording.
- Wikipedia is a starting point, not the evidence. Follow its footnotes.
- Screenshots of posts or headlines are easy to fake; find the live post or article before rating what it says.
- Do not post corrections or reply to anyone on the user's behalf; the report is the job.

name: file-organizer
text:
---
name: file-organizer
description: Use when the user wants a messy folder tidied: "clean up my Downloads", "organize my Desktop", "sort these files", "find duplicates". Plans first, moves instead of deleting, keeps an undo log.
---

# File Organizer

## When to use

- Tidying Downloads, Desktop, Documents or any folder the user names.
- Sorting files into folders by type, project or date.
- Finding duplicate files and large old files.
- Not for notes inside a Markdown vault: use `markdown-notes-vault`.
- Never for system folders (`/System`, `/Library`, `~/Library`) or app bundles.

## Steps

1. Scope. Work only in the folder the user named. Note it as `$TARGET`. Do not recurse into subfolders unless asked; treat existing subfolders as already organized.
2. Survey, read-only:
   - Count and size: `find "$TARGET" -maxdepth 1 -type f | wc -l` and `du -sh "$TARGET"`.
   - By extension: `find "$TARGET" -maxdepth 1 -type f | sed -E 's/.*\.([^.]+)$/\1/' | tr A-Z a-z | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`.
   - Largest: `find "$TARGET" -maxdepth 1 -type f -size +100M -exec ls -lh {} \;`.
   - Oldest untouched: `find "$TARGET" -maxdepth 1 -type f -atime +180`.
3. Find duplicates by content, not name (see Tools). Same size first, then hash.
4. Write the plan to `output/organize-plan.md`: proposed folders, how many files go where, duplicate groups (which copy is kept: the oldest or the one with the clearest name), and anything you will not touch. Suggested buckets for Downloads: `Documents`, `Images`, `Installers` (.dmg .pkg .zip of apps), `Archives`, `Audio`, `Video`, `Spreadsheets`, `Code`, `To review`.
5. Stop and show the plan. Reply with the summary and wait for the user's yes before moving anything.
6. On yes, move with `mv -n` (never overwrite). For every move append a line to `output/organize-undo.sh`: `mv -n "<new path>" "<old path>"`. Duplicates go to `$TARGET/_Duplicates/`, not the Trash.
7. Deleting: only if the user explicitly says delete, and then to the Trash so it is recoverable: `osascript -e 'tell application "Finder" to delete POSIX file "/full/path"'`. Never `rm`.
8. Verify: file count before equals file count after (across the new folders); run `ls` on each new folder.

## Tools on a Mac

- Hash for duplicates: `shasum -a 256 "$file"`. For a whole folder, group same-size files first, then hash only those:

```bash
python3 - "$TARGET" <<'PY'
import hashlib, os, sys, collections
by_size = collections.defaultdict(list)
for name in os.listdir(sys.argv[1]):
    path = os.path.join(sys.argv[1], name)
    if os.path.isfile(path): by_size[os.path.getsize(path)].append(path)
for paths in by_size.values():
    if len(paths) < 2: continue
    by_hash = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for path in paths:
        by_hash[hashlib.sha256(open(path, "rb").read()).hexdigest()].append(path)
    for group in by_hash.values():
        if len(group) > 1: print(" | ".join(group))
PY
```

- File kind and dates: `mdls -name kMDItemKind -name kMDItemContentCreationDate -name kMDItemWhereFroms "$file"` (WhereFroms tells where a download came from).
- Date taken for photos: `mdls -name kMDItemContentCreationDate photo.jpg` or `sips -g creation photo.jpg`.
- Safe move: `mkdir -p "$TARGET/Images" && mv -n "$file" "$TARGET/Images/"`.
- Undo: run the log newest move first, `tail -r output/organize-undo.sh | sh`.
- Reveal the result if the user asks: `open "$TARGET"`.

## Quality checklist

- The plan was shown and approved before any move.
- File count unchanged after moving; nothing deleted without an explicit request.
- Every move is in `output/organize-undo.sh`.
- No file overwritten (`mv -n`), no hidden files or app bundles moved.
- Duplicates kept one copy in place and moved the rest to `_Duplicates/`.

## Reply to the user

Plan stage: one to three sentences with the numbers, then the question. For example: "Downloads has 412 files; I'd sort them into 7 folders and set aside 38 duplicates (1.2 GB). The plan is in output/organize-plan.md. Go ahead?" After moving: what moved and that `output/organize-undo.sh` puts it all back.

## Pitfalls

- Moving files an app is still downloading (`.crdownload`, `.download`, `.part`): skip them.
- Matching duplicates by name ("report (1).pdf") instead of content; names lie.
- Moving `.app` bundles or folders that look like files (packages such as `.pages`, `.key`, `.photoslibrary`) breaks them; treat any directory as off-limits.
- iCloud "optimized" files are placeholders; hashing them downloads them. Skip files whose `mdls` shows they are not local, or warn about the download size.
- Desktop and Documents may sync to iCloud; huge moves cause long syncs. Mention it.
- Never empty the Trash.

text:
---
name: frontend-design
description: Use when the user asks to build, design or restyle a web page, UI, component, dashboard or small web app and wants it to look polished and distinctive rather than generic.
---

# Frontend Design

## When to use

- The user wants a web interface: a page, a component, a dashboard, a tool, a prototype, or a small app.
- The user says "make it look good", "redesign this", "make a UI for", "build a web app that".
- Not for a full marketing site with pricing and FAQ: use `landing-page`.
- Not for a fixed-size image (poster, thumbnail, social card): use `poster-and-graphics`.
- If the user has a brand file (`brand.md`), read it first and follow it (see `brand-guidelines`).

## Steps

1. Pin down the job in one line: who uses it, what they do on it, what the one main action is.
2. Pick an aesthetic direction on purpose and write it at the top of the file as a comment, e.g. "editorial, warm paper, serif headlines" or "dense terminal, monospace, one acid accent". Avoid the default look: purple-to-blue gradient, centered card, Inter everywhere, emoji icons.
3. Choose the format:
   - Default: one self-contained `output/<name>/index.html` with inline CSS and JS. No build step.
   - If the user wants a real app with several views or state: Vite + vanilla JS or React in `output/<name>/` (`npm create vite@latest <name> -- --template react`), only if Node is installed (`node -v`).
4. Set design tokens first as CSS custom properties on `:root`: 1 background, 1 surface, 1 text, 1 muted text, 1 border, 1 accent, plus a dark-mode set under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`.
5. Typography: pair one display face with one text face from Google Fonts (e.g. Fraunces + Inter Tight, Space Grotesk + IBM Plex Sans, Instrument Serif + Geist). Use a type scale (e.g. 14, 16, 20, 28, 40, 56 px). Body line-height 1.5, headings 1.1 to 1.2, line length 60 to 75 characters.
6. Spacing: use a 4 or 8 px scale (4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96). Keep generous outer margins; group related items tightly and separate groups widely.
7. Layout: CSS grid and flexbox, mobile first, one breakpoint around 768 px and one around 1100 px. No horizontal scroll at 375 px width.
8. Motion: a few meaningful transitions (hover, enter, state change), 150 to 300 ms, `ease-out` for entering. Respect `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`.
9. Build real content, not lorem ipsum. Use realistic labels, numbers and empty states.
10. Make every interactive element reachable by keyboard, with a visible `:focus-visible` style and `cursor: pointer`.
11. Preview with `open output/<name>/index.html` and take a screenshot to check it (see Tools).
12. Fix what looks off, then reply.

## Tools on a Mac

- Preview: `open output/<name>/index.html` (default browser).
- Screenshot without clicking: headless Chrome, if installed:
  `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --window-size=1440,900 --screenshot=tmp/desktop.png file://$PWD/output/<name>/index.html`
  Repeat with `--window-size=390,844` for phone width.
- Fallback thumbnail: `qlmanage -t -s 1200 -o tmp output/<name>/index.html`.
- Local server for apps that fetch files: `python3 -m http.server 8000 -d output/<name>` then `open http://localhost:8000`.
- Icons: inline SVG from Lucide or Heroicons (copy the path), not icon fonts.
- Vite apps: `npm install`, `npm run build` (static files land in `dist/`).

## Quality checklist

- A clear visual hierarchy: you can tell the main action within two seconds.
- Contrast at least 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and UI borders.
- Works at 390 px and 1440 px; no overflowing text or clipped buttons.
- Dark mode looks intentional, not inverted.
- No console errors (check with headless Chrome `--enable-logging=stderr --v=0` or open DevTools).
- Fonts load from one Google Fonts link with `display=swap`; fallbacks set.
- Images have `alt`, buttons have text or `aria-label`.
- Nothing points at files outside `output/<name>/`.

## Reply to the user

One to three plain sentences: what you built, the look you chose, and the path, e.g. "Built the habit tracker as one page with a warm editorial look. It's at output/habit-tracker/index.html and I opened it for you."

## Pitfalls

- Shipping the generic AI look (gradient hero, glassmorphism cards, three identical feature boxes). Commit to one idea.
- Too many fonts or accent colors. Two families, one accent.
- Hardcoding colors in components instead of the tokens, which breaks dark mode.
- Fixed pixel heights that clip text at phone width.
- Loading big frameworks from a CDN for a page that needs 40 lines of JS.
- Reporting "done" without looking at a screenshot.
- Publishing or deploying anywhere without the user's yes.

name: gif-maker
text:
---
name: gif-maker
description: Use when the user wants a GIF, looping animation, reaction GIF, sticker or emoji animation from a video, screen recording or images, or needs a GIF small enough for Slack, Discord or GitHub.
---

# GIF Maker

## When to use

- "Make a GIF of this", "turn this clip into a GIF", "a looping sticker", "an animated Slack emoji", "make it small enough for Discord".
- Input is a video, a screen recording, a set of frames, or a drawing you generate frame by frame.
- Not for a long video edit: use `video-editing-ffmpeg`. Not for a still image: use `poster-and-graphics` or `image-editing`.

## Steps

1. Check tools: `ffmpeg -version` (`brew install ffmpeg` if missing). `gifsicle` is optional for squeezing size (`brew install gifsicle`).
2. Find the target and its limits:
   - Slack custom emoji: 128x128 recommended, under 128 KB (bigger uploads may get resized or rejected).
   - Slack message GIF: aim under 2 to 5 MB and 480 to 640 px wide.
   - Discord: emoji 128x128 under 256 KB; stickers APNG/GIF 320x320 under 512 KB; message attachments 10 MB on free accounts.
   - GitHub README: under 10 MB, 800 px wide is plenty.
   - If unsure, default to 480 px wide, 12 to 15 fps, under 3 seconds, under 2 MB.
3. Pick the moment: a short section (1 to 4 s) that loops well. Find start and end with `ffprobe` and a few test frames.
4. Make it with the two-pass palette method (best quality per byte), output to `output/<name>.gif`.
5. Check size with `ls -lh`. If over the limit, shrink in this order: fewer seconds, smaller width, lower fps, fewer colors, then `gifsicle --lossy`.
6. For a perfect loop, cut on matching frames, or make a boomerang (forward then reverse).
7. For animations drawn from scratch: render numbered PNG frames into `tmp/frames/` (Python + Pillow, or HTML screenshots), then assemble.
8. Open the result and watch it loop at least twice.

## Tools on a Mac

- Two-pass high quality GIF:
  `ffmpeg -ss 2.0 -t 3 -i in.mp4 -vf "fps=15,scale=480:-1:flags=lanczos,palettegen=stats_mode=diff" -y tmp/palette.png`
  `ffmpeg -ss 2.0 -t 3 -i in.mp4 -i tmp/palette.png -lavfi "fps=15,scale=480:-1:flags=lanczos[x];[x][1:v]paletteuse=dither=bayer:bayer_scale=5:diff_mode=rectangle" -loop 0 -y output/clip.gif`
- One-line version: `-filter_complex "[0:v]fps=15,scale=480:-1:flags=lanczos,split[a][b];[a]palettegen[p];[b][p]paletteuse" -loop 0`.
- Square emoji: add `crop=min(iw\,ih):min(iw\,ih),scale=128:128` before `palettegen`/`paletteuse`.
- Fewer colors: `palettegen=max_colors=64`.
- Boomerang: `-filter_complex "[0:v]trim=0:2,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,split[f][r];[r]reverse[rv];[f][rv]concat=n=2:v=1,fps=15,scale=480:-1,split[a][b];[a]palettegen[p];[b][p]paletteuse"`.
- From frames: `ffmpeg -framerate 12 -i tmp/frames/%03d.png -vf "split[a][b];[a]palettegen[p];[b][p]paletteuse" -loop 0 output/anim.gif`.
- Squeeze: `gifsicle -O3 --lossy=60 --colors 128 output/clip.gif -o output/clip-small.gif`; resize `gifsicle --resize-width 320`.
- Text overlay: `drawtext=fontfile=/System/Library/Fonts/Helvetica.ttc:text='Ship it':fontsize=36:fontcolor=white:borderw=3:x=(w-text_w)/2:y=h-th-20` before `palettegen`.
- Transparent sticker: GIF transparency is 1-bit; for smooth edges use APNG `ffmpeg -i in.mov -plays 0 -f apng output/sticker.png` or animated WebP `-c:v libwebp -loop 0 -lossless 0 -q:v 70 output/sticker.webp`.
- MP4 instead of GIF (far smaller, for platforms that autoplay video): `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -an -vf scale=480:-2 -c:v libx264 -crf 26 -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart output/clip.mp4`.
- Watch it: `open -a Safari output/clip.gif` (Preview shows frames, not playback); `qlmanage -p output/clip.gif`.
- Info: `gifsicle --info output/clip.gif | head -5`.

## Quality checklist

- Under the size limit for where it is going (`ls -lh`).
- Loops cleanly with no visible jump or flash frame.
- No heavy banding or dither noise on flat areas; text is readable.
- Correct dimensions (square for emoji).
- Plays at a natural speed (12 to 20 fps for real footage, 8 to 12 fine for simple motion).
- Starts and ends on the moment the user wanted.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences with path, size and dimensions, e.g. "Here's a 3-second loop at 480 px, 1.4 MB, small enough for Slack: output/high-five.gif."

## Pitfalls

- Single-pass GIF without a palette looks grainy and is larger.
- `scale=-1` can give odd heights that some tools reject; `-2` keeps it even for MP4 (GIF is fine with odd).
- Long GIFs explode in size; 10 seconds at 640 px is often 20 MB or more.
- Previewing in Preview.app and thinking it does not animate.
- Using copyrighted clips as public stickers; uploading anything without the user's yes.
