name: git-workflow
text:
---
name: git-workflow
description: Use when working with git or GitHub ("commit this", "make a branch", "merge conflict", "undo my last commit", "push", ".gitignore"). Small commits, safe branches, no force-pushing shared work.
---

# Git Workflow

## When to use

- Starting work in a repository, committing, branching, merging, rebasing or pushing.
- Resolving merge conflicts or undoing a mistake.
- Setting up a new repository or its .gitignore.

Do not use when:

- The user only wants a review of changes. Use code-review.

## Steps

1. Look before acting: `git status`, `git branch --show-current`, `git log --oneline -10`, `git remote -v`. Note uncommitted changes that are not yours; never discard them.
2. New repository: `git init`, add a .gitignore first (step 9), then the first commit.
3. Branch for each piece of work from an up-to-date main: `git switch main && git pull --ff-only && git switch -c feature/short-description` (or `fix/...`). Do not commit straight to main unless the user works that way.
4. Commit small: one logical change per commit, with tests passing. Stage on purpose: `git add <files>` and check `git diff --staged` before committing. Avoid `git add -A` when there may be stray files.
5. Message format: a subject under about 60 characters in imperative mood ("Add CSV export", "Fix crash on empty playlist"), a blank line, then a body saying why if it is not obvious. No "WIP", "stuff", "fixes".
6. Push only when the user asked: `git push -u origin <branch>`. Opening a PR, merging into main, pushing tags or deleting remote branches also wait for the user's yes.
7. Keep a branch current: `git fetch origin` then `git rebase origin/main` for a branch only you use, or `git merge origin/main` for a branch others share.
8. Resolve conflicts:
   - `git status` lists conflicted files. Open each, find `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`.
   - Understand both sides (`git log --oneline -3 origin/main -- <file>`), then write the correct combined code. Do not just pick "ours" for everything.
   - Check no markers remain: `grep -rn '^<<<<<<<\|^>>>>>>>' .`
   - Run tests, then `git add <file>` and `git rebase --continue` or `git commit`. To give up: `git rebase --abort` or `git merge --abort`.
9. .gitignore: ignore build output, dependencies, caches, local env and secrets, OS junk. Typical lines: `.DS_Store`, `node_modules/`, `dist/`, `build/`, `.build/`, `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `.venv/`, `.env`, `*.log`, `DerivedData/`, `xcuserdata/`. If a file is already tracked, `git rm --cached <file>` stops tracking it.
10. Undo safely, least destructive first:
    - Unstage: `git restore --staged <file>`.
    - Throw away your own uncommitted edit to one file: `git restore <file>`.
    - Fix the last unpushed commit: `git commit --amend`.
    - Undo the last unpushed commit but keep the changes: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`.
    - Undo a pushed commit: `git revert <sha>` (adds a new commit; history stays intact).
    - Lost something: `git reflog` shows every recent HEAD; `git switch -c rescue <sha>` brings it back.
11. Before any `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fd`, `git checkout -- .` or branch delete, save a safety point: `git stash push -u -m "before reset"` or `git branch backup/<date>`.

## Tools on a Mac

- git ships with Xcode Command Line Tools: `xcode-select --install` if `git --version` fails.
- Readable history: `git log --oneline --graph --decorate -20`.
- Who changed a line: `git blame -L 40,60 path/to/file`.
- Find when something broke: `git bisect` (see systematic-debugging).
- GitHub CLI if wanted: `brew install gh`; the user signs in themselves with `gh auth login`. Never handle their token.
- Large binaries: `brew install git-lfs`, `git lfs track "*.psd"`.

## Quality checklist

- Work is on a branch with a descriptive name.
- Each commit builds and passes tests, with an imperative subject line.
- No secrets, .env files, build output or .DS_Store committed (`git diff --staged --name-only` checked).
- Nothing pushed, merged or deleted remotely without the user's yes.
- No conflict markers left; tests pass after resolving.

## Reply to the user

"Committed <N> changes on branch <name>: <subject of main commit>. Not pushed yet; say the word and I will push." One or two sentences.

## Pitfalls

- `git push --force` to main or any shared branch. If a force push is truly needed on your own branch, use `git push --force-with-lease` and only with the user's yes.
- `git reset --hard` or `git clean -fd` with someone's uncommitted work in the tree.
- Committing a secret, then "removing" it in the next commit; it stays in history. Tell the user to rotate it.
- One giant commit called "updates".
- Rebasing a branch other people have already pulled.
- Resolving conflicts by keeping one side wholesale without reading the other.

name: homebrew-cli-tools
text:
---
name: homebrew-cli-tools
description: Use when a task needs a command-line tool that isn't installed ("command not found", "install ffmpeg", "get me a tool for X"), or the user asks what was installed with Homebrew.
---

# Homebrew CLI Tools

## When to use

- A command you need is missing (`command not found`) and a well-known tool solves it: ffmpeg, pandoc, yt-dlp, tesseract, jq, imagemagick, poppler, ripgrep.
- The user asks to install, update or remove a command-line tool.
- The user asks what you installed.
- Not for Mac apps from the App Store or paid software: tell the user what to get instead.
- Prefer a built-in first (`sips`, `textutil`, `afconvert`, `qlmanage`, `curl`, `python3`). Install only if built-ins can't do the job well.

## Steps

1. Check before installing: `command -v toolname` and `brew list --formula | grep -x toolname`. If it exists, use it.
2. Check Homebrew itself: `command -v brew`. On Apple silicon it lives at `/opt/homebrew/bin/brew`, on Intel at `/usr/local/bin/brew`. If it is missing, do not install Homebrew yourself: tell the user it needs their admin password and give them the one line from brew.sh to paste in Terminal.
3. Find the right formula: `brew search name` then `brew info name`. Prefer the formula with many installs and a known homepage. Check `brew info --json=v2 name | python3 -c "import json,sys;d=json.load(sys.stdin)['formulae'][0];print(d['desc'],d['homepage'])"`.
4. Avoid unknown taps (`brew tap someone/thing`) and casks for GUI apps unless the user asked for that app by name.
5. Install: `brew install name`. It can take minutes; let it finish. Don't run `brew upgrade` on everything as a side effect; that changes other tools the user relies on.
6. Verify: `name --version`, then run the real command once on a small input.
7. Keep a note: append one line to `output/installed-tools.md` (create it if missing) with date, formula, version and why, for example `2026-10-22  ffmpeg 7.1  converting the user's screen recordings`.
8. Uninstalling or upgrading tools the user already had waits for their yes.

## Tools on a Mac

- `brew search <term>`, `brew info <formula>`, `brew install <formula>`, `brew list --versions`
- `brew uses --installed <formula>` before removing anything (shows what depends on it).
- `brew uninstall <formula>`, `brew upgrade <formula>` (one at a time, with the user's yes).
- `brew doctor` when installs fail; read its first warnings only.
- `brew install --dry-run <formula>` (recent Homebrew) shows what would be pulled in without installing.
- `brew deps --tree <formula>` to see how heavy an install will be.
- `brew --prefix` to find where things live.
- `brew outdated <formula>` to see if one tool is behind, without touching others.
- `brew cleanup <formula>` frees space from old versions of that one formula.
- For Python packages: `python3 -m pip install --user <package>` for well-known ones (requests, pillow, python-docx). If pip refuses with "externally managed", use `brew install pipx` then `pipx install <tool>` for CLI tools.
- Well-known formulae by job: media `ffmpeg`; documents `pandoc`, `poppler` (pdftotext, pdftoppm), `qpdf`; images `imagemagick`, `exiftool`; OCR `tesseract`; data `jq`, `csvkit`, `sqlite`; web `wget`, `yt-dlp`; search `ripgrep`, `fd`.

## Quality checklist

- Checked it was not already installed.
- The formula is the well-known one (core tap, real homepage), not a look-alike.
- Version printed and a real test run passed.
- The note in `output/installed-tools.md` was added.
- No `sudo`, no piping random scripts into a shell, no system-wide upgrades.

## Reply to the user

One sentence: what you installed and why, for example "I installed ffmpeg with Homebrew to convert the videos; it's noted in output/installed-tools.md." If Homebrew is missing, say that plainly and what they need to do.

## Pitfalls

- `brew install` auto-updates Homebrew first and can be slow; that is normal. `HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1 brew install x` skips it when time matters.
- PATH: a fresh install may not be on the helper's PATH. Call it by full path (`/opt/homebrew/bin/ffmpeg`) if `command -v` fails right after install.
- Name clashes: `brew install imagemagick` gives `magick`, not `convert` on newer versions; `poppler` gives `pdftotext`, not a `poppler` command.
- Never use `sudo brew`. It breaks permissions.
- `brew search` matches loosely; `brew info` on the exact name before installing avoids grabbing a fork or a cask by mistake.
- A tool may already exist under another manager (pip, npm, a download in `~/bin`); check `which -a name` before adding a second copy.
- Casks (`--cask`) install GUI apps and may ask for a password; leave those to the user.
- Big installs (like `ffmpeg` with many dependencies) pull hundreds of MB; mention it if the user is on a slow connection.

name: image-editing
text:
---
name: image-editing
description: Use when the user wants to resize, crop, convert (HEIC, PNG, JPG, WebP), compress, rotate, add borders or watermarks, remove a background, or batch-process a folder of images.
---

# Image Editing

## When to use

- "Resize these photos", "convert HEIC to JPG", "make this smaller for email", "crop to square", "remove the background", "turn these into WebP", "do this to the whole folder".
- Not for making a new graphic or poster from scratch: use `poster-and-graphics`.
- Not for animated output: use `gif-maker`.

## Steps

1. Find the inputs. Never edit originals in place: copy or write results to `output/` (or `output/<batch-name>/` for many files).
2. Inspect first: `sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight -g format -g dpiWidth file`, and `ls -lh` for size. For a folder, count files and types.
3. Pick the tool: `sips` for simple resize, rotate, convert and crop (always present); `magick` for anything more (exact crops, padding, watermarks, quality control, sharpening); `cwebp` for WebP; `rembg` only for background removal.
4. Do one file first, show or check the result, then run the batch.
5. For batches, loop in the shell with quoted paths: `for f in in/*.HEIC; do sips -s format jpeg "$f" --out "output/$(basename "${f%.*}").jpg"; done`.
6. Verify outputs: dimensions, format, file size, count matches input count.
7. Keep metadata decisions explicit: strip location (EXIF GPS) for anything to be shared publicly with `magick in.jpg -strip out.jpg`; keep it for personal archives unless asked.

## Tools on a Mac

Built in (`sips`):
- Resize longest side to 1600 px: `sips -Z 1600 in.jpg --out output/in.jpg`
- Exact size (may distort): `sips -z 1080 1920 in.png --out out.png` (height first, then width).
- Convert: `sips -s format jpeg -s formatOptions 82 in.heic --out out.jpg` (formats: jpeg, png, heic, tiff, gif, pdf, bmp).
- Rotate / flip: `sips -r 90 in.jpg --out out.jpg`; `sips -f horizontal in.jpg --out out.jpg`.
- Center crop: `sips -c 1080 1080 in.jpg --out out.jpg` (height, width).
- Pad to canvas: `sips -p 1080 1080 --padColor FFFFFF in.png --out out.png`.
- Quick view: `qlmanage -p out.jpg` or `open out.jpg`.

ImageMagick (`brew install imagemagick`, command `magick`):
- Fill-crop to exact size: `magick in.jpg -resize 1080x1080^ -gravity center -extent 1080x1080 out.jpg`
- Crop region: `magick in.png -crop 800x600+120+40 +repage out.png`
- Compress JPEG: `magick in.jpg -sampling-factor 4:2:0 -strip -quality 80 -interlace JPEG out.jpg`
- Watermark text: `magick in.jpg -gravity southeast -fill "rgba(255,255,255,0.7)" -pointsize 36 -annotate +24+24 "(c) Name" out.jpg`
- Border: `magick in.jpg -bordercolor white -border 40 out.jpg`
- Batch to a folder: `magick mogrify -path output/small -resize 1200x1200\> -quality 82 *.jpg` (the `\>` means only shrink).
- Contact sheet: `magick montage *.jpg -tile 4x -geometry 300x300+8+8 output/sheet.jpg`

WebP and PNG size:
- `cwebp -q 80 in.png -o out.webp` (`brew install webp`); back with `dwebp in.webp -o out.png`.
- `pngquant --quality 65-85 --output out.png in.png` (`brew install pngquant`); lossless `oxipng -o 3 in.png` (`brew install oxipng`).

Background removal (optional, downloads a model on first run, about 170 MB):
- `python3 -m pip install --user "rembg[cli]"` then `rembg i in.jpg output/in-cutout.png`; batch `rembg p in/ output/cutouts/`.
- Output must be PNG or WebP to keep transparency.

## Quality checklist

- Originals untouched; results in `output/`.
- Output count equals input count; no zero-byte files.
- Dimensions and format are what the user asked for (`sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight`).
- Faces and subjects not cut off by crops; aspect ratio not distorted unless asked.
- Compressed files are visibly fine at 100 percent zoom (no banding or blocky skies).
- Transparent cutouts saved as PNG/WebP with clean edges (check on a dark and light background).
- Sizes meet any stated limit (e.g. under 1 MB for a form upload).

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: what changed, how many files, where, and a size note, e.g. "Converted 42 HEIC photos to JPG at 2000 px wide in output/trip-jpg/, about 600 KB each."

## Pitfalls

- `sips -z` and `-c` take height before width.
- `mogrify` without `-path` overwrites the originals.
- Saving a cutout as JPEG kills the transparency.
- Upscaling small images and calling them high resolution.
- Unquoted paths breaking on spaces in file names.
- HEIC from iPhone may carry rotation in EXIF; `magick -auto-orient` fixes it.
- Deleting originals; never do that without the user's yes.

name: internal-comms
text:
---
name: internal-comms
description: Use when the user needs a message for their team or company: status update, weekly report, project update, announcement, incident note, newsletter, or FAQ.
---

# Internal Comms

## When to use

- Status updates and weekly reports (to a manager, team or leadership).
- Announcements: launches, changes, new hires, policy updates, events.
- Incident notes: what happened, impact, what is being done.
- Team newsletters and FAQs.
- Not for one-to-one email: use `email-drafting`.
- Not for notes from a single meeting: use `meeting-notes` (then feed its output here).

## Steps

1. Identify the type, the audience and the channel (Slack, email, wiki, all-hands slide). Channel decides length: Slack posts under 150 words, emails under 300, wiki pages can be longer.
2. Gather inputs: the user's notes, meeting notes, files, previous updates in the workspace (match their format if one exists). Never invent progress, numbers or dates.
3. Pick the format below and fill it. Lead with what matters most to this audience.
4. Save to `output/comms/<yyyy-mm-dd>-<type>.md`. For Slack, also produce a plain-text version (Slack uses `*bold*`, not `**bold**`).
5. Reread as the busiest person on the list: can they get the point from the first two lines?

### Formats

Status update or weekly report:
```
<Project> update - week of <date>
Status: On track | At risk | Off track (one line why)
Done: 2 to 4 bullets with outcomes, not activity
Next: 2 to 4 bullets with owners and dates
Risks / help needed: bullets, or "None"
```

Leadership summary (3P): Progress, Plans, Problems, 1 to 3 bullets each, metrics where they exist.

Announcement:
```
<Headline that states the news>
What: one or two sentences.
Why: the reason, in one or two sentences.
What it means for you: concrete changes, dates.
Questions: where to ask.
```

Incident note:
```
[Investigating | Identified | Monitoring | Resolved] <short title>
Impact: who or what is affected, since when (time zone).
Current status and next step.
Next update by: <time>.
```
After resolution add: cause in plain words, what fixed it, follow-ups with owners. Blameless: describe systems and steps, not people's mistakes.

Newsletter: 3 to 6 short items, each a bold one-line headline plus two sentences and a link.

FAQ: questions in the reader's words, answers of 1 to 3 sentences, most-asked first.

## Tools on a Mac

- Draft and read in Markdown with `cat`, `rg`.
- Gather recent work if the user points at a git repo: `git -C <repo> log --since="1 week ago" --pretty="- %s (%an)"`.
- Copy the final text: `pbcopy < output/comms/<file>.md`.
- Convert for email or docs: `pandoc in.md -o out.html` or `-o out.docx` (`brew install pandoc`).
- Date math for "week of": `date -v-mon +%Y-%m-%d` (start of this week on macOS `date`).

## Quality checklist

- The first line says the news or the status; no warm-up.
- Every "next" item has an owner and a date.
- Numbers and dates match the sources; nothing invented or rounded into a different claim.
- Bad news is stated plainly, with what is being done about it.
- Fits the channel length; jargon and acronyms explained for the audience.
- Consistent with the format of earlier updates if there are any.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences: the type of message, its key line, the path. For example: "Wrote the weekly update marking the launch at risk because of the API delay; it's in output/comms/2026-10-22-weekly.md and on your clipboard."

## Pitfalls

- Never post to Slack, send email or publish to a wiki yourself. The user posts it.
- Listing activity ("had meetings about X") instead of outcomes.
- Hiding a slipped date under good news.
- Incident notes that guess at the cause before it is known; say "under investigation".
- Naming or blaming individuals in incident write-ups.
- Markdown that will not render in the target channel (tables in Slack, headings in plain email).

name: landing-page
text:
---
name: landing-page
description: Use when the user wants a landing page, product page, one-page site or marketing site with hero, features, pricing, testimonials, FAQ and a call to action, as static files ready to deploy.
---

# Landing Page

## When to use

- "Make a landing page for my app", "a one-page site for my product", "a waitlist page", "a sales page".
- The result is a single scrolling marketing page that sells one thing.
- Not for an app UI, dashboard or tool: use `frontend-design`.
- Not for a single image or ad: use `poster-and-graphics`.
- If a `brand.md` exists in the folder or the skills library, follow it (see `brand-guidelines`).

## Steps

1. Gather the facts from the user's message and any files or URL they gave: product name, what it does, who it is for, the one action you want (sign up, buy, download, join waitlist), price, real quotes or numbers. Never invent testimonials, logos, user counts or reviews; use clearly marked placeholders like `[Customer quote]` instead.
2. Write the copy first in `tmp/copy.md`:
   - Hero: headline under 10 words that states the outcome, a subhead of one sentence on how, one primary button, one secondary link.
   - Value props: 3 or 4 benefits, each a short title plus one sentence, written as what the user gets.
   - How it works: 3 numbered steps.
   - Social proof: quotes, logos or numbers (real or placeholders).
   - Pricing: 1 to 3 tiers, the recommended one marked; what is included as bullets.
   - FAQ: 5 to 8 real objections (price, privacy, cancel, platforms, support).
   - Final CTA: restate the outcome and repeat the button.
   - Footer: name, contact, privacy and terms links.
3. Build `output/<slug>/index.html` with inline or one `styles.css`. Semantic HTML: `header`, `main`, `section` with `id`s, `footer`. FAQ with `<details><summary>`.
4. Style: tokens on `:root`, one accent color for every CTA, a type scale, 8 px spacing grid, section padding 64 to 120 px on desktop and 48 px on phone. Mobile first; breakpoints near 768 and 1100 px.
5. Add `<head>` essentials: `<title>`, meta description under 160 characters, viewport, Open Graph tags (`og:title`, `og:description`, `og:image`), a favicon (inline SVG data URL is fine).
6. Images: put them in `output/<slug>/assets/`, compress them (see `image-editing`), give width, height and `alt`, and `loading="lazy"` below the fold.
7. Forms: by default the button links to a `mailto:` or a placeholder `#signup`. Only wire a form service if the user names one, and never put keys in the page.
8. Preview and screenshot at desktop and phone width; fix and repeat.
9. Offer deployment, but do not deploy until the user says yes.

## Tools on a Mac

- Preview: `open output/<slug>/index.html`.
- Screenshots: `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --hide-scrollbars --window-size=1440,4000 --screenshot=tmp/full.png file://$PWD/output/<slug>/index.html` and again with `--window-size=390,6000`.
- Local server: `python3 -m http.server 8080 -d output/<slug>`.
- Compress images: `sips -Z 1600 in.png --out assets/in.png`; WebP with `cwebp -q 80` (`brew install webp`).
- Deploy after a yes: Netlify (`npx netlify-cli deploy --dir output/<slug>` then `--prod`), Cloudflare Pages (`npx wrangler pages deploy output/<slug>`), or Vercel (`npx vercel output/<slug>`). These open a browser login; the user signs in themselves.
- Zip to hand off: `ditto -c -k --keepParent output/<slug> output/<slug>.zip`.

## Quality checklist

- The hero says what it is and who it is for without scrolling, at 390 px wide.
- One primary CTA style, repeated at least in the hero and at the end.
- No fabricated claims, customers or numbers; placeholders are obvious.
- Total page weight under about 1.5 MB; largest image under 300 KB.
- Headings in order (one `h1`), links work, `#anchors` scroll to sections.
- Contrast 4.5:1 for text; buttons have hover and `:focus-visible` states.
- Meta description and OG tags filled in.
- Opens correctly straight from the file and from a local server.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: the page is ready, the path, and the next step, e.g. "Your landing page is in output/nimbus-site/index.html. I left two testimonial placeholders for real quotes. Want me to deploy it to Netlify?"

## Pitfalls

- Feature-speak headlines ("AI-powered workflow platform") instead of the outcome.
- Five buttons in different colors fighting for attention.
- Made-up testimonials or "trusted by 10,000 teams".
- Absolute paths (`/assets/x.png`) that break when opened as a file; use relative paths.
- Huge unoptimized PNG heroes.
- Deploying, buying a domain or connecting a form service without asking.

name: mac-automation-applescript
text:
--- name: mac-automation-applescript description: Use when a task means driving a Mac app by script: "add a reminder", "make a calendar event", "save Safari tabs", "rename these Finder files", Mail, Notes, Music, System Events, via osascript. --- # Mac Automation with AppleScript ## When to use - Reading or changing data in scriptable Mac apps: Finder, Safari, Mail, Calendar, Reminders, Notes, Music, Contacts, System Events. - Small repeatable jobs: list open Safari tabs, add reminders from a list, file Finder items, read today's events. - Not for running the user's own Shortcuts: use `apple-shortcuts`. - Not for clicking around apps that have no scripting support: that needs the computer-use skill, if it is on. - Plain file work (rename, move, convert) is usually simpler with shell commands than with Finder scripting. ## Steps 1. Check that the app is scriptable: `sdef /System/Applications/Reminders.app | grep -m5 ' Privacy & Security > Automation, then retry. Never try to bypass it. 6. For writes, do one item first, check it landed, then the rest. 7. Deleting, moving to Trash, sending mail or messages, or changing many items waits for the user's yes. For mail, create a visible draft (`make new outgoing message with properties {visible:true}`) and let the user press Send. 8. Save useful output (lists, exports) to `output/` as `.txt`, `.csv` or `.md`. ## Tools on a Mac - `osascript -e 'tell application "Safari" to get URL of every tab of front window'` - `osascript -l JavaScript -e 'Application("Reminders").lists.name()'` for JXA; returns JSON-friendly arrays. - Reminders: `tell application "Reminders" to make new reminder at end of list "Inbox" with properties {name:"Call Sam", due date:(date "Friday, 1 November 2026 at 09:00")}`. Date strings follow the user's locale; safer to build the date with `current date` and set year, month, day, hours. - Calendar: `tell application "Calendar" to tell calendar "Home" to make new event with properties {summary:"Dentist", start date:d, end date:d + 3600}`. Reading many events is slow; limit by date with `whose start date > (current date)`. - Notes: `tell application "Notes" to make new note at folder "Notes" with properties {body:"

Title

Text

"}` (body is HTML). - Mail: `tell application "Mail" to get subject of messages 1 thru 10 of inbox`. - Music: `tell application "Music" to play playlist "Focus"`, `get name of current track`. - Finder: `tell application "Finder" to get name of every file of (path to downloads folder)`, `reveal POSIX file "/path"`. - System Events: `tell application "System Events" to get name of every process whose background only is false`; UI scripting (`click menu item ...`) needs Accessibility and breaks easily, so use it last. - `sdef /Applications/App.app > tmp/app.sdef` to read a full dictionary. - `open -a "Notes"`, `open -b com.apple.iCal` to launch apps. - Get JSON out of JXA for parsing: `osascript -l JavaScript -e 'JSON.stringify(Application("Safari").windows[0].tabs.url())' > tmp/tabs.json`. ## Quality checklist - The script ran on one item before the batch, and the result was checked by reading it back. - No user text pasted unescaped into script source; arguments used instead. - Nothing sent, deleted or moved to Trash without the user's yes. - Dates and times checked in the app (time zone, AM/PM, locale). - Errors are reported with their number and plain meaning, not swallowed with `try` and ignored. ## Reply to the user One or two sentences on what changed, for example "I added 5 reminders to your Inbox list, due Friday at 9." If a permission prompt blocked you, say exactly which setting to allow. Point to any export in `output/`. ## Pitfalls - Error -1743 (not authorized) and -1728 (can't get object) are the common ones; the first is a permission, the second a wrong name or list. - Calendar and Mail scripts on big accounts can take minutes; filter with `whose` and use `with timeout of 120 seconds`. - iCloud Notes and Reminders sync slowly; a just-made item may not show on the iPhone right away. - `display dialog` blocks a headless script waiting for a click nobody sees. Avoid it. - AppleScript lists start at 1, not 0. - Quoting: wrap one-liners in single quotes in the shell and use double quotes inside AppleScript; anything more complex goes in a file. - UI scripting depends on menu names in the user's language and app version. - Apps launched by a script steal focus; mention it if that may surprise the user. name: markdown-notes-vault
text:
---
name: markdown-notes-vault
description: Use when the user keeps notes in a Markdown folder or Obsidian vault and wants notes added, linked, tagged, found or tidied: "add to my notes", "daily note", "find my note about".
---

# Markdown Notes Vault

## When to use

- Adding a note, a daily note, or a clipping to a folder of Markdown notes (Obsidian, Logseq-style, iA Writer or plain folders).
- Finding notes by text, tag, link or date.
- Linking related notes, fixing broken links, adding front matter, building index notes.
- Not for moving or renaming many non-note files: use `file-organizer`.
- Not for writing a long document: use `doc-coauthoring`, then save the result into the vault.

## Steps

1. Find the vault. Use the path the user gives. Otherwise look for a `.obsidian` folder: `mdfind -name .obsidian 2>/dev/null | head` or check `~/Documents`, `~/Obsidian`, iCloud at `~/Library/Mobile Documents/iCloud~md~obsidian/Documents/`. Confirm the path in your reply the first time.
2. Learn its conventions before writing: list folders (`ls`), read 3 recent notes (`ls -t **/*.md | head`), and check `.obsidian/daily-notes.json` and `.obsidian/templates.json` for the daily note folder, date format and template. Copy what the vault already does.
3. Write notes in this shape unless the vault does something else:

```markdown
---
title: Kitchen renovation
created: 2026-10-22
tags: [home, projects]
aliases: [kitchen reno]
---

# Kitchen renovation

Short summary line.

- Quote from [[Sam Builders]] due Friday
- See also [[Home budget 2026]]
```

4. File names: the title in plain words, `Kitchen renovation.md`; no dates in the name except daily notes (`2026-10-22.md` in the daily folder).
5. Links: use `[[Note name]]` for notes that exist or should exist; check the target exists with `ls`, and create a stub if the user wants it. Use `[[Note name#Heading]]` for sections.
6. Tags: lowercase, hyphenated, few. Reuse existing tags; list them first (see Tools).
7. Daily note: append under a heading (`## Log`, or whatever the template uses) with a time stamp; create the note from the template if it does not exist.
8. Edit by appending or inserting; never rewrite a whole note the user wrote.

## Tools on a Mac

- Search text: `rg -n -i "renovation" "$VAULT" --glob '*.md'` (`brew install ripgrep`; fallback `grep -rni`).
- Find by tag: `rg -n "(^tags:.*\bhome\b|#home\b)" "$VAULT" --glob '*.md'`.
- List all tags: `rg -o --no-filename "#[a-z][a-z0-9/_-]+" "$VAULT" --glob '*.md' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -40`.
- Backlinks to a note: `rg -l "\[\[Kitchen renovation(\|[^]]*)?(#[^]]*)?\]\]" "$VAULT"`.
- Broken links: extract `[[...]]` targets with `rg -o --no-filename "\[\[[^]|#]+" "$VAULT" | sort -u` and compare with `find "$VAULT" -name '*.md'` basenames.
- Recent notes: `find "$VAULT" -name '*.md' -mtime -7 -not -path '*/.obsidian/*'`.
- Spotlight search across the vault: `mdfind -onlyin "$VAULT" "renovation"`.
- Today's date: `date +%Y-%m-%d`; time: `date +%H:%M`.
- Open a note in Obsidian if asked: `open "obsidian://open?path=$(python3 -c 'import urllib.parse,sys;print(urllib.parse.quote(sys.argv[1]))' "$NOTE_PATH")"`.

## Quality checklist

- Front matter is valid YAML (dashes on their own lines, lists in brackets or dashes, colons in values quoted).
- New links point at notes that exist, or the stub was created on purpose.
- Tags reuse existing ones; no near-duplicates (`project` vs `projects`).
- File name has no `/ \ : * ? " < > |` and no `#`, `^`, `[`, `]`.
- Nothing outside the vault changed; no note the user wrote lost text.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences: what you added or found, and where. For example: "Added today's log entry to Daily/2026-10-22.md and linked it to Kitchen renovation." For searches, name the top one to three notes.

## Pitfalls

- Editing `.obsidian/` settings or plugin files. Leave them alone.
- Writing while Obsidian Sync or iCloud is mid-sync can create "conflicted copy" files; write once, do not rewrite rapidly.
- Renaming a note breaks every `[[link]]` to it; if you must rename, update the links with care and list them.
- Using Markdown links `[x](x.md)` in a vault that uses wikilinks, or the other way round.
- Inventing a folder layout the user does not use.
- Large vaults: always scope searches to `*.md` and skip `.obsidian`, `.trash` and attachments.

name: mcp-server-builder
text:
---
name: mcp-server-builder
description: Use when building or fixing an MCP server ("make an MCP server", "MCP tool for X", "connect Claude or Gemini to my API"). Covers TypeScript SDK or Python FastMCP, tool design, testing and registering it.
---

# MCP Server Builder

## When to use

- The user wants an AI client (Gemini CLI, Claude Code, Claude Desktop) to reach an API, database, app or files through tools.
- An existing MCP server needs new tools, fixes or testing.

Do not use when:

- A plain script the user runs by hand would do. Write the script.
- The idea is still vague (which service, which actions). Use brainstorming-before-building first.

## Steps

1. Pin down the service and the 3 to 8 jobs the user wants done ("find an issue", "create a note"). Read the service's API docs. Design tools around those jobs, not one tool per endpoint.
2. Pick the stack: Python with FastMCP for quick, small servers; TypeScript SDK when the project is already Node or needs npm libraries. Use stdio transport for local servers (the client starts it as a subprocess).
3. Tool design rules:
   - Names: `snake_case` verbs with a service prefix, e.g. `notes_search`, `notes_create`.
   - Description: what it does, when to use it, what it returns, in two or three sentences. The model only sees this.
   - Inputs: typed and described, with sensible defaults and limits (`limit` default 20, max 100).
   - Output: concise and readable; return the fields a model needs, paginate long lists, offer a `detail` or `format` option instead of dumping raw JSON.
   - Errors: return a clear message saying what went wrong and what to try next, never a stack trace.
   - Mark read-only tools as read-only; make destructive tools need explicit arguments (an id, not "all").
4. Secrets: read API tokens from environment variables (`os.environ["NOTES_TOKEN"]`, `process.env.NOTES_TOKEN`). Never hard-code them or ask the user to paste them into the chat; tell them which variable to set in the client config.
5. Python (FastMCP), in the project folder:
   ```
   python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
   python3 -m pip install "mcp[cli]" httpx
   ```
   `server.py`: `from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP`, `mcp = FastMCP("notes")`, decorate typed functions with `@mcp.tool()` (the docstring becomes the description), end with `if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run()`.
6. TypeScript: `npm init -y`, `npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk zod`, `npm install -D typescript @types/node`, set `"type": "module"`. In `src/index.ts` create `new McpServer({ name: "notes", version: "1.0.0" })`, add tools with `server.registerTool(name, { description, inputSchema: { query: z.string() } }, handler)` returning `{ content: [{ type: "text", text }] }`, then `await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport())`. Build with `npx tsc`.
7. Never write to stdout except through the SDK on stdio servers; log to stderr (`console.error`, `print(..., file=sys.stderr)`), or the protocol breaks.
8. Test with MCP Inspector: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python3 server.py` or `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node build/index.js`. It opens a local web page: list tools, call each with normal, empty and bad inputs, read the results. Also add unit tests for the logic behind each tool (test-driven-development).
9. Register it, after showing the user the exact entry and getting their yes (it changes their client config):
   - Gemini CLI: add to `.gemini/settings.json` in the project (or `~/.gemini/settings.json` for all projects):
     ```
     { "mcpServers": { "notes": { "command": "/abs/path/.venv/bin/python3",
       "args": ["/abs/path/server.py"], "env": { "NOTES_TOKEN": "$NOTES_TOKEN" }, "timeout": 30000 } } }
     ```
     or run `gemini mcp add notes /abs/path/.venv/bin/python3 /abs/path/server.py`. Check with `/mcp` inside gemini or `gemini mcp list`.
   - Claude Code: `claude mcp add notes -- /abs/path/.venv/bin/python3 /abs/path/server.py` (add `--scope project` to write `.mcp.json` for the repo, `-e NOTES_TOKEN=...` for env). Check with `claude mcp list`.
10. Write a short `README.md` next to the server: what it does, each tool, required env vars, the config snippets above.

## Tools on a Mac

- Runtimes: `python3 --version` (3.10+ needed for the mcp package), `node --version` (18+). Missing: `brew install python node`.
- Faster Python setup if the user has it: `brew install uv`, then `uv init`, `uv add "mcp[cli]"`, `uv run mcp dev server.py` (dev also opens Inspector).
- Absolute paths for configs: `realpath server.py`, `which node`.
- Try the API before wrapping it: `curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $NOTES_TOKEN" https://api.example.com/v1/notes | python3 -m json.tool | head -40`.
- Validate config JSON: `python3 -m json.tool .gemini/settings.json > /dev/null && echo ok`.

## Quality checklist

- Every tool has a clear description, typed and described inputs, and limits on output size.
- Each tool was called in Inspector with good and bad input and returned a readable result.
- No secrets in code or README; tokens come from env vars.
- Nothing printed to stdout outside the protocol.
- Config uses absolute paths and was added only with the user's yes.

## Reply to the user

"Built the <name> MCP server in output/<folder> with <N> tools; all tested in MCP Inspector. To use it, set <ENV_VAR> and add the entry from the README; want me to register it?"

## Pitfalls

- One tool per REST endpoint, leaving the model to chain ten calls for one job.
- Returning huge raw JSON that floods the model's context.
- `print()` debugging on a stdio server, which corrupts the stream.
- Relative paths or a bare `python3` in config, which resolve differently when the client launches it.
- Using a Python older than 3.10 for the mcp package.
- Tool descriptions that say what the code does but not when to call it.

name: meeting-notes
text:
---
name: meeting-notes
description: Use when the user gives a meeting transcript, recording or rough notes and wants clean notes: "summarize this call", "action items from the meeting", "transcribe this recording".
---

# Meeting Notes

## When to use

- A transcript (txt, vtt, srt, docx, pasted text) or rough notes to turn into structured notes.
- An audio or video recording to transcribe first, then summarize.
- Pulling only action items or decisions out of a long call.
- Not for writing the follow-up email: do the notes here, then use `email-drafting`.
- Not for a status report across many meetings: use `internal-comms`.

## Steps

1. Get the text.
   - Text files: read directly. Strip timestamps from .vtt/.srt with `sed -E '/-->/d;/^[0-9]+$/d;/^WEBVTT/d;/^$/d' in.vtt > tmp/transcript.txt`.
   - Word or PDF: `textutil -convert txt -stdout in.docx`, `pdftotext -layout in.pdf -`.
   - Audio or video: convert, then transcribe with Whisper (see Tools). Save the full transcript to `output/<date>-<topic>/transcript.txt`.
2. Find the basics: date, title, who attended (from speaker labels or names mentioned), length.
3. Read the whole transcript before writing. Mark every decision, commitment, open question and number.
4. Write `output/<date>-<topic>/notes.md` with this structure:

```markdown
# <Meeting title> - <YYYY-MM-DD>
Attendees: ...

## Summary
2 to 4 sentences: why the meeting happened and what came out of it.

## Decisions
- <decision>, (who decided, if clear)

## Action items
| Owner | Task | Due |
|-------|------|-----|
| Maya  | Send revised quote to client | 2026-10-29 |

## Open questions
- <question> (who should answer it)

## Discussion
Short bullets by topic, only what someone would need later.
```

5. Owners and dates: use only what was said. If no owner was named write `Unassigned`; if no date write `No date`. Turn relative dates ("next Friday") into real dates using the meeting date and note it.
6. Optionally export: `pandoc notes.md -o notes.docx` if the user wants Word.

## Tools on a Mac

- Convert audio to 16 kHz WAV (built in): `afconvert -f WAVE -d LEI16@16000 -c 1 in.m4a tmp/audio.wav`.
- Video or odd formats: `brew install ffmpeg`, then `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -ar 16000 -ac 1 tmp/audio.wav`.
- Whisper, local and private:
  - `brew install whisper-cpp`, download a model once, for example `curl -L -o tmp/ggml-base.en.bin https://huggingface.co/ggerganov/whisper.cpp/resolve/main/ggml-base.en.bin`, then `whisper-cli -m tmp/ggml-base.en.bin -f tmp/audio.wav -otxt -of tmp/transcript`.
  - Or `python3 -m pip install --user openai-whisper` then `whisper tmp/audio.wav --model base --language en --output_format txt --output_dir tmp`.
  - Use `small` or `medium` models for accents or poor audio; `base` is fine for clear calls.
- Duration: `afinfo in.m4a | grep duration` or `mdls -name kMDItemDurationSeconds in.m4a`.
- Search a long transcript: `rg -n -i "action|follow up|by friday|decide|agreed" tmp/transcript.txt`.
- Copy the action items to the clipboard if asked: `pbcopy < tmp/actions.md`.

## Quality checklist

- Every action item has an owner (or `Unassigned`) and a due date (or `No date`).
- Decisions are things actually agreed, not ideas floated.
- Names spelled as in the transcript or attendee list; no invented attendees.
- Numbers, dates and amounts match the transcript exactly.
- Summary readable in 20 seconds.
- Transcript saved next to the notes when you made it.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: the headline outcome, how many action items, the path. For example: "The team agreed to launch on Nov 12; there are 5 action items, two for you. Notes are in output/2026-10-22-launch-sync/notes.md."

## Pitfalls

- Whisper invents words in silence and music; skim the transcript for repeated or nonsense lines and drop them.
- Speaker labels from Whisper do not exist; do not guess who said what unless the transcript has names.
- Treating "we should maybe" as a decision. Put it under open questions.
- Assigning tasks to the user that someone else volunteered for.
- Long recordings take time: whisper `base` runs roughly real-time-to-faster on Apple silicon; tell the user if a 2-hour file will take a while.
- Recordings and transcripts are private; never upload them to a web service.

name: news-briefing
text:
---
name: news-briefing
description: Use when the user wants a short news update on topics they follow: "brief me on", "what's new with", "daily AI news", "weekly roundup of", "catch me up on". Also for repeating briefings.
---

# News Briefing

## When to use

- A daily or weekly digest on a few topics, companies, people or places the user follows.
- "Catch me up" requests after the user was away.
- Repeating briefings that should stay quiet when nothing happened.
- Not for a deep report on one question: use `deep-research`.
- Not for checking whether a specific story is true: use `fact-checking`.

## Steps

1. Keep the topic list in `briefing-topics.md` in the helper folder: one topic per line with optional notes ("Apple: only product and legal news", "local: Austin, TX"). Create it from the user's request the first time; update it when they add or drop topics.
2. Read `briefing-log.md` (create it if missing). It holds the date of the last briefing and the headlines and URLs already reported, so you do not repeat them.
3. Set the window: since the last briefing, or the last 24 hours for daily and 7 days for weekly when there is no log.
4. For each topic, run 2 or 3 searches with the date in mind ("<topic> news this week", the key names, official sources). Prefer:
   - Original reporting from established outlets (Reuters, AP, BBC, Bloomberg, FT, the major national papers, respected trade press).
   - Primary sources: official announcements, filings, release notes, government sites.
   - Avoid content farms, AI-rewritten aggregators and anonymous social posts as the only source.
5. Open each candidate story and confirm its publish date falls inside the window. Drop rewrites of old news.
6. Merge duplicates: one item per event, linked to the best original source, with a second source for anything surprising.
7. Rank by how much it matters to the user's stated interest, not by how loud it is. Keep 3 to 8 items in total.
8. If nothing new and meaningful happened on any topic, do not pad. Write nothing and reply with exactly `NOTHING NEW`.
9. Otherwise write `output/briefing-YYYY-MM-DD.md`:
   - Title with the date and window ("Oct 15 to Oct 22").
   - Per topic, items as: **Headline in plain words** (date) one or two sentences on what happened and why it matters. [Source](url)
   - "Quiet" line listing topics with no news.
10. Append the reported headlines, URLs and today's date to `briefing-log.md`. Trim entries older than 60 days.

## Tools on a Mac

- The helper's web search and fetch tools.
- RSS feeds are reliable and cheap: `curl -sL https://feeds.example.com/rss.xml -o tmp/feed.xml`, then parse with `python3 -m pip install --user feedparser` and filter by `entry.published_parsed`.
- Google News RSS for a query: `curl -sL "https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=%22Rivian%22+when:7d&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US:en"` (use it to find stories, then cite the original outlet).
- `date -v-7d +%Y-%m-%d` gives the date a week ago on macOS.
- `say -f output/briefing-2026-10-22.md` only if the user asks to hear the whole file.

## Quality checklist

- Every item has a date and a working link to the original source.
- Nothing is older than the window, and nothing repeats the log.
- Each item says why it matters in one clause, without hype words.
- Rumors and single-source claims are labeled as such.
- The briefing reads in under two minutes.
- `briefing-log.md` was updated.

## Reply to the user

Short enough to be read aloud: the one or two biggest items in a sentence each, then the path, for example "Big one: the EU fined Apple 500 million euros over App Store rules. Four more items are in output/briefing-2026-10-22.md." When nothing changed, the whole reply is `NOTHING NEW`.

## Pitfalls

- Reporting an article's crawl date instead of its publish date.
- Padding a quiet day with background pieces, opinion columns or old news.
- Citing an aggregator when the original outlet is available.
- Paywalled stories: summarize only what is visible and say it is paywalled; do not bypass.
- Political and contested topics: report what happened and who said what, without taking sides.
- Do not share, post or email the briefing anywhere; saving it is the job.

name: pdf-tools
text:
---
name: pdf-tools
description: Use when the task involves a PDF: read or summarize it, pull out text or tables, merge, split, rotate, fill a form, compress, or make a new PDF from a page, doc or notes.
---

# PDF Tools

## When to use

- Reading a PDF to answer questions or summarize it.
- Extracting text, tables or images.
- Merging, splitting, reordering, rotating, compressing or password-removing (with a password the user gives for this one file) PDFs.
- Filling a PDF form.
- Making a PDF from HTML, Markdown, a Word file or images.
- Not for editing the content of a Word file: use `word-documents`, then export.

## Steps

1. Copy the input to `tmp/` and work on copies. Never change the user's original.
2. Inspect first: `pdfinfo tmp/in.pdf` (pages, size, encrypted?) and `pdffonts tmp/in.pdf` (no fonts listed usually means a scanned image PDF).
3. Do the task with the matching recipe below.
4. Write results to `output/` with a descriptive name, for example `output/contract-signed-pages-1-3.pdf`.
5. Verify: `pdfinfo` on the output (page count right?), and `qlmanage -t -s 1000 -o tmp output/x.pdf` to look at page one.

## Tools on a Mac

Built in:
- `mdls -name kMDItemNumberOfPages in.pdf` for a page count.
- `textutil -convert html notes.txt -output tmp/notes.html` then `cupsfilter tmp/notes.html > output/notes.pdf` to make a simple PDF.
- `sips -s format pdf photo.jpg --out tmp/photo.pdf` for one image to PDF.
- `qlmanage -t -s 1000 -o tmp in.pdf` for a thumbnail.
- `open -a Preview output/x.pdf` only if the user asks to see it.

Homebrew (`brew install poppler qpdf`):
- Text: `pdftotext -layout in.pdf tmp/in.txt` (keeps columns; add `-f 3 -l 5` for pages 3 to 5).
- Images: `pdfimages -png in.pdf tmp/img`.
- Pages to PNG: `pdftoppm -png -r 150 -f 1 -l 1 in.pdf tmp/page`.
- Merge: `qpdf --empty --pages a.pdf b.pdf -- output/merged.pdf`.
- Split pages 1-3: `qpdf in.pdf --pages . 1-3 -- output/part1.pdf`; every page: `qpdf --split-pages in.pdf tmp/page-%d.pdf`.
- Rotate page 2 by 90: `qpdf in.pdf output/rotated.pdf --rotate=+90:2`.
- Compress and fix: `qpdf --linearize --object-streams=generate in.pdf output/smaller.pdf`.
- Remove a known password: `qpdf --password='...' --decrypt in.pdf output/open.pdf` (the user types it for this run; never save it).

Python (`python3 -m pip install --user pypdf pdfplumber`):

```python
import pdfplumber
with pdfplumber.open("tmp/in.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        for table in page.extract_tables():
            print(table)
```

Form filling with pypdf:

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
reader = PdfReader("tmp/form.pdf")
print(reader.get_fields().keys())   # learn the real field names first
writer = PdfWriter(clone_from=reader)
writer.update_page_form_field_values(writer.pages[0], {"Name": "Ada Lovelace"}, auto_regenerate=False)
writer.set_need_appearances_writer(True)
writer.write("output/form-filled.pdf")
```

- Tables to CSV: write `extract_tables()` rows with the `csv` module to `output/tables.csv`.
- Markdown to PDF: `pandoc in.md -o tmp/in.html --standalone` then `cupsfilter tmp/in.html > output/in.pdf`.
- Scanned PDFs (no text): `brew install ocrmypdf` then `ocrmypdf in.pdf output/searchable.pdf`.

## Quality checklist

- Output page count matches what you expected.
- Extracted text is not empty or garbled; if it is, the PDF is scanned, so OCR it.
- Filled forms show the values when rendered (check the thumbnail), not only in field data.
- Rotations and page order look right in the preview.
- Nothing was printed, uploaded or shared.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences with the result and the path, for example "Merged the three invoices into one 7-page PDF at output/invoices-march.pdf." For a summary, give the two or three key points and say the full text is in `output/`.

## Pitfalls

- `pdftotext` without `-layout` scrambles tables and multi-column pages.
- Form field names in the file rarely match the labels on the page; read them with `get_fields()` before filling.
- Flattened or XFA forms cannot be filled with pypdf; say so and offer to overlay text instead.
- `cupsfilter` prints a harmless "using default" warning; check the output size, not the warning.
- Large scanned PDFs can be hundreds of MB after `pdftoppm`; keep renders in `tmp/` and delete them when done.
- Never guess or brute-force passwords on encrypted PDFs.

name: poster-and-graphics
text:
---
name: poster-and-graphics
description: Use when the user wants a poster, flyer, social media image, YouTube thumbnail, banner, cover, quote card or other static graphic made as a PNG or PDF.
---

# Poster and Graphics

## When to use

- "Make a poster for", "an Instagram post", "a YouTube thumbnail", "a banner for LinkedIn", "a flyer", "an event graphic", "a cover image".
- The output is a fixed-size picture, built as SVG or HTML and rendered to PNG (and PDF for print).
- Not for editing an existing photo (resize, crop, background removal): use `image-editing`.
- Not for a scrolling web page: use `frontend-design` or `landing-page`.
- Not for animation: use `gif-maker` or `video-editing-ffmpeg`.

## Steps

1. Pick the exact canvas size:
   - Instagram post 1080x1350 (4:5) or 1080x1080; story/reel cover 1080x1920.
   - YouTube thumbnail 1280x720 (under 2 MB).
   - X/Twitter 1600x900; LinkedIn post 1200x1200, banner 1584x396.
   - Open Graph 1200x630. Facebook cover 1640x624.
   - Print poster: A3 is 297x420 mm; render at 300 dpi (3508x4961 px) or export PDF; 18x24 in is 5400x7200 px.
2. Decide the one message and the reading order: headline, then image, then detail, then call to action. If it has more than 3 levels, cut.
3. Compose:
   - Use a grid (e.g. 12 columns, margins 5 to 8 percent of width). Align everything to it.
   - One focal point, large. Headline at least 8 percent of canvas height for thumbnails, and readable at 20 percent scale.
   - 2 typefaces max, 1 accent color plus neutrals (from `brand.md` if present).
   - Leave real empty space; keep text out of the outer 5 percent (safe area) and out of platform overlays (bottom 20 percent of stories, bottom-right of YouTube where the timestamp sits).
   - Contrast: put text on flat color or a darkened area of the photo, never straight over a busy region.
4. Build it as `tmp/<name>.html` (a fixed-size `body` with `margin:0`, exact `width` and `height` in px) or `tmp/<name>.svg` with a matching `viewBox`. Embed fonts via Google Fonts or `@font-face` to a local file.
5. Render to PNG at exact size (see Tools). Check the pixel size with `sips`.
6. Look at the PNG, also shrunk to 25 percent, and fix legibility and balance.
7. For several sizes, keep one source and change only the canvas and layout per size. Name files `output/<name>-<width>x<height>.png`.
8. For print, also save a PDF and note bleed (3 mm) if the user is printing professionally.

## Tools on a Mac

- HTML to PNG at an exact size (Chrome):
  `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --force-device-scale-factor=1 --window-size=1280,720 --screenshot=$PWD/output/thumb-1280x720.png file://$PWD/tmp/thumb.html`
  Use `--force-device-scale-factor=2` for a 2x crisp version, then downscale with `sips`.
- HTML to PDF: same Chrome with `--print-to-pdf=$PWD/output/poster.pdf --no-pdf-header-footer` and an `@page { size: 297mm 420mm; margin: 0 }` rule.
- SVG to PNG: `rsvg-convert -w 1080 -h 1350 in.svg -o out.png` (`brew install librsvg`), or `magick -density 300 in.svg out.png`. Quick preview: `qlmanage -t -s 1080 -o tmp in.svg` (thumbnail quality, not for final).
- Check size: `sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight output/thumb-1280x720.png`.
- Shrink to check legibility: `sips -Z 320 output/thumb-1280x720.png --out tmp/small.png`.
- Compress PNG: `pngquant --quality 70-90 --output out.png in.png` (`brew install pngquant`); JPEG with `sips -s format jpeg -s formatOptions 85`.
- Open to look: `open output/thumb-1280x720.png`.

## Quality checklist

- Exact pixel size for the target platform; file size within its limit.
- Headline readable at thumbnail size (25 percent scale).
- Nothing important in the safe-area margins or overlay zones.
- Text contrast at least 4.5:1, or large text 3:1.
- Fonts actually rendered (no fallback serif where you meant a custom font).
- No spelling mistakes; dates, times, prices and URLs checked against the user's message.
- Only images the user supplied, made, or that are clearly free to use.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences with the file paths, e.g. "Made the event poster at A3 as output/jazz-night-poster.pdf and a 1080x1350 Instagram version as output/jazz-night-1080x1350.png."

## Pitfalls

- Rendering before web fonts load: add a short delay (`--virtual-time-budget=3000`) or use local font files.
- Retina screenshots doubling the size; set `--force-device-scale-factor`.
- Cramming every detail onto the poster. One message.
- Thin light fonts that vanish when compressed.
- Using logos, characters or photos the user has no rights to.
- Posting the graphic anywhere without the user's yes.

name: pricing-and-competitor-research
text:
---
name: pricing-and-competitor-research
description: Use when the user wants competitors compared or a price set: "who are my competitors", "compare these apps", "how should I price this", "what do others charge", "make a competitor table".
---

# Pricing and Competitor Research

## When to use

- Mapping the competitors of a product, app, service or small business.
- Comparing features, prices and positioning in a table.
- Choosing a pricing model and price points with reasons.
- Not for a general market or industry report: use `deep-research`.
- Not for launch plans and post copy: use `product-launch-marketing`.

## Steps

1. Write down the user's product in `tmp/brief.md`: what it does, for whom, platform, current or planned price, and region and currency. Fill gaps with stated assumptions.
2. Find competitors in three rings:
   - Direct: same job, same audience (search "<job> app", "<competitor> alternatives", app store categories, Product Hunt, G2 or Capterra categories).
   - Indirect: different product, same job (spreadsheets, a general tool, an agency).
   - Free or built-in options (what the OS or a big platform already gives away).
   Keep 5 to 10, mostly direct.
3. For each, open the official pricing page and record the facts in `tmp/competitors.csv`: `name,url,pricing_page,checked_on,model,free_tier,plans_and_prices,billing,key_features,limits,target_customer,positioning_line,notes`. Note monthly versus annual price, currency and whether tax is included.
4. Positioning: copy the headline from each homepage in your own short paraphrase (who it is for, main promise). Note review themes from app stores or review sites: what users praise and complain about.
5. Build the comparison in `output/competitors.md`:
   - A table: Name | For whom | Model | Free tier | Entry price | Top price | Standout features | Weak spots.
   - A feature matrix (yes/no/partial) for the 6 to 10 features that matter to the user's buyers.
   - Gaps: what nobody does well, which audience is underserved.
6. Pricing models to weigh, with their fit:
   - Freemium: wide funnel, needs a clear paid line (limits on usage, seats, or pro features).
   - Free trial then paid: works when value shows within 7 to 14 days.
   - Tiers (Good/Better/Best): anchor with a high tier; most buyers pick the middle.
   - Usage-based: fits costs that scale with use (API calls, storage, minutes).
   - One-time purchase: common for Mac utilities; plan for paid major upgrades.
   - Per seat: for team tools.
7. Recommend: one model and 2 or 3 concrete price points, each with its reasoning (competitor range, cost to serve, perceived value, audience budget). Give one alternative and what would make it the better choice. Suggest a simple test (for example, two prices for new visitors for two weeks).
8. Put the recommendation at the top of `output/competitors.md`, and save the raw data as `output/competitors.csv`.

## Tools on a Mac

- The helper's web search and fetch tools for pricing pages and reviews.
- `curl -sL -A "Mozilla/5.0" https://competitor.example/pricing -o tmp/pricing-competitor.html` then `textutil -convert txt -stdout tmp/pricing-competitor.html | grep -iE '\$|per month|/mo|year'`.
- App Store data without scraping: `curl -s "https://itunes.apple.com/search?term=habit+tracker&entity=software&country=us&limit=25"` (JSON with price, rating, review count, seller).
- Single app lookup: `curl -s "https://itunes.apple.com/lookup?id=<app id>&country=us"`.
- Pricing pages that need JavaScript: Playwright as in `web-scraping-politely`.
- `python3 -m pip install --user pandas tabulate` and `df.to_markdown()` to turn the CSV into a table.

## Quality checklist

- Every price has its source URL, currency, billing period and the date it was checked.
- Competitors are real and current (site live, product still sold).
- The table compares like with like (monthly vs monthly, per user vs per user).
- The recommendation follows from the data and says what assumption it rests on.
- Opinions about competitors are framed as review themes, with where they came from.

## Reply to the user

Two or three sentences: the key insight, the recommended price, and the path, for example "Most rivals charge $4 to $8 a month with a free tier; I'd suggest freemium with Pro at $5.99 a month or $39 a year. The table and reasoning are in output/competitors.md."

## Pitfalls

- Using prices from articles or memory; pricing pages change often. Always check the live page.
- Missing regional pricing; App Store prices differ by country.
- Counting "contact sales" as free or missing; record it as custom pricing.
- Copying a competitor's price without asking whether the user's costs and audience match.
- Signing up for trials, entering payment details or contacting competitors. Do not.

text:
---
name: product-launch-marketing
description: Use when the user is launching an app or product and wants a plan or posts: "help me launch", "write my Product Hunt post", "launch plan", "draft tweets for launch", "how do I market my app".
---

# Product Launch Marketing

## When to use

- Planning a launch for an app, tool, side project or small product.
- Writing launch copy drafts: Product Hunt, Reddit, X, TikTok scripts, email, landing page headline.
- A checklist for launch day.
- Not for pricing decisions or competitor tables: use `pricing-and-competitor-research` first.
- Not for ongoing social posting after launch: use `social-media-content`; for full video scripts use `youtube-tiktok-scripts`; for building the landing page itself use `landing-page`.
- Never posts, submits, emails or schedules anything. Drafts only; the user publishes.

## Steps

1. Gather the facts in `tmp/brief.md`: what the product does in one sentence, who it is for, the problem it solves, what makes it different, price, platform, launch date, links, and any proof (beta users, numbers, quotes). Read the user's site or README if given. Mark gaps as assumptions.
2. Positioning: write a one-line statement, "For <audience> who <problem>, <product> is a <category> that <main benefit>. Unlike <alternative>, it <difference>." Then 3 headline options under 10 words each.
3. Audience: describe 1 or 2 specific groups, where they already hang out online (named subreddits, communities, hashtags, newsletters), and what words they use for the problem.
4. Channels, chosen for the audience, each with how to show up there:
   - **Product Hunt**: launch 12:01 am Pacific, Tuesday to Thursday; tagline up to 60 characters; first comment from the maker telling the story; gallery images 1270x760.
   - **Reddit**: only subreddits whose rules allow self-promotion; lead with the story or a useful lesson; be present to answer comments; no reposting the same text across many subs.
   - **X**: a thread with a short demo video or GIF in the first post; the link in a reply; tag tools used only when relevant.
   - **TikTok / Reels / Shorts**: 15 to 45 second vertical script with a hook in the first 2 seconds, the problem, the product solving it on screen, and a call to action.
   - Also consider: Hacker News "Show HN" (plain, technical, no hype), an email to waitlist or friends, relevant newsletters and communities.
5. Timeline in `output/launch-plan.md`: 2 weeks before (assets, landing page, waitlist), launch week, launch day hour by hour, the week after (reply, thank, collect feedback, share results).
6. Launch-day checklist: site and signup tested on phone and desktop, analytics working, download or payment link working, support email monitored, assets ready, posts drafted, someone available for replies all day.
7. Write drafts in `output/launch-posts.md`, one section per channel, each in that channel's tone and length limits (X 280 characters per post; Product Hunt tagline 60 and description 260). Give 2 variants for the most important post.
8. Add simple measures: what to count (visits, signups, upvotes, comments, conversion), where, and a goal for each.

## Tools on a Mac

- The helper's web search and fetch to read subreddit rules (`https://www.reddit.com/r/<sub>/about/rules.json`) and current Product Hunt guidelines.
- `wc -m` to check character counts: `printf %s "draft text" | wc -m`.
- `sips -z 760 1270 in.png --out output/ph-gallery-1.png` to size a Product Hunt image (crop first if the ratio differs).
- `screencapture -x tmp/shot.png` is for the user's own screen only when the user asks for screenshots of their app.
- `pbcopy < output/launch-posts.md` only if the user asks to copy something.
- `say -v Samantha -f tmp/tiktok-script.txt -o tmp/script.aiff` to hear a video script's pacing.

## Quality checklist

- The positioning names a specific audience and one main benefit, not a list of features.
- Every draft respects its channel's limits and rules; Reddit picks name communities that allow it.
- No invented numbers, testimonials or user counts; claims match the brief.
- Each post has one clear call to action and the right link placeholder (`<LINK>`) where the user must fill it in.
- The checklist has owners and times, not only items.
- Nothing was posted, submitted or sent.

## Reply to the user

Two or three sentences: the positioning line, the recommended main channel and day, and the paths, for example "I'd lead with Product Hunt on Tuesday and r/macapps the same morning. The plan is in output/launch-plan.md and post drafts are in output/launch-posts.md; nothing has been posted."

## Pitfalls

- Spamming many subreddits with the same post gets accounts banned; pick a few and tailor each.
- Asking for upvotes violates Product Hunt and Reddit rules; ask people to check it out and leave feedback instead.
- Hype words ("revolutionary", "game-changing") lower trust, especially on Hacker News.
- Writing for "everyone"; vague audiences make vague copy.
- Fake scarcity or made-up social proof. Do not.
- Launching on a day with a big competing event (a major Apple keynote, a holiday) buries the news; check the calendar.
- Broken links on launch morning; test every link in the drafts the day before.
- Posting, scheduling or DMing on the user's behalf. Hand over drafts; publishing waits for the user.

name: routine-reports
text:
---
name: routine-reports
description: Use when running a repeating check or routine ("check every hour", "tell me when this changes", "daily summary of X"), so each run compares with the last and reports only what's new.
---

# Routine Reports

## When to use

- Any run of a routine: watching a page, a price, a feed, an inbox count, a folder, a release list, a search result.
- Setting up a new repeating check, so the first run leaves good notes for the next.
- Not for one-off research: just answer it.

## Steps

1. Start every run by reading your notes: `state.json` and `last-report.md` in the folder (create both on the first run). They are your memory between runs; the conversation may have been reset.
2. Fetch the current data the same way every time (same URL, same query, same sort). Save the raw copy to `tmp/run-latest.<ext>`.
3. Reduce it to comparable items, each with a stable id: a URL, a SKU, a title plus date, a file path. Store a short fingerprint per item (price, status, a hash of the text) rather than whole pages.
4. Compare with `state.json`: new items, removed items, changed fields. Ignore noise that changes every load (timestamps, view counts, ad blocks, "updated 3 minutes ago").
5. Decide:
   - Nothing meaningful changed: reply exactly `NOTHING NEW` and nothing else. Still update `last_checked` in `state.json`.
   - Something changed: write a short report of only the changes, newest first, each with its link.
6. Write the new state atomically: write `state.tmp.json`, then `mv state.tmp.json state.json`, so a crash never leaves half a file.
7. Save the report to `last-report.md` and append a one-line entry to `output/routine-log.md` (date, what changed).
8. If the source failed (timeout, 404, login wall, captcha), don't report a change. Record `consecutive_failures` and say plainly that the check failed and why. Never treat an error page as "everything was removed".

## Tools on a Mac

- `curl -sL --max-time 30 -A "Mozilla/5.0" URL -o tmp/run-latest.html`
- `python3` for parsing and diffing; `json`, `hashlib` and `html.parser` are built in.
- `shasum -a 256 file` for a quick fingerprint.
- `diff -u old.txt new.txt` for text lists.
- `textutil -convert txt -stdout page.html` to strip HTML to text.
- `brew install jq` for poking at JSON APIs: `jq '.items[] | {id, price}'`.
- A minimal state file:

```json
{
  "source": "https://example.com/deals",
  "last_checked": "2026-10-22T09:00:00Z",
  "last_changed": "2026-10-21T15:00:00Z",
  "consecutive_failures": 0,
  "items": {
    "sku-123": {"title": "Desk lamp", "price": 39.0, "first_seen": "2026-10-20"}
  }
}
```

## Quality checklist

- Read the previous state before fetching.
- Every reported item is actually new or changed since the last run, not since the first.
- No change means the reply is exactly `NOTHING NEW`, with no greeting or punctuation added.
- Thresholds the user set are respected (for example "only if the price drops below 50").
- `state.json` was saved even when nothing changed, and parses: `python3 -m json.tool state.json > /dev/null`.
- Links included for each change.

## Reply to the user

When something changed: one to three short sentences that lead with the change, for example "The lamp dropped from $39 to $29, and two new desks were listed. Details in output/routine-log.md." When nothing changed: exactly `NOTHING NEW`.

## Pitfalls

- Reporting the same item twice because its id was unstable (tracking parameters in URLs). Strip `utm_*` and similar before using a URL as an id.
- Pages that change layout make everything look "new". If more than half the items changed at once, suspect the parser, check, and say so instead of flooding the user.
- Saying "nothing new" on the first run. The first run reports the starting picture briefly and sets the baseline.
- Taking actions on a change (buying, replying, posting) without the user's yes. A routine reports; it doesn't act unless the user set that up and confirmed it.
- Dates in different time zones; store UTC ISO 8601.
- Letting `output/routine-log.md` grow forever; keep the last 200 lines.

name: screen-recording-edits
text:
---
name: screen-recording-edits
description: Use when the user wants to turn a screen recording into a polished demo, tutorial, product video or commercial clip: cut dead time, zoom in, add captions, music and a clean export.
---

# Screen Recording Edits

## When to use

- "Clean up this screen recording", "make a demo video from this", "cut the boring parts", "zoom in on the button", "add captions and music", "make it a commercial clip".
- Input is a `.mov` or `.mp4` from QuickTime, `screencapture -v`, Cmd+Shift+5, or another recorder.
- Not for simple trims or conversions: use `video-editing-ffmpeg`. For planning what to record: use `commercial-script-and-shotlist`.

## Steps

1. Inspect: `ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration:stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,codec_name -of compact rec.mov`. Retina recordings are often 2880x1800 or larger at 60 fps.
2. Find dead time:
   - Silence: `ffmpeg -i rec.mov -af silencedetect=noise=-35dB:d=1.2 -f null - 2>&1 | grep silence_`.
   - Frozen screen: `ffmpeg -i rec.mov -vf "freezedetect=n=0.003:d=1.5" -map 0:v -f null - 2>&1 | grep freeze_`.
   - Gaps that are both silent and frozen are safe to cut. Keep 0.3 s of padding on each side.
3. Write an edit decision list in `tmp/edl.csv`: `start,end,zoom_x,zoom_y,zoom_w,caption`. Times in seconds of the source. Leave zoom empty for full frame.
4. Zoom crops: for each moment where the action is small, crop to a 16:9 region around it (at least 1/3 of the frame width so it is not blurry) and scale back up: `crop=960:540:1200:300,scale=1920:1080:flags=lanczos`. Use a cut into the zoom, or a smooth push-in with `zoompan` only on short segments.
5. Cursor: if the cursor is too small, recommend re-recording with a larger pointer (System Settings > Accessibility > Display > Pointer size). Cursor highlights or click rings need the click times; add them with a PNG ring overlaid `enable='between(t,a,b)'`.
6. Render each segment to `tmp/seg-NN.mp4` with identical settings (1920x1080, 30 fps, H.264 CRF 18, AAC 48 kHz), then join with the concat demuxer.
7. Captions: transcribe the voiceover to SRT (whisper), fix names and terms by hand, keep lines under 42 characters and 2 lines, then burn in.
8. Music and ducking: lower music under speech with sidechain compression (see Tools). Music only if the user supplied it or it is clearly royalty-free.
9. Add a 0.5 s fade in and out, normalize loudness, and export the presets the user needs.
10. Watch the full result once, start to end, before replying.

## Tools on a Mac

- Record (if asked, after the user says go): `screencapture -v -C -k output/rec.mov` (`-C` cursor, `-k` show clicks); stop with Ctrl+C or via `-V <seconds>`.
- Segment render: `ffmpeg -ss <a> -to <b> -i rec.mov -vf "fps=30,crop=W:H:X:Y,scale=1920:1080:flags=lanczos,format=yuv420p" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -preset slow -c:a aac -b:a 192k -ar 48000 tmp/seg-01.mp4`
- Join: `ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i tmp/list.txt -c copy tmp/joined.mp4`.
- Captions: `whisper tmp/joined.mp4 --model small --output_format srt --output_dir tmp` (`python3 -m pip install --user openai-whisper`), then `-vf "subtitles=tmp/joined.srt:force_style='FontName=Helvetica Neue,FontSize=20,PrimaryColour=&HFFFFFF&,OutlineColour=&H80000000&,BorderStyle=3,MarginV=40'"`.
- Music ducking: `ffmpeg -i tmp/joined.mp4 -i music.m4a -filter_complex "[1:a]volume=0.35[m];[m][0:a]sidechaincompress=threshold=0.03:ratio=10:attack=20:release=400[duck];[0:a][duck]amix=inputs=2:duration=first:normalize=0,loudnorm=I=-14:TP=-1.5[a]" -map 0:v -map "[a]" -c:v copy -c:a aac -b:a 192k output/demo.mp4`
- Voiceover placeholder: `say -v Samantha -o tmp/vo.aiff -f tmp/vo.txt`, then `afconvert -f m4af -d aac tmp/vo.aiff tmp/vo.m4a`.
- Title card: render a 1920x1080 PNG (see `poster-and-graphics`), then `ffmpeg -loop 1 -t 2 -i title.png -f lavfi -t 2 -i anullsrc=r=48000:cl=stereo -vf format=yuv420p -c:v libx264 -c:a aac tmp/seg-00.mp4`.
- Export presets:
  - Web/YouTube 16:9: 1920x1080, 30 fps, CRF 18, `-movflags +faststart`, loudnorm -14.
  - Vertical social: 1080x1920 with the demo scaled to width over a blurred or brand-color background, captions in the middle third.
  - Square: 1080x1080. Small share: 1280x720 CRF 26, under 25 MB.
- Check: `open output/demo.mp4`.

## Quality checklist

- No pauses over about 1 second without something happening on screen or in audio.
- Every zoomed segment is sharp (crop at least 960 px wide on a 1920 output).
- Captions match the words, with correct product names, and never cover the UI being shown.
- Music is quieter than speech everywhere; no clipping; loudness near -14 LUFS.
- No private info visible: emails, notifications, tokens, other tabs, desktop files. Blur with `boxblur` on a crop overlay if needed, and tell the user.
- Exports match the requested platforms and play in QuickTime.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: length before and after, what was added, paths, e.g. "Cut your 6-minute recording to a 1:48 demo with 4 zooms, captions and ducked music: output/demo-16x9.mp4 and output/demo-9x16.mp4."

## Pitfalls

- Mixing segments with different fps or sizes, which breaks the concat or desyncs audio.
- Zooming into regions so small the text turns to mush.
- Cutting mid-word; keep padding around speech.
- Leaving notifications or personal data on screen.
- Variable frame rate from screen recorders; force `fps=30` on every segment.
- Starting a recording or posting the video without the user's yes.

text:
---
name: screenshot-ocr
description: Use when text must be read out of an image, screenshot or scanned PDF: "copy the text from this screenshot", "OCR this scan", "get the table out of this picture", "what does this photo say".
---

# Screenshot OCR

## When to use

- Pulling text from screenshots, photos of documents, receipts, slides or scanned PDFs.
- Rebuilding a table seen in an image as CSV.
- Putting the extracted text on the clipboard.
- Not for PDFs that already have a text layer: try `pdftotext` first (see the `pdf-tools` skill). Only OCR when that returns nothing.

## Steps

1. Find the input. Screenshots are usually on the Desktop: `ls -t ~/Desktop/*.png | head -5`. Copy the file into `tmp/`.
2. If it's a PDF, check for real text first: `pdftotext -layout tmp/in.pdf - | head`. Empty output means it's a scan; turn pages into images: `pdftoppm -r 300 -png tmp/in.pdf tmp/page` (poppler) or, built in, `sips -s format png tmp/in.pdf --out tmp/page.png` (first page only).
3. Prepare small or blurry images: upscale with `sips -Z 3000 tmp/in.png` when the text is tiny. Leave clear images alone.
4. OCR with macOS Vision (best quality, no install) using the Swift script below. Fall back to tesseract if Swift is unavailable.
5. Read the result and fix obvious OCR errors only when certain (0/O, 1/l, broken hyphenation). Never guess numbers, names or amounts; mark unsure parts with `[?]`.
6. Tables: Vision returns lines with bounding boxes. Group words into rows by their y position and into columns by x gaps, then write `output/<name>.csv`. Check the column count is the same on every row.
7. Save the text to `output/<name>.txt` (or `.md`/`.csv`) and, if the user asked, copy it: `pbcopy < output/name.txt`.

## Tools on a Mac

- Vision OCR, saved as `tmp/ocr.swift` and run with `swift tmp/ocr.swift tmp/in.png > tmp/out.txt`:

```swift
import Vision
import AppKit
let imageURL = URL(fileURLWithPath: CommandLine.arguments[1])
guard let image = NSImage(contentsOf: imageURL),
      let cgImage = image.cgImage(forProposedRect: nil, context: nil, hints: nil) else { exit(1) }
let request = VNRecognizeTextRequest()
request.recognitionLevel = .accurate
request.usesLanguageCorrection = true
try VNImageRequestHandler(cgImage: cgImage).perform([request])
for observation in request.results ?? [] {
    guard let best = observation.topCandidates(1).first else { continue }
    let box = observation.boundingBox
    print(String(format: "%.3f\t%.3f\t%@", box.minY, box.minX, best.string))
}
```

  Output is `y<TAB>x<TAB>text`, y measured from the bottom. Sort by y descending for reading order; strip the first two columns for plain text: `sort -t$'\t' -k1,1nr -k2,2n tmp/out.txt | cut -f3-`.
- Other languages: set `request.recognitionLanguages = ["de-DE", "en-US"]`.
- `swift` needs the Xcode command line tools. If missing (`xcode-select -p` fails), use tesseract.
- `brew install tesseract` then `tesseract tmp/in.png stdout` or `tesseract tmp/in.png tmp/out --psm 6` (block of text); add `-l deu` with `brew install tesseract-lang` for other languages; `tesseract tmp/in.png tmp/out tsv` gives word positions for tables.
- `brew install poppler` for `pdftotext` and `pdftoppm`.
- `sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight file.png` for size; `sips -Z 3000` to upscale; `sips -s format png in.heic --out tmp/in.png` for iPhone photos.
- `screencapture -x tmp/screen.png` captures the screen if the user says "read what's on my screen" (needs Screen Recording permission).
- `pbcopy < file` puts text on the clipboard.

## Quality checklist

- Reading order is right (top to bottom, columns not interleaved).
- Numbers, dates, amounts and names match the image when spot-checked.
- Unsure characters are marked, not invented.
- Tables have the same number of columns on every row and a header row.
- The original file is untouched; output is in `output/`.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences, for example "I pulled the text from the receipt; it's in output/receipt.txt and on your clipboard." If a part was unreadable, say which part. For short text (a line or two), you can include it in the reply.

## Pitfalls

- Low-resolution screenshots of small fonts: upscale before OCR, never after.
- Multi-column layouts read across columns; split by x position before joining lines.
- Handwriting is unreliable with tesseract; Vision does better but still check.
- HEIC photos must be converted first for tesseract.
- `pdftotext` on a scan returns blank pages, not an error. Check for empty output.
- Don't paste sensitive text (IDs, account numbers) into the reply to be read aloud; point to the file.
