text:
---
name: secure-coding
description: Use when writing or checking code that handles user input, logins, files, databases, secrets or the web ("is this secure", "security audit", "check for vulnerabilities", building an API or web app).
---

# Secure Coding

## When to use

- Building anything that takes input from users, files, URLs or other programs.
- Code with accounts, sessions, payments, uploads, database queries or shell commands.
- The user asks for a security check, audit or "is this safe".

Do not use when:

- The user wants a general review covering style and performance too. Use code-review, and use this checklist for its security part.

## Steps

1. Map the attack surface: list every entry point (HTTP routes, CLI args, file readers, webhooks, message handlers) and every sensitive sink (database, shell, file system, HTML output, outbound requests, eval). Write it in `tmp/security-notes.md`.
2. Secrets out of code. Search for keys and passwords (see Tools). Secrets belong in environment variables or the platform's secret store, read at runtime; `.env` is listed in .gitignore and an `.env.example` holds names only. If a real secret was committed, tell the user to rotate it; deleting it from the file does not remove it from git history. Never ask for, copy or store the secret yourself.
3. Validate input at the boundary: check type, length, range and format with an allowlist (expected values) rather than a blocklist. Reject early with a clear error. Use a schema library where the project has one (zod, pydantic, Codable).
4. Injection, for each sink:
   - SQL: parameterized queries or the ORM's binding (`cursor.execute("... WHERE id = ?", (user_id,))`), never string formatting.
   - Shell: pass an argument list (`subprocess.run(["convert", path])`, `execFile`), never `shell=True` or `exec` with user text.
   - HTML: let the template engine escape; avoid `innerHTML`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `|safe` with user data.
   - Paths: resolve and confirm the result stays inside the allowed folder (block `../`).
   - Never `eval`, `pickle.loads`, or `yaml.load` (use `yaml.safe_load`) on untrusted data.
5. Auth and access control: every route that reads or changes private data checks who the user is and that they own that record (not just that they are logged in). Check on the server, never only in the UI. Deny by default.
6. Passwords and sessions: hash with bcrypt, scrypt or argon2, never plain SHA; cookies `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` or stricter; CSRF protection for cookie-based forms; rate-limit login.
7. Outbound requests built from user input (SSRF): allowlist hosts; block internal addresses like `127.0.0.1`, `169.254.169.254`, `10.x`.
8. Errors and logs: users see generic messages; logs never contain passwords, tokens or full card numbers.
9. Dependencies: run the audit for the stack and upgrade anything high or critical that has a fix.
10. Walk the OWASP Top 10 (2021) checklist: A01 broken access control, A02 crypto failures (TLS, hashing, no home-made crypto), A03 injection (including XSS), A04 insecure design (abuse cases, limits), A05 misconfiguration (debug off, default passwords, CORS not `*` with credentials, security headers), A06 vulnerable components, A07 auth failures, A08 integrity (unsigned updates, unsafe deserialization), A09 logging and monitoring gaps, A10 SSRF.
11. Write findings to `output/security-review.md`, each with severity (critical, high, medium, low), file:line, how it could be exploited in one line, and the fix. Fix only when the user asked for fixes.

## Tools on a Mac

- Secret search: `grep -rnEi '(api[_-]?key|secret|token|passw(or)?d|private[_-]?key)\s*[:=]' --exclude-dir={node_modules,.git,.venv} .` and `git log -p | grep -nEi 'BEGIN (RSA|OPENSSH) PRIVATE KEY|sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'`.
- Dedicated scanner: `brew install gitleaks`, then `gitleaks detect --source . --no-banner`.
- Node: `npm audit`, `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high`; fix with `npm audit fix` (not `--force` without checking the changes).
- Python: `python3 -m pip install --user pip-audit bandit`, then `pip-audit -r requirements.txt` and `bandit -r src -ll`.
- Multi-language static checks: `python3 -m pip install --user semgrep`, then `semgrep --config auto .`.
- Headers on a running site: `curl -sI https://localhost:3000 | grep -iE 'content-security|strict-transport|x-frame|x-content-type'`.
- Open ports a local app exposes: `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN`.

## Quality checklist

- No secrets in code, config committed to git, logs or replies.
- Every entry point validates input; every sink uses safe APIs.
- Every private-data route checks ownership on the server.
- Dependency audit run and its result reported.
- Each OWASP item checked or marked not applicable.
- Findings have severity, location, exploit line and fix.

## Reply to the user

"Security review in output/security-review.md: <N> issues, <M> high or critical. The most urgent is <one line>." If a secret leaked: say plainly that they should rotate it now.

## Pitfalls

- Validating in the browser only; attackers call the API directly.
- Escaping input on the way in instead of output encoding for each context.
- Checking "is logged in" but not "owns this record" (IDOR).
- Running audit fix with `--force` and breaking the app with a major upgrade.
- Testing exploits against systems the user does not own. Only test locally or on their own setup, with their yes.
- Printing a found secret in full in the reply; show only the first few characters and the file.

---
name: skill-creator
description: Use when the user says "make a skill", "save this as a skill", "remember how to do this" or wants a repeatable how-to added to the skills library, or an existing skill fixed or sharpened.
---

# Skill Creator

## When to use

- The user asks to turn a task, a workflow or a set of house rules into a skill.
- You just finished a task that took real trial and error and the user is likely to ask again (same file type, same site, same report). Offer to save it; write it only on a yes.
- An existing skill fired at the wrong time, missed a step or gave stale commands: edit it.
- Not worth a skill: a one-off task, a single command, a fact about the user (that belongs in your notes), or something any helper already does well without help.

## Steps

1. Name the job in one line: what input, what output, what makes it done. If you cannot, it is not ready to be a skill.
2. Pick a name: lowercase words joined by hyphens, two or three words, saying the job (`invoice-pdfs`, `weekly-sales-report`). Check the library first so you do not duplicate one: `ls "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Dottie/Skills"` and `grep -l "^name:" */SKILL.md`.
3. Write the description first, because it is the only part a helper sees before loading. Start with "Use when", then the phrases a user would actually say and the kind of file or site involved. One or two sentences, under 220 characters. Bad: "Helps with reports." Good: "Use when the user wants the Monday sales report from Stripe exports: 'do the weekly numbers', 'sales recap'."
4. Create the folder and file: `<library>/<name>/SKILL.md`, starting with front matter:

```
---
name: weekly-sales-report
description: Use when ...
---
```

5. Write the body with `##` sections in this order: When to use (and when a sibling skill fits better), Steps (numbered, concrete), Tools on a Mac (exact commands and flags), Quality checklist, Reply to the user, Pitfalls. Keep it between about 60 and 130 lines.
6. Put the hard-won details in: the exact command that worked, the flag that broke it, the file path, the column name, the limit you hit. Leave out what a capable helper knows already.
7. Supporting files (a script, a template) go in the same folder; reference them by relative path, for example `scripts/clean.py`, and keep them small.
8. Test it on a real task: in `tmp/`, follow only what the skill says, from a fresh start, on a real input the user gave you. Note every place you had to guess.
9. Fix the guesses, then test once more. If the description would not have triggered for the user's real phrasing, add that phrasing.

## Tools on a Mac

- `ls`, `cat`, `grep -n` to read the library and check for overlaps.
- `mkdir -p "<library>/<name>"` and your file tools to write `SKILL.md`.
- `head -5 SKILL.md` to check the front matter; `wc -l SKILL.md` for length.
- `awk '/^description:/{print length($0)-13}' SKILL.md` to count description characters.
- `python3 -c "import sys,re;t=open(sys.argv[1]).read();print(bool(re.match(r'---\nname: [a-z0-9-]+\ndescription: Use when',t)))" SKILL.md` as a quick format check.
- `grep -nP '[^\x00-\x7F]' SKILL.md` finds curly quotes and long dashes; replace them with plain ASCII.

## Quality checklist

- Folder name and `name:` match exactly and use only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.
- Description starts "Use when", names real trigger words, is under 220 characters.
- Steps are numbered, each one an action with a command, path or check.
- Every command was run at least once during testing, or is clearly marked as untested.
- No passwords, API keys, tokens or personal data inside the skill. Anything that sends, posts, buys or deletes says to wait for the user's yes.
- Pitfalls list real failures you saw, not generic advice.
- Ends with a `Based on:` line.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences: the skill's name, what it is for, and that it is saved in the library, for example "I saved a skill called weekly-sales-report that rebuilds the Monday numbers from your Stripe export; it's on for this helper." Mention if it still needs a test on a real file.

## Pitfalls

- A vague description means the skill never loads. Write it for the moment of decision, with the user's words.
- Long essays get skimmed. Cut background; keep commands and checks.
- Copying a chat transcript into a skill. Distill it into steps.
- Hard-coding one file name or date that will be different next time. Use placeholders like `<export.csv>`.
- Two skills for the same job confuse helpers. Extend the existing one instead.
- Saving secrets from the conversation into the skill file. Never.

---
name: slide-decks
description: Use when the user wants a presentation: "make slides", "build a deck", "turn this into a PowerPoint/Keynote", pitch decks, talks, or editing an existing .pptx or .key file.
---

# Slide Decks

## When to use

- Building a new deck as .pptx (opens in PowerPoint, Keynote and Google Slides).
- Building one in Keynote when the user asks for Keynote by name.
- Editing, reordering or pulling text out of an existing .pptx.
- Exporting a deck to PDF.
- Not for a written report: use `word-documents` or `doc-coauthoring`.

## Steps

1. Get the point of the talk in one sentence, the audience and the length (minutes or slide count). If the user gave none, assume 10 minutes and 8 to 12 slides.
2. Write the outline in `tmp/outline.md` first: one line per slide stating the single idea it carries, as a full sentence ("Churn fell 20% after onboarding changes"), not a topic ("Churn").
3. Shape it: title slide, the problem or question, 3 to 7 body slides, a summary or ask, a closing slide. One idea per slide; at most 5 bullets of at most 8 words each.
4. Put detail in speaker notes, not on the slide. Every body slide gets 2 to 5 sentences of notes the presenter could read.
5. Build with python-pptx (below). Use the built-in layouts so the deck stays editable: 0 title, 1 title and content, 5 title only, 6 blank.
6. Add visuals where they carry the idea: a chart from real numbers, an image the user gave, or a big single number. No decorative clip art.
7. Save `output/<topic>-deck.pptx`. Render a check: `qlmanage -t -s 1200 -o tmp output/<topic>-deck.pptx` for slide one, and export to PDF (below) to review every slide.

## Tools on a Mac

- `python3 -m pip install --user python-pptx`

```python
from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
deck = Presentation()
deck.slide_width, deck.slide_height = Inches(13.333), Inches(7.5)   # 16:9
slide = deck.slides.add_slide(deck.slide_layouts[1])
slide.shapes.title.text = "Churn fell 20% after the new onboarding"
body = slide.placeholders[1].text_frame
body.text = "Trial-to-paid up from 31% to 38%"
body.add_paragraph().text = "Biggest gain: teams of 5 to 20"
slide.notes_slide.notes_text_frame.text = "Start with the number, then explain why."
deck.save("output/churn-deck.pptx")
```

- Charts: `from pptx.chart.data import CategoryChartData` and `slide.shapes.add_chart(XL_CHART_TYPE.COLUMN_CLUSTERED, x, y, cx, cy, chart_data)`.
- Images: `slide.shapes.add_picture("photo.png", Inches(1), Inches(1.5), height=Inches(5))`. Resize big photos first: `sips -Z 1920 photo.jpg --out tmp/photo.jpg`.
- Read a deck: loop `deck.slides`, then `shape.has_text_frame` and `shape.text_frame.text`; notes in `slide.notes_slide.notes_text_frame.text`.
- Keynote export to PDF (Keynote installed):

```bash
osascript -e 'tell application "Keynote"
  set theDoc to open POSIX file "/full/path/output/deck.pptx"
  export theDoc to POSIX file "/full/path/output/deck.pdf" as PDF
  close theDoc saving no
end tell'
```

- Without Keynote: `brew install --cask libreoffice` then `soffice --headless --convert-to pdf --outdir output output/deck.pptx` (large install; ask first).
- Check every slide: `pdftoppm -png -r 60 output/deck.pdf tmp/slide` (from `brew install poppler`) and look at the images.

## Quality checklist

- Each slide title is a sentence that states its point; reading only the titles tells the story.
- No slide has more than 5 bullets or text below 18 pt.
- Nothing overflows its box (check the rendered PDF or PNGs).
- Every body slide has speaker notes.
- Numbers on slides match the source; chart axes are labeled.
- 16:9 unless the user asked for 4:3.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences: slide count, the storyline in a phrase, the path. For example: "Made a 9-slide deck on the Q3 churn results with speaker notes; it's at output/churn-deck.pptx, plus a PDF copy."

## Pitfalls

- python-pptx does not auto-shrink text; long bullets spill off the slide silently. Keep bullets short or lower the font size yourself.
- Default python-pptx decks are 4:3. Set the width and height for 16:9 before adding slides.
- `slide_layouts` indexes differ in custom templates; print `[layout.name for layout in deck.slide_layouts]` first.
- Keynote scripting needs Automation permission and opens the app on screen; use it only when asked.
- Do not fill slides with paragraphs copied from the source document.
- Fonts not on the Mac fall back silently; stick to system fonts like Helvetica Neue or the template's.

name: social-media-content
text:
---
name: social-media-content
description: Use when the user wants posts written for X, Instagram, TikTok or LinkedIn: "write a tweet about", "caption for this photo", "LinkedIn post", "content calendar", "hooks for my video". Drafts only.
---

# Social Media Content

## When to use

- Drafting posts, captions, threads, video scripts or hooks for X, Instagram, TikTok or LinkedIn.
- Turning one idea, article or launch into versions per platform.
- Planning a two-week content calendar.
- You never post, schedule, like, follow or reply on the user's accounts. You write drafts the user copies and posts.
- Not for long blog posts or newsletters: write those as a document.

## Steps

1. Get the basics, from the request or by asking once: who it's for, the one point of the post, the platform(s), the voice (look at two or three of the user's past posts if they share them), and any link or call to action.
2. Write the hook first. The first line decides whether anyone keeps reading. Patterns that work: a specific number ("I cut our bill 40% in a week"), a surprising claim, a clear promise ("3 settings every Mac user should change"), a question the reader has. Write three hooks and pick the strongest.
3. Write the body for the platform (limits below). One idea per post. Short lines, plain words, concrete details over adjectives.
4. End with one call to action at most: a question, "link in bio", "save this", or the link.
5. Hashtags: 0 to 2 on X and LinkedIn, 3 to 5 relevant ones on Instagram and TikTok. Real tags people use, not a wall of them.
6. Check length per platform with `wc -m` and trim.
7. Save drafts to `output/social-drafts.md`, one `##` heading per platform with the character count after each draft. For a calendar, write `output/content-calendar.csv` (see below) and a short `.md` version.
8. Copy one draft to the clipboard if the user asks: `pbcopy < tmp/x-post.txt`.

## Tools on a Mac

- `wc -m < tmp/post.txt` counts characters (emoji may count as 2 on X; leave margin).
- `pbcopy` to put a draft on the clipboard; `open output/social-drafts.md` to show it.
- `sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight image.jpg` to check image size; `sips -c 1350 1080 in.jpg --out output/ig.jpg` crops to 4:5 for Instagram.
- Platform limits and fits:
  - X: 280 characters for standard accounts (longer only with a paid tier); links count as 23. Threads: 3 to 7 posts, number them.
  - Instagram: caption up to 2,200 characters, about 125 show before "more"; up to 30 hashtags allowed, use 3 to 5. Feed images 1080x1350 (4:5).
  - TikTok: caption up to 4,000 characters; a script with the hook spoken in the first 2 seconds; 9:16, 1080x1920.
  - LinkedIn: posts up to 3,000 characters, about 210 show before "see more"; first two lines carry it; line breaks help.
- Calendar CSV columns: `date,platform,format,hook,post,cta,asset_needed,status` with status `draft`.
- A good two-week mix: about 40% teaching (tips, how-tos), 30% story or behind the scenes, 20% proof (results, examples the user supplied), 10% direct ask (launch, sign-up). Spread posts 3 to 5 per week per platform rather than daily if the user posts alone.
- Video scripts (TikTok, Reels): write as `0-2s hook | 2-20s point | last 3s call to action`, with on-screen text lines marked separately from spoken lines.

## Quality checklist

- Each draft is under the platform limit, with the count shown.
- The hook is in the first line and is specific.
- Facts, numbers and claims come from the user or a source; nothing invented about results or customers.
- No fake testimonials, no impersonating anyone, no misleading health, money or legal claims.
- Paid partnerships or sponsored content are labeled (#ad or the platform's tag) if the user mentioned a sponsor.
- The calendar has 14 days, mixes formats, and doesn't repeat the same hook.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences, for example "I wrote drafts for X, Instagram and LinkedIn in output/social-drafts.md; the X one is 241 characters and on your clipboard." Remind them you didn't post anything only if they might assume you did.

## Pitfalls

- Pasting the same text everywhere. Each platform reads differently; at least rewrite the hook and length.
- Hashtag walls look like spam and reduce reach on LinkedIn and X.
- Links in the post body can lower reach on some platforms; offer the link as a first comment the user adds, and say why.
- Burying the point after a long setup.
- Trend audio, memes and current events go stale fast; check they're still current before suggesting them.
- Mentioning or tagging real people or brands in a way that suggests they endorse the user.
- Never log in to, post to, or schedule on any account, even if asked to "just post it"; hand the draft back and let the user post.

---
name: spreadsheets
description: Use when the task is a spreadsheet: make, clean, analyze or fix an .xlsx, .csv or Numbers file, add formulas, totals, charts or formatting, or convert between spreadsheet formats.
---

# Spreadsheets

## When to use

- Creating a workbook from data, a budget, a tracker or a model.
- Cleaning a messy CSV or .xlsx (headers, dates, duplicates, types).
- Adding formulas, summaries, pivots, conditional formatting or charts.
- Converting .xlsx, .csv and Numbers files.
- Not when the user only wants a number answered: compute it and reply, no file needed.

## Steps

1. Copy inputs to `tmp/` and look before changing anything: sheet names, header row, row count, column types.
   `python3 -c "import pandas as pd; x=pd.read_excel('tmp/in.xlsx', sheet_name=None); [print(k, v.shape, list(v.columns)) for k,v in x.items()]"`
2. Plan the layout: one table per sheet, headers in row 1, one row per record, no merged cells inside data, inputs and assumptions on their own sheet or clearly marked block.
3. Use pandas for cleaning and analysis, openpyxl for the final workbook with formulas and formatting.
4. Write formulas, not computed values, for anything the user might change: totals, ratios, growth, lookups. A cell that holds `=SUM(B2:B13)` stays right when inputs change; a pasted number does not.
5. Format: bold header, freeze the top row, sensible column widths, number formats (currency, percent, dates), an autofilter on tables.
6. Add a chart only if it helps answer the question.
7. Save to `output/<name>.xlsx` (and `.csv` if asked). Recalculate and check for errors (below).

## Tools on a Mac

- `python3 -m pip install --user openpyxl pandas`

```python
from openpyxl import Workbook
from openpyxl.styles import Font
from openpyxl.chart import BarChart, Reference
workbook = Workbook()
sheet = workbook.active
sheet.title = "Budget"
sheet.append(["Month", "Income", "Spend", "Saved"])
for row_number, (month, income, spend) in enumerate(data, start=2):
    sheet.append([month, income, spend, f"=B{row_number}-C{row_number}"])
last_row = sheet.max_row
sheet.append(["Total", f"=SUM(B2:B{last_row})", f"=SUM(C2:C{last_row})", f"=SUM(D2:D{last_row})"])
for cell in sheet[1]:
    cell.font = Font(bold=True)
sheet.freeze_panes = "A2"
for column in "BCD":
    for cell in sheet[column][1:]:
        cell.number_format = '"$"#,##0.00'
chart = BarChart()
chart.add_data(Reference(sheet, min_col=4, min_row=1, max_row=last_row), titles_from_data=True)
chart.set_categories(Reference(sheet, min_col=1, min_row=2, max_row=last_row))
sheet.add_chart(chart, "F2")
workbook.save("output/budget.xlsx")
```

- Read values a formula produced: `openpyxl.load_workbook(path, data_only=True)` (only works after Excel or Numbers has saved the file).
- Recalculate and check formulas without Excel: `brew install --cask libreoffice`, then `soffice --headless --convert-to xlsx --outdir tmp output/budget.xlsx` and load `tmp/budget.xlsx` with `data_only=True`; scan every cell for `#REF!`, `#DIV/0!`, `#VALUE!`, `#NAME?`. Ask before installing LibreOffice.
- Numbers to Excel or CSV (Numbers installed):

```bash
osascript -e 'tell application "Numbers"
  set theDoc to open POSIX file "/full/path/in.numbers"
  export theDoc to POSIX file "/full/path/tmp/in.xlsx" as Microsoft Excel
  close theDoc saving no
end tell'
```

- CSV quick look: `head -5 file.csv`, `wc -l file.csv`, `file file.csv` (encoding).
- `qlmanage -t -s 1200 -o tmp output/budget.xlsx` for a preview image.

## Quality checklist

- Totals and derived columns are formulas; spot-check two by hand.
- No formula errors anywhere after recalculation.
- Headers in row 1, frozen, bold; no blank rows inside tables.
- Dates are real dates, numbers are numbers (not text with spaces or currency symbols).
- Row count after cleaning matches what you expect; note any rows dropped and why.
- Original file untouched.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: what the sheet holds, the headline number if there is one, the path. For example: "Built a 12-month budget with live totals and a savings chart; you'd save $4,210 at this pace. It's at output/budget.xlsx."

## Pitfalls

- pandas `to_excel` writes values only and loses formatting; build the final file with openpyxl or style it after.
- Saving with openpyxl drops existing charts, images and pivot tables in a workbook you loaded. For those files, write a new sheet or a new workbook instead of rewriting the old one.
- `data_only=True` then `save()` replaces every formula with its cached value. Never save a workbook you opened that way.
- CSV from Excel on a Mac may be UTF-16 or use semicolons; pass `encoding` and `sep` to `read_csv`.
- Leading zeros (zip codes, IDs) vanish unless the column is read as `dtype=str`.
- Hardcoding a total because the formula was fiddly defeats the purpose of the sheet.

name: systematic-debugging
text:
---
name: systematic-debugging
description: Use when something is broken or behaves wrong ("it crashes", "this error", "tests fail", "it worked yesterday", "why does it..."). Reproduce, gather evidence, find the root cause, then fix.
---

# Systematic Debugging

## When to use

- An error message, crash, failing test, wrong output, hang or slowdown.
- A fix was already tried and did not work. That is a strong signal to slow down and use this.
- Behavior differs between two places (your Mac and CI, yesterday and today).

Do not use when:

- The cause is plain from the error and the fix is one line you can test at once. Fix it, add a regression test, verify.
- The user wants a new feature, not a fix. Use brainstorming-before-building or writing-plans.

## Steps

1. Read the whole error. Read the full stack trace, top and bottom, and note the first line that is in the project's own code. Copy the exact message into `tmp/debug-notes.md`.
2. Reproduce it. Find the smallest command that shows the problem every time, and write it in the notes. If it only happens sometimes, run it in a loop (`for i in $(seq 20); do <cmd> || break; done`) and note how often.
3. Check what changed. `git status`, `git diff`, `git log --oneline -15`, and recently updated dependencies (lock file diffs). If it worked at a known commit, use `git bisect` (see Tools).
4. Gather evidence at the boundaries. Where data passes between parts (function call, file, network, process), print or log what goes in and what comes out. Find the first place where the data is wrong. The bug is between the last good point and the first bad one.
5. Form one hypothesis, written as "X happens because Y". Pick a test that would prove it wrong: a print, a smaller input, a changed variable. Run it.
6. If the hypothesis fails, cross it out in the notes and form the next one. Change one thing at a time. Revert experiments that did not help.
7. Keep tracing backward until you reach the root cause: the original wrong value or wrong assumption, not the line where it finally blew up.
8. Write a failing test that reproduces the bug (see test-driven-development). See it fail.
9. Fix the root cause with the smallest change. Do not also tidy unrelated code.
10. Run the new test, then the whole suite, then the original reproduction command. All must pass.
11. Search for the same mistake elsewhere: `grep -rn` for the pattern you just fixed.
12. If three fixes in a row fail, stop. The model of the system is wrong. Re-read the code from the entry point and question the architecture, and tell the user what you have learned so far.

## Tools on a Mac

- Find a culprit commit: `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad`, `git bisect good <sha>`, then `git bisect run <test command>`; finish with `git bisect reset`.
- Mac app and system logs: `log show --last 10m --predicate 'process == "AppName"' --style compact`; crash reports in `~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/` (`ls -t | head`).
- Python: `python3 -X dev script.py` (extra warnings), `python3 -m pdb script.py`, `python3 -m pytest -x --pdb`, `traceback.print_exc()`.
- Node: `node --trace-warnings app.js`, `node --inspect-brk app.js`, `DEBUG=* npm start` for libraries using the debug package.
- Swift: `swift test --filter Name`, `lldb .build/debug/<binary>` then `run`, `bt` after a crash.
- Network: `curl -v <url>` to see headers and status; `nc -vz host 443` to check a port opens.
- Processes and ports: `lsof -i :3000`, `ps aux | grep <name>`, `top -o cpu -l 1 | head -20`.
- Environment differences: `env | sort > tmp/env.txt`, `which -a python3`, `sw_vers`.

## Quality checklist

- You can state the root cause in one sentence, and the evidence that proves it.
- A regression test exists, failed before the fix and passes after.
- The original reproduction now behaves correctly.
- All debug prints and temporary logging are removed.
- The full test suite passes.

## Reply to the user

"Found it: <root cause in plain words>. Fixed in <file> and added a test so it stays fixed; all tests pass." If not solved: say what is ruled out and the next thing to try.

## Pitfalls

- Guessing a fix from the error line and shipping it without understanding why the bad value got there.
- Changing several things at once, so you cannot tell which one mattered.
- Wrapping the failure in try/except or a nil check that hides the symptom.
- Trusting the error message's location when the real fault is upstream.
- Debugging a stale build: rebuild, clear caches (`rm -rf node_modules/.cache`, `.build`, `__pycache__`) when results look impossible.
- Claiming "fixed" without rerunning the original reproduction.

name: test-driven-development
text:
---
name: test-driven-development
description: Use when writing or changing code that has behavior worth checking ("add a feature", "write a function", "fix this bug", "write tests"). Write the failing test first, watch it fail, then make it pass.
---

# Test-Driven Development

## When to use

- Any new function, feature or bug fix in a project that has, or can have, automated tests.
- Fixing a bug: the regression test that reproduces it comes first.
- Refactoring: tests that pin current behavior come before the change.

Do not use when:

- Throwaway exploration ("try calling this API and see what comes back"). Explore, then delete the spike and do it properly with tests.
- Pure config or copy changes with no logic. Verify them with verification-before-done instead.
- You are hunting an unknown cause. Use systematic-debugging, then come back here for the fix.

## Steps

1. Find the test command. Look in package.json "scripts", pyproject.toml, setup.cfg, Package.swift, Makefile. If none exists, set one up (see Tools on a Mac) and commit that first.
2. Red: write one small test for the next bit of behavior. Name it after the behavior: `test_empty_input_returns_empty_list`, `it("rejects a negative amount")`.
3. Run only that test and watch it fail. Read the failure. It must fail for the reason you expect (assertion mismatch, function missing), not a typo, import error or syntax error. If it passes already, the test is wrong or the behavior exists; find out which.
4. Green: write the least code that makes it pass. Hard-coding is fine at this point if the next test will force the general version.
5. Run the test again and see it pass. Then run the whole suite to make sure nothing else broke.
6. Refactor: clean up names and duplication in both code and tests, running the suite after each change. Behavior must not change in this step.
7. Repeat from step 2 with the next behavior: edge cases (empty, zero, one, many, unicode, very large), error paths, then the happy path variants.
8. For a bug: write a test that reproduces the exact bug report, see it fail, fix, see it pass. Keep the test forever.
9. Commit after each green-and-refactored cycle with a message describing the behavior added.

## Tools on a Mac

Python:
- Install once: `python3 -m pip install --user pytest`
- Run all: `python3 -m pytest -q`; one test: `python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_parser.py::test_empty_input -x`
- Stop at first failure and show locals: `python3 -m pytest -x -l`
- Built-in fallback with no install: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`

JavaScript and TypeScript:
- Run all: `npm test`; pass a filter: `npm test -- parser` (Jest and Vitest both take a name pattern).
- Node 18+ has a built-in runner: `node --test`, test files named `*.test.js` or `*.test.mjs`.
- Add Vitest to a project: `npm install --save-dev vitest`, then `"test": "vitest run"` in package.json.

Swift:
- Swift packages: `swift test`; one test: `swift test --filter ParserTests/testEmptyInput`.
- Tests live in `Tests/<Target>Tests/` and import the module with `@testable import <Target>`.
- Xcode app projects: do not run `xcodebuild` from a helper unless the user asks; it can reset the app's privacy permissions. Put testable logic in a Swift package and `swift test` that.

Other:
- Go: `go test ./...`; Rust: `cargo test`; Ruby: `bundle exec rspec`.
- Watch mode while iterating: `npx vitest`, `python3 -m pip install --user pytest-watch && ptw`.

## Quality checklist

- You saw every new test fail before you wrote the code that passes it.
- Each test checks one behavior and has a name that says which.
- Tests use real inputs and assert on outputs, not on internal calls, unless the outside effect cannot be observed any other way.
- No test depends on the network, the clock or test order; fake or freeze those.
- The full suite passes at the end, and you read the final summary line.

## Reply to the user

"Added <behavior> with <N> new tests; the full suite passes (<X> passed). Code is in <path>." One or two sentences.

## Pitfalls

- Writing the code first and the test after, then never seeing the test fail. A test that never failed may test nothing.
- A test that fails because of an import error, counted as a "red" step.
- Mocking so much that the test only checks the mocks.
- Changing a test's expected value to match buggy output.
- Leaving `.only`, `fit`, `@pytest.mark.skip` or `-x` filters in committed code.
- Huge tests covering five behaviors, so a failure says nothing about which broke.

name: verification-before-done
text:
---
name: verification-before-done
description: Use before saying any task is done, fixed, working or passing, for code, files, scripts or documents. Run the real check, read its output, and put the evidence in the reply.
---

# Verification Before Done

## When to use

- At the end of every task, right before the final reply.
- Before any reply containing "done", "fixed", "works", "passes", "ready", "should work".
- Before committing, or before handing work to the user or another helper.

There is no "too small to verify". If a check takes too long to run, say that plainly instead of claiming success.

## Steps

1. Name the claim you are about to make, for example "the tests pass", "the script converts all 40 files", "the bug is fixed".
2. Pick the check that proves exactly that claim:
   - Tests pass: the full test command, not a filtered subset.
   - Build works: the build command, run fresh.
   - Bug fixed: the original reproduction steps, plus the regression test.
   - File created: the file exists, is not empty, and opens as the right type.
   - Script works: run it on real input and inspect the output.
   - Requirements met: re-read the user's request line by line and tick each item.
3. Run the check now, in this turn. Earlier runs do not count after any edit.
4. Read the whole output. Look at the exit code (`echo $?`), the summary line, warnings and counts. "No errors printed" is not the same as success.
5. If the check fails or is unclear, you are not done. Go back to the work (use systematic-debugging if the cause is unknown) and check again.
6. If something cannot be checked here (needs the user's account, another device, a real payment), say exactly what is unverified and how the user can check it.
7. Put the evidence in the reply: the command and the key result, in a few words.

## Tools on a Mac

- Exit codes: `<command>; echo "exit=$?"`. Zero means success for almost every tool.
- Tests: `python3 -m pytest -q`, `npm test`, `swift test`; read the last line (e.g. "42 passed", "Tests: 18 passed").
- Type and lint checks: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `python3 -m pyflakes .` (after `python3 -m pip install --user pyflakes`), `swiftc -typecheck file.swift`.
- Files: `ls -la output/`, `wc -l output/*.csv`, `file output/report.pdf`, `mdls -name kMDItemNumberOfPages output/report.pdf`.
- Images: `sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight output/*.png`.
- Documents: `textutil -convert txt -stdout output/report.docx | head -40` to read what is actually inside.
- JSON and CSV: `python3 -m json.tool output/data.json > /dev/null && echo valid`, `head -5 output/data.csv`.
- Web pages and servers: `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000`.
- Quick visual check: `qlmanage -t -s 800 -o tmp output/report.pdf` makes a thumbnail you can look at.
- Diff against the request: `git diff --stat` to confirm you changed only what was asked.

## Quality checklist

- The check was run after the last edit, in this turn.
- You read the exit code and summary, not just the first lines.
- The check matches the claim (a passing lint is not a passing test).
- Every requirement in the user's message is either met with evidence or listed as not done.
- Nothing in the reply says "should", "probably" or "I believe" about something you could have checked.

## Reply to the user

Lead with the result and the evidence: "Done: all 42 tests pass (pytest) and the report is at output/report.pdf, 6 pages." If partly done: "3 of 4 done; the upload is not tested because it needs your login."

## Pitfalls

- Saying "fixed" because the code looks right.
- Running a filtered test and reporting the whole suite as passing.
- Trusting a helper or a previous run's report instead of checking yourself.
- Missing a failure because output was piped through `head` or `tail` and the exit code was lost.
- Creating a file of 0 bytes, or a .pdf that is really HTML, and calling it done.
- Hiding a failing check by skipping the test or loosening the assertion.

name: video-downloads
text:
---
name: video-downloads
description: Use when the user wants a video or its audio saved from a link they have the right to keep: "download my YouTube video", "save this talk as mp3", "get the subtitles", Creative Commons or public domain clips.
---

# Video Downloads

## When to use

- Downloading the user's own uploads, Creative Commons or public domain videos, or clips the site lets everyone download.
- Getting audio only, a lower resolution, or subtitles from such a video.
- Not for DRM-protected or paid content: Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video, Spotify, Apple Music, paid courses, members-only or paywalled videos. Say no plainly and suggest the service's own offline download feature.
- Not for converting or editing files already on the Mac: use ffmpeg directly.

## Steps

1. Check the rights. Look at the page: is it the user's channel, marked Creative Commons, public domain (archive.org, government sources), or a site with a download button? If unclear, ask the user whether it is theirs or licensed for reuse. If it's a paid or DRM service, stop.
2. Check tools: `command -v yt-dlp ffmpeg`. Install missing ones with `brew install yt-dlp ffmpeg` (see `homebrew-cli-tools`).
3. Look before downloading: `yt-dlp -F URL` lists formats; `yt-dlp --print "%(title)s | %(duration_string)s | %(license)s" URL` shows title, length and the license if the site reports it.
4. Download into `output/`, named by title:
   - Best quality as MP4: `yt-dlp -f "bv*[ext=mp4]+ba[ext=m4a]/b[ext=mp4]/b" --merge-output-format mp4 -o "output/%(title)s.%(ext)s" URL`
   - Capped at 1080p: `-f "bv*[height<=1080]+ba/b[height<=1080]"`
   - Audio only as MP3: `yt-dlp -x --audio-format mp3 --audio-quality 0 -o "output/%(title)s.%(ext)s" URL`
   - Subtitles only: `yt-dlp --skip-download --write-subs --write-auto-subs --sub-langs "en.*" --convert-subs srt -o "output/%(title)s" URL`
   - A section: `--download-sections "*00:01:30-00:03:00"`
5. Playlists: confirm the count first (`yt-dlp --flat-playlist --print title URL | wc -l`) and ask before pulling more than about 20 videos. Add `--no-playlist` when the user meant one video from a playlist link.
6. Verify the file: `ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration,size -of default=nw=1 output/file.mp4`, and that it plays (`qlmanage -p` previews it).

## Tools on a Mac

- `yt-dlp` (Homebrew): `-F`, `-f`, `-x`, `--audio-format`, `--write-subs`, `--embed-subs`, `--embed-thumbnail`, `--restrict-filenames`, `--no-playlist`, `-o` templates.
- `ffmpeg`/`ffprobe` (Homebrew), needed for merging video and audio and for MP3.
- `afconvert -f m4af -d aac in.wav out.m4a` (built in) for simple audio conversions without ffmpeg.
- `qlmanage -p file` to preview; `open output/` to show the folder.
- `yt-dlp --list-subs URL` to see which subtitle languages exist before asking for them.
- `yt-dlp --embed-subs --embed-thumbnail --add-metadata` to keep subtitles, cover art and title inside the MP4.
- `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vn -c:a copy output/audio.m4a` pulls audio from a file already downloaded without re-encoding.
- `brew upgrade yt-dlp` when sites change and downloads start failing (only that formula).

- `yt-dlp --download-archive tmp/archive.txt` skips videos already fetched when the user asks again for the same channel or playlist.
- `yt-dlp --print filename -o "output/%(title)s.%(ext)s" URL` shows the final file name before downloading.

## Quality checklist

- Rights checked; nothing from a DRM, paid or members-only source.
- File plays, has sound, and the duration matches the page.
- Saved in `output/` with a readable name; `--restrict-filenames` if the title has odd characters.
- For Creative Commons, note the license and creator in `output/<title>-credits.txt` so the user can attribute it.
- No cookies, logins or browser sessions used to reach content the user couldn't otherwise download.

## Reply to the user

One sentence with what and where, for example "I saved the talk as an MP3 (42 minutes) in output/." If you refused, say why in one sentence and name the legitimate route (the app's offline download).

## Pitfalls

- "HTTP Error 403" or "Requested format is not available" usually means an outdated yt-dlp; upgrade it once and retry.
- Without ffmpeg, yt-dlp downloads separate video and audio files instead of one MP4.
- `--cookies-from-browser` exists but is a way around access controls; don't use it for content the user doesn't own or isn't allowed to save.
- Auto-generated subtitles can be poor; say they're automatic.
- Big files: a 1-hour 4K video can be several GB. Check `df -h ~` first and cap the height if space is tight.
- Long titles with slashes or emoji break paths; use `--restrict-filenames` or `-o "output/%(id)s.%(ext)s"`.
- Uploading or re-sharing the file anywhere waits for the user's yes, and the license still applies.

name: video-editing-ffmpeg
text:
---
name: video-editing-ffmpeg
description: Use when the user wants to trim, cut, join, convert, compress, resize, speed up, crop to vertical, add subtitles or music, or extract audio from a video file, or make it fit a social platform.
---

# Video Editing with ffmpeg

## When to use

- "Trim this video", "join these clips", "make it smaller", "convert MOV to MP4", "make it vertical for TikTok", "add captions", "pull the audio out", "speed it up 2x".
- Not for turning a screen recording into a polished demo with zooms and ducked music: use `screen-recording-edits`.
- Not for short looping animations: use `gif-maker`.
- Not for writing the script: use `youtube-tiktok-scripts` or `commercial-script-and-shotlist`.

## Steps

1. Check ffmpeg: `ffmpeg -version`; if missing, `brew install ffmpeg`.
2. Inspect the input: `ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration:stream=codec_name,width,height,r_frame_rate,sample_rate -of compact in.mov`. Note rotation, frame rate and whether there is audio.
3. Plan the command and write it to `tmp/edit.sh` so it can be rerun. Write results to `output/`, never over the input.
4. Run on a short section first (`-t 10`) when the job is long, check it, then do the full file.
5. Verify the output with `ffprobe` (duration, size, codec) and open it with `open output/x.mp4` or `qlmanage -p`.

## Tools on a Mac

Common recipes (H.264 + AAC MP4 plays everywhere):
- Trim, exact: `ffmpeg -ss 00:00:05 -to 00:00:32 -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 20 -preset medium -c:a aac -b:a 160k output/trim.mp4`
- Trim, instant (cuts on keyframes, may be off by a second): `ffmpeg -ss 5 -to 32 -i in.mp4 -c copy output/trim.mp4`
- Convert MOV to MP4: `ffmpeg -i in.mov -c:v libx264 -crf 20 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -movflags +faststart output/out.mp4`
- Compress: raise `-crf` (23 to 28 = smaller) and cap size with `-vf "scale=-2:1080"`. To hit a size, bitrate = target MB x 8192 / seconds minus audio kbps; then `-b:v <n>k -maxrate <n>k -bufsize <2n>k`.
- Hardware encode (fast, bigger files): `-c:v h264_videotoolbox -b:v 8M` or `hevc_videotoolbox -tag:v hvc1`.
- Join same-format clips: write `tmp/list.txt` lines `file '/full/path/a.mp4'`, then `ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i tmp/list.txt -c copy output/joined.mp4`. Different formats: re-encode each to the same size, fps and codec first.
- Vertical 9:16 center crop: `-vf "crop=ih*9/16:ih,scale=1080:1920"`. Blurred-background fit instead: `-filter_complex "[0:v]scale=1080:1920:force_original_aspect_ratio=increase,crop=1080:1920,boxblur=20[bg];[0:v]scale=1080:-2[fg];[bg][fg]overlay=(W-w)/2:(H-h)/2"`.
- Speed 2x: `-filter_complex "[0:v]setpts=0.5*PTS[v];[0:a]atempo=2.0[a]" -map "[v]" -map "[a]"` (atempo takes 0.5 to 2.0 per stage; chain for more).
- Extract audio: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vn -c:a aac -b:a 192k output/audio.m4a`, or `-vn -c:a libmp3lame -q:a 2 output/audio.mp3`, or WAV `-vn -c:a pcm_s16le output/audio.wav`.
- Remove audio: `-an`. Replace audio: `ffmpeg -i v.mp4 -i music.m4a -map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v copy -shortest output/out.mp4`.
- Burn subtitles: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "subtitles=subs.srt:force_style='FontName=Helvetica,FontSize=18,Outline=2,MarginV=60'" -c:a copy output/captioned.mp4`. Soft subtitles in MP4: `-i subs.srt -c copy -c:s mov_text`.
- Make an SRT: transcribe with `whisper in.mp4 --model small --output_format srt` (`python3 -m pip install --user openai-whisper`, runs locally) or `whisper-cli` from `brew install whisper-cpp`.
- Thumbnail frame: `ffmpeg -ss 3 -i in.mp4 -frames:v 1 output/thumb.jpg`.
- Fade in/out: `-vf "fade=t=in:d=0.5,fade=t=out:st=<dur-0.5>:d=0.5" -af "afade=t=in:d=0.5,afade=t=out:st=<dur-0.5>:d=0.5"`.
- Normalize loudness: `-af loudnorm=I=-14:TP=-1.5:LRA=11` (social), `I=-16` for podcasts.

Platform targets:
- TikTok / Reels / Shorts: 1080x1920, 30 fps, H.264, AAC 44.1 or 48 kHz, under 60 s for Shorts (up to 3 min now allowed), keep captions out of the bottom 20 percent.
- YouTube: keep source resolution and fps, `-crf 18`, `-movflags +faststart`.
- X: up to 1920x1200, 140 s, 512 MB. Slack/email: aim under 25 MB.
- Always add `-pix_fmt yuv420p` for compatibility (QuickTime, iPhone, web).

## Quality checklist

- Output plays in QuickTime (`open`) with sound in sync.
- Duration matches the plan; cuts land where intended (check a frame near each cut with `-ss`).
- Resolution, aspect and file size meet the platform.
- Text and faces not cropped off in vertical crops.
- Audio not clipping; loudness reasonable.
- Input file unchanged.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences with the path and key facts, e.g. "Made a 9:16 version for TikTok, 42 seconds, 18 MB, at output/launch-vertical.mp4."

## Pitfalls

- `-c copy` with `-ss` cuts on keyframes and can start with a frozen frame; re-encode for exact cuts.
- Odd widths/heights fail with libx264; use `-2` in `scale` to keep them even.
- Forgetting `-pix_fmt yuv420p` makes files that will not play on some devices.
- iPhone HDR/HEVC clips look washed out when converted; add `-vf "zscale=t=linear,tonemap=hable,zscale=t=bt709,format=yuv420p"` if needed.
- Concat demuxer silently breaks with mismatched codecs.
- Uploading or posting anything without the user's yes.

text:
---
name: video-game-guides
description: Use when the user wants help with a video game or Roblox experience: "how do I play X", "make me a guide for this game", "what are the controls", "best first steps in X", "how do I beat this boss".
---

# Video Game Guides

## When to use

- Writing a short starter guide for a game or Roblox experience the user is about to play or is stuck in.
- Answering a focused question (a boss, a quest, a crafting recipe, a control) with sources.
- Not for long lore essays or full walkthroughs; keep the guide to what helps the next hour of play.

## Steps

1. Pin down the exact game: full title, platform (PC, console, mobile, Roblox), and version or season if it matters. Roblox experiences need the experience name and creator, since many share names.
2. Search in this order and open the best two or three:
   - The official site, patch notes or Steam page (for current controls and mechanics).
   - The official or main wiki (Fandom or a dedicated wiki like wiki.gg). Prefer the one with recent edits.
   - Reddit (`site:reddit.com <game> beginner tips`) for what players actually recommend now.
   - YouTube guides: read titles, descriptions and transcripts rather than watching. Prefer recent ones.
   - Roblox: the experience page (description, updates), its Discord or Trello linked from that page, and its wiki if it has one.
3. Check dates. Patches change builds, prices and controls. Prefer sources from the current version; note anything that may be outdated.
4. Write `output/game-guide.md` (or `output/<game>-guide.md` if one already exists for a different game) with these sections, short and scannable:
   - **Game**: title, platform, version checked, date.
   - **Controls**: a table of key or button and action, default bindings for the user's platform.
   - **Goal**: what you are trying to do, in two or three sentences.
   - **First hour**: a numbered route, 5 to 10 steps.
   - **Tips**: 5 to 8 that save the most time or deaths.
   - **Avoid**: common beginner mistakes.
   - **Roblox specifics** (Roblox only): game passes and what is free, codes from the official page (with date checked), trading and scam warnings, private server notes.
   - **Sources**: links used.
5. Cross-check any number (damage, prices, drop rates, codes) against a second source; drop it if they disagree and you can't tell which is current.

## Tools on a Mac

- Web search and fetch for pages; `curl -sL URL | textutil -stdin -format html -convert txt -stdout` to read a page as text.
- `brew install yt-dlp`, then `yt-dlp --skip-download --write-auto-subs --sub-langs en --convert-subs srt -o "tmp/%(id)s" URL` for a YouTube transcript.
- `open output/game-guide.md` to show the file.
- `screencapture -x tmp/game.png` plus the `screenshot-ocr` skill if the user asks about what's on screen right now.

## Quality checklist

- Right game and platform; controls match that platform.
- Every claim about current content comes from a source dated near the current version.
- Codes and prices listed with the date checked.
- First-hour route is something a new player can actually follow in order.
- The guide fits on about one screen per section; no padding.
- Sources listed.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences with the single most useful tip and the path, for example "Your Grow a Garden guide is in output/game-guide.md; the big one is to sell crops before the shop restocks." Spoken aloud, so no tables or lists in the reply.

## Pitfalls

- Wikis for games with similar names (or Roblox clones of popular experiences). Check the creator and links.
- Outdated tier lists and meta builds after a patch.
- Roblox "free Robux" or code generator sites are scams; never link them. Codes only from the experience's own page, Discord or social accounts.
- Cheats, exploits, scripts and account sharing: don't help; they risk bans.
- Spoilers: keep story spoilers out unless the user asked.
- Don't buy, trade, or join anything on the user's behalf.

name: web-scraping-politely
text:
---
name: web-scraping-politely
description: Use when the user wants data collected from websites into a file: "scrape this site", "pull all the listings from", "get every product and price into a spreadsheet", "download the table on this page".
---

# Web Scraping Politely

## When to use

- Collecting structured data (lists, tables, prices, listings, article titles) from public web pages into CSV or JSON.
- Pages that need JavaScript to show their content (use Playwright, see Steps).
- Not for reading one page to answer a question: the helper's web fetch is enough.
- Not for analyzing the data afterwards: hand the CSV to `csv-data-analysis`.
- Not for anything behind a login, a paywall or a CAPTCHA. Stop and tell the user.

## Steps

1. Look for an official way first: a public API, an RSS feed, a download link, or a sitemap (`/sitemap.xml`). Use it if it exists.
2. Read the rules. Fetch `https://site.example/robots.txt` and check the paths you need against it with `urllib.robotparser`. Skim the site's terms for a ban on automated access. If either forbids it, stop and tell the user.
3. Fetch one sample page with `curl` and save it to `tmp/sample.html`. If the data is in the HTML, use requests + BeautifulSoup. If the HTML is nearly empty and the data appears only in the browser, look in the page for a JSON API call (often under `/api/` or in a `<script type="application/json">`) before reaching for Playwright.
4. Write the scraper in `tmp/scrape.py`:
   - Identify yourself: a User-Agent like `DottieHelper/1.0 (personal research)`.
   - One request at a time, at least 1 to 2 seconds apart (more if robots.txt sets `Crawl-delay`).
   - Timeouts (`timeout=20`), up to 3 retries with growing waits on 429 and 5xx, stop on 403.
   - Cache each fetched page in `tmp/cache/` so reruns do not hit the site again.
5. Parse with CSS selectors that describe meaning (`article h2 a`, `table#prices tr`), not long brittle paths. Strip whitespace, convert prices and dates to plain values, keep the source URL for each row.
6. Run on 2 or 3 pages first and check the output by eye. Then run the full job, with a hard cap on pages (for example 500) unless the user set one.
7. Save results to `output/<name>.csv` (UTF-8, header row) and, for nested data, `output/<name>.json`. Add a `scraped_at` column with the date.
8. Report counts: pages fetched, rows saved, pages that failed.

## Tools on a Mac

- `curl -sL -A "DottieHelper/1.0" https://site.example/robots.txt`.
- `python3 -m pip install --user requests beautifulsoup4 lxml`.

```python
import time, requests, urllib.robotparser
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
robots = urllib.robotparser.RobotFileParser("https://site.example/robots.txt"); robots.read()
session = requests.Session(); session.headers["User-Agent"] = "DottieHelper/1.0 (personal research)"
url = "https://site.example/catalog?page=1"
assert robots.can_fetch(session.headers["User-Agent"], url)
soup = BeautifulSoup(session.get(url, timeout=20).text, "lxml")
rows = [{"title": card.select_one("h2").get_text(strip=True), "url": url} for card in soup.select("article")]
time.sleep(2)
```

- JavaScript pages: `python3 -m pip install --user playwright && python3 -m playwright install chromium`, then `page.goto(url, wait_until="networkidle")` and `page.content()` into BeautifulSoup.
- HTML tables: `pandas.read_html("tmp/sample.html")` returns every `<table>` as a DataFrame.
- `python3 -m json.tool output/items.json | head` to check JSON.

## Quality checklist

- robots.txt was checked and the scraper obeys it, including Crawl-delay.
- Requests were spaced out; no parallel hammering.
- Row count is plausible against what the site shows (for example "1,240 results").
- No empty or shifted columns; spot-check 5 rows against the live pages.
- Each row has its source URL and the scrape date.
- No personal data about private individuals was collected beyond what the user's task needs.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: what you collected, how many rows, anything skipped, and the path, for example "I saved 1,236 listings with price and location to output/listings.csv; 4 pages failed and are noted in the file's log."

## Pitfalls

- Ignoring robots.txt or terms "just this once". If it is disallowed, say so and suggest the official API or a manual export.
- Logging in, solving CAPTCHAs, rotating IPs or faking browsers to get around blocks. Do not.
- Pagination that loops forever; track seen URLs and stop on repeats.
- Selectors that silently match nothing after a layout change: fail loudly when a page yields zero rows.
- Prices in the HTML may differ by region or need a cookie; note which version you got.
- Never store the user's passwords or cookies in scripts.

name: webapp-testing
text:
---
name: webapp-testing
description: Use when the user wants a local web app checked or tested in a browser: "test my site", "does the signup flow work", "take screenshots of localhost", "why is the page blank", "check for console errors".
---

# Webapp Testing

## When to use

- Testing a web app the user is building, running on `localhost` or from a folder on the Mac.
- Walking through user flows (sign up, add to cart, submit a form), catching console errors, taking screenshots at different sizes.
- Not for collecting data from other people's sites: use `web-scraping-politely`.
- Not for testing live production sites with real accounts or payments without the user's explicit yes.

## Steps

1. Find out how the app starts. Read `package.json` scripts, `README`, `Makefile`, `manage.py` or `vite.config.*`. Note the port.
2. Check whether it is already running: `lsof -nP -iTCP:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN`. If not, start it in the background and log output: `npm run dev > tmp/server.log 2>&1 &` and save the PID (`echo $! > tmp/server.pid`).
3. Wait until it answers: `for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -sf http://localhost:3000 >/dev/null && break; sleep 1; done`. If it never comes up, read `tmp/server.log` and report the error.
4. Do a first look: load the page in headless Chromium, take a full-page screenshot, and collect console messages and failed requests.
5. Find selectors from what is actually rendered: dump `page.content()` or list `page.get_by_role("button").all_inner_texts()`. Prefer role and text locators (`get_by_role("button", name="Sign up")`, `get_by_label("Email")`) over CSS classes.
6. Write each flow as a small script in `tmp/test_<flow>.py`: steps, an `expect(...)` assertion after each important step, and a screenshot at the end or on failure.
7. Check common sizes: desktop 1440x900 and phone 390x844.
8. Run, read the results, and if something fails, look at the screenshot and console log before deciding if it is an app bug or a test mistake.
9. Write `output/test-report.md`: what was tested, pass/fail per flow, each bug with steps to reproduce, console errors, and screenshot paths in `output/screenshots/`.
10. Stop the server you started: `kill $(cat tmp/server.pid)`. Leave alone a server the user had running.

## Tools on a Mac

- `python3 -m pip install --user playwright pytest-playwright && python3 -m playwright install chromium`.

```python
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, expect
with sync_playwright() as playwright:
    browser = playwright.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page(viewport={"width": 1440, "height": 900})
    console_messages, failed_requests = [], []
    page.on("console", lambda message: console_messages.append(f"{message.type}: {message.text}"))
    page.on("requestfailed", lambda request: failed_requests.append(request.url))
    page.goto("http://localhost:3000", wait_until="networkidle")
    page.get_by_label("Email").fill("test@example.com")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign up").click()
    expect(page.get_by_text("Check your inbox")).to_be_visible()
    page.screenshot(path="output/screenshots/signup-done.png", full_page=True)
    browser.close()
```

- `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` lists servers that are running; `curl -sI http://localhost:3000` checks status.
- Static folder with no server: `python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory site/`.
- `qlmanage -t -s 1000 -o tmp output/screenshots/home.png` for a quick thumbnail.

## Quality checklist

- The app was confirmed up before testing, and the URL and port are in the report.
- Every flow has an assertion, not only clicks.
- Console errors and failed network requests are listed, even when flows pass.
- Screenshots exist for each flow and each failure.
- Bugs have clear reproduction steps.
- Any server you started is stopped; no stray processes left (`pgrep -fl node`).

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: how many flows passed, the most important bug, and the path, for example "3 of 4 flows pass; checkout fails because the Pay button stays disabled on phone width. The report and screenshots are in output/test-report.md."

## Pitfalls

- Clicking before the page is ready. Use locators and `expect`, not `time.sleep`.
- Using `wait_until="networkidle"` on apps that keep a socket open; fall back to `"load"` plus an `expect`.
- Fixing the app's code when asked only to test it. Report bugs; change code only if the user asked.
- Real emails, payments or production data: use test accounts and fake data like `test@example.com`.
- Leaving a dev server running on the user's port.

---
name: word-documents
description: Use when the user wants a Word file (.docx) made, edited, filled in or converted: "make this a Word doc", "fix the formatting in report.docx", "turn my notes into a docx".
---

# Word Documents

## When to use

- Creating a new .docx from notes, Markdown or an outline.
- Editing an existing .docx: replacing text, adding sections or tables, fixing headings, filling a template.
- Converting between .docx and .md, .html, .rtf, .txt or .pdf.
- Not for long writing done with the user over several rounds: use `doc-coauthoring` for the writing, then this skill for the file.
- Not for PDFs as the main input or output: use `pdf-tools`.

## Steps

1. Find the source. Copy any file the user names into `tmp/` and work on the copy; never edit the original in place.
2. Read before you write. Dump the text with `textutil -convert txt -stdout file.docx` or `pandoc file.docx -t markdown`. For styles and structure, list paragraphs with python-docx (see below).
3. Pick the route:
   - New document from plain content: write Markdown in `tmp/draft.md`, then `pandoc tmp/draft.md -o output/name.docx`. Add `--reference-doc=template.docx` when the user has a house style.
   - Small edits that must keep the original look: python-docx, changing text inside existing runs so fonts and styles survive.
   - Template filling: put placeholders like `{{client_name}}` in the template and replace them run by run.
4. Use real styles, not manual formatting: `Heading 1`, `Heading 2`, `List Bullet`, `Title`. That keeps the navigation pane and table of contents working.
5. Save to `output/` with a clear name, for example `output/project-brief-v2.docx`. Never overwrite the user's file unless they asked.
6. Check the result: convert back to text and read it, and render a preview with `qlmanage -t -s 1200 -o tmp output/name.docx` to see the first page.

## Tools on a Mac

- `textutil -convert docx notes.rtf -output output/notes.docx` (built in; handles txt, rtf, html, doc, docx, odt).
- `textutil -convert txt -stdout report.docx` to read text quickly.
- `textutil -convert html report.docx -output tmp/report.html` then `cupsfilter tmp/report.html > output/report.pdf` for a quick PDF.
- `qlmanage -t -s 1200 -o tmp file.docx` for a PNG thumbnail of page one.
- `mdls -name kMDItemNumberOfPages file.docx` sometimes has a page count.
- `brew install pandoc` for Markdown to Word with headings, lists, tables and footnotes:
  `pandoc in.md -o out.docx --toc --reference-doc=ref.docx`.
- `python3 -m pip install --user python-docx` for editing:

```python
from docx import Document
document = Document("tmp/report.docx")
for paragraph in document.paragraphs:
    print(paragraph.style.name, "|", paragraph.text)
document.add_heading("Next steps", level=2)
document.add_paragraph("Ship the beta on Friday.", style="List Bullet")
document.save("output/report-edited.docx")
```

- Replacing text without losing formatting: loop `paragraph.runs` and change `run.text`. Setting `paragraph.text` wipes the runs and their formatting.
- Tables: `document.tables[0].cell(row, column).text`; add with `document.add_table(rows=1, cols=3, style="Table Grid")`.

## Quality checklist

- Opens without errors: `python3 -c "import docx; docx.Document('output/x.docx')"`.
- Headings use heading styles; the outline reads correctly in `pandoc -t markdown`.
- No leftover placeholders: `textutil -convert txt -stdout output/x.docx | grep -n '{{'` finds nothing.
- Fonts, header, footer and page size match the original when editing.
- Tables have a header row and no empty columns.
- File name says what it is; the original file is untouched.

## Reply to the user

One or two sentences: what you made or changed and where it is, for example "I made the project brief as a Word file with four sections; it's in output/project-brief.docx." Mention anything you could not keep, like tracked changes.

## Pitfalls

- Tracked changes and comments: python-docx cannot accept, reject or create tracked changes, and pandoc drops them unless you pass `--track-changes=all` when reading. If the user's file has revisions, say so and ask whether to keep, accept or ignore them before editing.
- Editing `paragraph.text` destroys bold, italics and links in that paragraph. Edit runs.
- Placeholders split across runs (Word often breaks `{{name}}` into pieces) will not match. Join the runs' text, replace, and write it back into the first run.
- `.doc` (old binary format) is not readable by python-docx. Convert first: `textutil -convert docx old.doc -output tmp/old.docx`.
- textutil conversions lose complex layout (columns, text boxes). Use it for reading and simple files only.
- Pandoc ignores the styles of a docx you did not pass as `--reference-doc`.
- Do not email or upload the file; saving it in `output/` is the job.

text:
---
name: writing-plans
description: Use when there is an agreed design or clear feature request and the work needs splitting into steps ("plan this", "break it down", "how would we build it"). Writes plan.md with files and checks.
---

# Writing Plans

## When to use

- A design exists (often `output/design.md` from brainstorming-before-building) and the user wants it built.
- A request is clear but touches several files or takes more than one sitting.
- Work will be resumed later, by you or another helper, and needs a written trail.

Do not use when:

- The idea is still vague. Use brainstorming-before-building first.
- The change is one file and a few lines. Just make it and verify it (verification-before-done).

## Steps

1. Read the design and the code it touches. List the existing files you will change with `git ls-files` or `find . -type f -not -path './node_modules/*' -not -path './.git/*'`.
2. Find how the project runs its tests and build: look in package.json "scripts", Makefile, pyproject.toml, Package.swift, README. Note the exact commands. If there is no test setup, the first task is to add one.
3. Split the work into tasks of 2 to 15 minutes each. A task changes one behavior, touches few files and ends in a passing check. If a task needs "and" in its title, split it.
4. Order tasks so each one builds on working code: data model first, then logic, then interface, then polish. Put the riskiest unknown early so it fails fast.
5. Write `output/plan.md` (or `plan.md` in the project root if the user keeps docs there) in this shape:

   ```
   # Plan: <feature>
   Design: output/design.md
   Test command: npm test   (or pytest -q, swift test)

   ## Task 1: <short imperative title>
   Files: src/parser.ts (new), test/parser.test.ts (new)
   Do: <2-5 lines: what to write, function names, inputs and outputs>
   Test first: <the failing test to write and what it asserts>
   Check: npm test -- parser  -> 3 passing
   Commit: "Add parser for routine blocks"
   ```

6. Every task has a Check line: an exact command and the result that means it worked. "Looks right" is not a check.
7. Include the edge cases from the design as their own tests (empty input, huge input, missing file, no network).
8. End the plan with a "Done when" list copied from the design's success criteria, plus "all tests pass" and "README updated if usage changed".
9. Show the user the task titles only (not the whole file) and ask whether to start. When building, tick tasks off in plan.md (`- [x]`) as each check passes, so progress survives a restart.
10. If the plan proves wrong while building, edit plan.md first, then the code. Never let the plan and the code silently drift apart.

## Tools on a Mac

- Map the project: `git ls-files | head -100`, `find . -name '*.swift' | xargs wc -l | sort -n | tail -20`.
- Find where something is defined: `grep -rn "functionName" --include='*.py' .`
- Read scripts: `cat package.json | python3 -m json.tool`, `cat Makefile`.
- Count tasks and progress: `grep -c '^## Task' output/plan.md`, `grep -c '\[x\]' output/plan.md`.
- Open the plan for the user: `open output/plan.md`.
- If `rg` (ripgrep) speeds up searching a big repo: `brew install ripgrep`, then `rg -n "pattern"`.

## Quality checklist

- Each task names exact files (new or changed) and exact functions or types.
- Each task has a runnable check with an expected result.
- No task is bigger than about 15 minutes or touches more than about 3 files.
- Tests come before code inside each task (see test-driven-development).
- The plan covers everything in the design's scope and nothing in "Not in this version".
- A stranger could pick up the plan cold and do task 4 without asking you anything.

## Reply to the user

"The plan is in output/plan.md: <N> tasks, starting with <task 1 title>. Shall I start?" Keep it to one or two sentences.

## Pitfalls

- Tasks like "Implement the backend": too big to check, so nothing is ever clearly done.
- Check lines that say "verify it works" instead of a command.
- Planning against files you have not opened, then discovering they look nothing like you assumed.
- Saving all testing for a final "write tests" task at the end.
- Planning features the design left out because they seemed useful.
- Forgetting setup tasks: installing a test runner, creating a config file, adding a .gitignore.

text:
---
name: youtube-tiktok-scripts
description: Use when the user wants a script, hook, outline, titles or thumbnail ideas for a YouTube video, TikTok, Reel, Short or other short-form or long-form creator video.
---

# YouTube and TikTok Scripts

## When to use

- "Write a TikTok script about", "script my YouTube video", "give me hooks", "title and thumbnail ideas", "turn this blog post into a Short".
- Creator content: tutorials, explainers, reviews, vlogs, storytime, listicles.
- Not for a paid ad or product commercial with a shot list: use `commercial-script-and-shotlist`.
- For editing the footage afterwards: `video-editing-ffmpeg` or `screen-recording-edits`. For the thumbnail image itself: `poster-and-graphics`.

## Steps

1. Pin down: platform and length (Short/TikTok/Reel 15 to 60 s, up to 3 min; YouTube long-form 6 to 15 min), topic, audience, the one takeaway, the call to action, and the creator's on-camera style (talking head, voiceover, screen recording, faceless).
2. If facts are involved, research with web search and keep source links in `tmp/sources.md`. Do not invent stats.
3. Write 5 hooks, each a different type, and pick the best:
   - Outcome ("This one setting doubled my battery life").
   - Curiosity gap ("Nobody tells you why ... ").
   - Contrarian ("Stop using to-do lists").
   - Pattern interrupt (a surprising visual in the first frame).
   - Direct callout ("If you edit on a Mac, watch this").
   The hook must land in the first 2 seconds (about 5 to 7 spoken words) with the visual already moving.
4. Short-form structure (about 2.5 words per second, so 30 s is 70 to 80 words):
   - 0 to 2 s hook, 2 to 5 s stakes or promise, then 3 to 5 beats of one idea each, a payoff, and a quick CTA. Cut every sentence that does not move it forward. Optional loop: last line leads back into the first.
5. Long-form structure: cold open hook (0 to 15 s) that shows the payoff, a 15 to 30 s promise of what they will get, chapters each opening with an open question and closing with a mini-payoff, a re-hook every 60 to 90 s, a mid-roll CTA only after delivering value, an ending that pays off the title without a long goodbye.
6. Write the script as a table in `output/<slug>-script.md` with columns: Time, Spoken words (VO / on camera), On-screen visual or b-roll, On-screen text (caption, max 6 words).
7. Add a b-roll and shot list: each shot, where it comes from (record on Mac, phone, stock, screen recording), and duration.
8. Add captions guidance: burned-in captions for short-form, 1 to 3 words per card for punchy styles, keep in the middle third away from UI overlays.
9. Add 5 titles (under 60 characters, specific, no clickbait the video does not pay off) and 3 thumbnail concepts (subject, expression or object, 2 to 4 words of text, contrast colors). For Shorts/TikTok add a caption and 3 to 5 hashtags.
10. Add retention notes: where viewers may drop and what fixes it (cut, visual change, new question).
11. Read the script aloud with `say` to check timing.

## Tools on a Mac

- Timing check: `say -r 170 -f tmp/vo.txt -o tmp/vo.aiff && afinfo tmp/vo.aiff | grep duration` (170 wpm is a brisk creator pace).
- Word count: `wc -w tmp/vo.txt`.
- Copy the spoken lines to paste into a teleprompter: `pbcopy < tmp/vo.txt`.
- Research: web search and fetch; transcripts of the user's own past videos if they give links.
- Word file if asked: `textutil` does not read Markdown, so write the script as `tmp/script.html` and run `textutil -convert docx tmp/script.html -output output/<slug>-script.docx`.
- Preview: `open output/<slug>-script.md`.

## Quality checklist

- Hook works with sound off (on-screen text) and in under 2 seconds.
- One clear takeaway; every beat earns its place.
- Spoken word count fits the target length.
- Every line has a visual; no 5-second stretches of the same shot.
- Facts have sources; no invented numbers or quotes.
- Titles and thumbnails promise only what the video delivers.
- CTA is one action, not three.

## Reply to the user

One to three sentences: the hook you chose, the length, the path, e.g. "Wrote a 45-second TikTok script opening with 'Your Mac has a hidden screen recorder' plus 5 titles and a b-roll list: output/mac-recorder-script.md."

## Pitfalls

- Slow intros ("Hey guys, welcome back") before the hook.
- Writing for reading instead of speaking: long sentences, nested clauses.
- Over-packing a Short with several ideas.
- Clickbait titles that hurt retention when the video does not deliver.
- Using music or clips without rights; posting anything without the user's yes.
